MONASTIC, something belonging to monks, or the monkish life. The monastic profession is a kind of civil death, which in all worldly matters has the same effect as the natural death. The council of Trent fix sixteen years as the age at which a person may be admitted into the monastic state. St Anthony was the person who, in the fourth century, first established monastic institutions; as St Pachomius, in the same century, is said to have first set on foot the cenobitical life, or regular communities of religious. In a short time the deserts of Egypt became inhabited with a set of solitaries, who took upon them the monastic profession. St Basil carried the same spirit into the East, where he composed a rule, which afterwards obtained throughout a great part of the West. In the eleventh century the monastic discipline had become very remiss. St Odo first began to retrieve it in the monastery of Cluny; that establishment, by the conditions of its erection, was put under the immediate protection of the holy see, with a prohibition to all powers, both secular and ecclesiastical, to disturb the monks in the possession of their effects or the election of their abbot. In virtue of this they pleaded an exemption from the jurisdiction of the bishop, and extended this privilege to all the houses dependent on Cluny. This made the first congregation of several houses, under one chief immediately subject to the pope, so as to constitute one body, or, as it is called, one religious order. Till then, each monastery was independent, and subject to the bishop.

MONAVAR

Pages 392-392

MONAVAR, a Spanish town in the province of Valencia, containing 8000 inhabitants; it has a manufacture of linen, and several medicinal baths.

MONDOVI

Pages 392-392

MONDOVI, a province of Piedmont, in the Sardinian dominions. It extends over seven hundred and sixty-two square miles, and comprises four cities, eighty-one towns and villages, and ninety-six rural establishments, with 136,934 inhabitants. Although the Apennines form a part of the southern division of the province, it is on the whole fruitful in corn, wine, hemp, and silk. It has some mines of iron, and several valuable marble quarries. The capital is the city of the same name situated on the river Ellero. It is fortified, is the seat of a bishop, and contains a cathedral, five parish churches, four convents of nuns and eleven of monks, 4000 houses, and 22,570 inhabitants. It is a place of considerable manufacturing industry, making both printed cottons, cloth, silks, and paper. It was the birthplace of the celebrated Beccaria. Long. 7. 45. E. Lat. 44. 23. N.

MONETARIUS

Pages 392-392

MONETARIUS, or Moneyer, a name which antiquaries and medallists give to those who struck the ancient coins or moneys. Many of the old Roman coins have the name of the monetarius, either written at length, or at least the initial letters of it. See the article Medals. Money is a term used to designate whatever commodity the inhabitants of any particular country, accept either voluntarily or by compulsion, as an equivalent for their labour, and for whatever else they have to dispose of. Sect. I.—Circumstances which led to the use of money. Principal properties that every commodity used as such ought to possess. Not a sign or a measure of value, but a real equivalent. A country in which the division of labour was unknown, and where every individual or family directly produced the commodities necessary for his or their consumption, would have no exchanges, and consequently no money. But, after the division of labour has been established, the introduction of money becomes necessary, or, at least, highly advantageous. A very small part only of a man's wants is then directly supplied by his own labour. The greater part is indirectly supplied by exchanging that part of the produce of his labour which exceeds his own consumption, for such parts of the produce of other men's labour as he has occasion for, and they are willing to part with. Every man thus lives by exchanging, or becomes in some measure a merchant, and the society itself grows to be what is properly a commercial society. "But when the division of labour first began to take place, this power of exchanging must frequently have been very much clogged and embarrassed in its operations. One man we shall suppose, has more of a certain commodity than he himself has occasion for, while another has less. The former, consequently, would be glad to dispose of, and the latter to purchase, a part of this superfluity. But, if this latter should chance to have nothing that the former stands in need of, no exchange can be made between them. The butcher has more meat in his shop than he himself can consume, and the brewer and the baker would each be willing to purchase a part of it; but they have nothing to offer in exchange except the different productions of their respective trades, and the butcher is already provided with all the bread and beer which he has immediate occasion for. No exchange can, in this case, be made between them. He cannot be their merchant, nor they his customers; and they are all of them thus mutually less serviceable to one another. To avoid the inconveniency of such situations, every prudent man, in every period of society, after the establishment of the division of labour, must naturally have endeavoured to manage his affairs in such a manner as to have at all times by him, besides the peculiar produce of his own industry, a certain quantity of some one commodity or another, such as he imagined few people would be likely to refuse in exchange for the produce of their industry." Money. (Wealth of Nations, vol. i. p.43. McCulloch's ed.) This commodity, whatever it may be, is money. An infinite variety of commodities have been used as Commodity-money in different countries and states of society. Those ties used as nations who chiefly subsist by the chase, such as the ancients in Russia, and the greater part of the Indians who now occupy the uncultivated portion of America, use the skins of wild animals as money. In a pastoral state of society cattle are most commonly used for that purpose. Homer tells us, that the armour of Diomed cost only nine oxen, whilst that of Glaucon cost one hundred. (Ilias, lib. 6, lin. 235.) The etymology of the Latin word pecunia, signifying money, and of all its derivatives, proves that cattle (pecus) had been the primitive money of the Romans. They had also been used as such by the ancient Germans; for their laws uniformly fix the amount of the penalties to be paid for particular offences in cattle. (Storch, in loco citato.) In remoter ages corn was very generally used, in agricultural countries, as money; and even now, it is by no means uncommon to stipulate for corn rents and wages. Other commodities have been used in different countries. Salt is said to be the common money of Abyssinia (Wealth of Nations, i. p. 45.); a species of shells, called cowries, gathered on the shores of the Maldivian Islands, are used in smaller payments throughout Hindustan, and form the only money of extensive districts in Africa. Dried fish forms the money of Iceland and Newfoundland; sugar of some of the West India islands; and Dr. Smith mentions that there was, at the period of the publication of the Wealth of Nations, a village in Scotland where it was customary for a workman to carry nails, as money, to the baker's shop or the alehouse. (Wealth of Nations, i. p. 45.) But these commodities are universally deficient in some Defects of the principal requisites which every commodity used as money ought to possess. Products must frequently be brought to market worth only half an ox, or half a skin; but as an ox could not be divided, and as the division of a skin would most probably deprive it of the greater part of its value, it would be impossible to exchange them for such money. Divisibility is not, however, the only indispensable requisite in a commodity used as a medium of exchange. It is necessary that it should admit of being kept for an indefinite period without deteriorating; that it should, by possessing great value in small bulk, be easily transported; and that one piece of money, of a certain denomination, should always be precisely equivalent to every other piece of money of the same denomination. But none of the commodities above named as having been used as money possesses these properties. Though cattle had been sufficiently 1 Etymologists differ respecting the derivation of the word money. Some contend that it comes from monere, (quid nota inscripta de valore admodum,) because the stamp impressed on coined money indicates its weight and fineness (Boutroux, Recherches sur les Monnaies de France, p. 1.); and others, that it originates in the circumstance of silver being first coined at Rome in the temple of Juno Moneta. (Suidas, in voce Monera.) 2 Storch, Traité d'Economie Politique, tome iii. p. 16.; and Ullon, Memoires Philosophiques sur l'Amérique, tome ii. p. 100. 3 Morellet, Prospectus d'un Nouveau Dictionnaire de Commerce, p. 115. 4 "Dans les pays où le cuivre a trop de valeur pour pouvoir représenter celle des plus menues denrées, on est encore obligé de lui substituer quelque autre matière plus commune. C'est cette circonstance qui a fait adopter aux Indiens l'usage des cuivres en guise des petits monnaies. Cet usage pouvait paraître étrange dans les pays aussi riches et d'une civilisation aussi ancienne que le Borneo et l'Indonésie; mais le cuivre y est si rare, et les vivres y sont à si bon marché, qu'une pièce de la valeur de 1 cop. est à (about a halfpenny English) peut y acheter une quantité des denrées suffisante pour la subsistance journalière d'un homme du peuple. On est donc obligé de diviser la plus petite monnaie de cuivre en plusieurs fractions; et comme une monnaie d'aussi peu de valeur coûteur plus à fabriquer qu'elle ne peut valoir, on la remplace par un coquillage dont la nature fait presque tous les frais. Quelque mince que soit la valeur d'un cuivre, elle suffit dans ces contrées isolées pour acheter une pièce des bananes ou quelque autre fruit commun." (Le Goux de Flaux, Essai sur l'Indonésie, tom. i. pp. 143—200, quoted by Storch, Économie Politique, tom. iii. p. 133.) 5 Smith, ubi supra; and Horrebou, Description de l'Islande, tome ii. p. 90.

or Manfalout, a town of Upper Egypt, situated on the left bank of the Nile, about a mile from the river, in a fertile and beautiful country. It is well built, of considerable magnitude, and carries on an extensive commerce in every species of grain. There is likewise a large manufactory of cloth here. Long. 31.36. E. Lat. 27.42. N.

MONFLA

one of the Querimba <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>, which are situated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOZAMBIQUE">Mozambique</a>, off the western <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOT_AND_GARONNE"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a> and Garonne, and arrondissement of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VILLENEUVE_D_AGEN">Villeneuve d'<a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGEN">Agen</a>. MONGE

Pages 423-424

Gaspar, the inventor of descriptive <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a>, and one of the founders of the Polytechnic School, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol2.html#article-BEAUNE">Beaune</a> in 1746. His father was a dealer in small wares, who had much difficulty in supporting his family, consisting of three sons, all of whom were inclined to the sciences; but having the good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> to appreciate the importance of instruction, he employed every means in his power to procure this benefit to his children. The subject of this notice, being the eldest, received the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of the Oratory in his native town, where he was initiated in the elements of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and whence, having completed the usual course, he was removed to a superior school at Lyons, where his precocious talents quickly developed themselves. At the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of sixteen, he was judged qualified to assist his new masters in teaching physics; and before he had completed his nineteenth year, he had been admitted into the school which had been founded at Mézières for the instruction of engineers. But this establishment was only opened to privileged scholars, twenty in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, of whom one half left, and as many joined it, every year. In order to participate in its advantages, it was essential to possess an elevated station in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>; and the humble fortune of Monge was therefore a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a>. He was placed as a pupil and modeller in the class, with the superintendence and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of works in fortification; and amidst these obscure labours, where dexterity was of more importance than intelligence, the qualities of his mind remained unobserved. He was considered merely as an expert modeller, and he longed to escape from a reputation which was equally unworthy of his genius and offensive to his self-<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. Meanwhile, the commandant of the school selected him to make the practical calculations of an operation of deployment, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> defiling, which had been prescribed as a task. But Monge, dissatisfied with the tentative means by which the problem was usually resolved, and impressed with the importance of signalizing the commencement of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a>, imagined a more expeditious and not less certain, though far more scientific method, for attaining the result desired, by the instrumentality of geometry. His solution was contested, upon the ground that he had not made allowance for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> required to exhaust the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of calculations; but its merit was nevertheless recognised, and the capacity of the pupil strongly exemplified. The latter was then nineteen. Bossut, who professed mathematics at Mézières, now appointed Monge his assistant; and he was attached, in the same capacity, to Abbé Nollet, professor of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, whom he soon afterwards succeeded in that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>. In this situation he made a number of curious experiments on <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAS">gas</a>, molecular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a>, and the effects of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OPTICS">optics</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>, as well as refined deductions on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METEOROLOGY">meteorology</a>, and on the important discovery of the production of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMBUSTION">combustion</a> of inflammable <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Anticipated by Cavendish, without being aware of it, he examined this phenomenon with scrupulous <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and assigned the share of caloric and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> in its production. About the same time Monge extended and generalised his first mathematical essays, and setting out from the principle which refers to three rectangular coordinates the position of any point whatever taken in space, he made it the foundation of a new and fruitful doctrine, indispensable for all the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, and to which, when completed by successive developments, he applied the name of Descriptive Geometry. This collection of simple and uniform methods was, however, at variance with the incoherent practices which had been sanctioned by time; the attempt made by the inventor to introduce his innovations into the course of instruction in the school encountered strenuous opposition; and more than twenty years elapsed before he succeeded in obtaining the application of his geometry to the tracings of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARPENTRY">carpentry</a>. Monge generally passed his vacations at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he mingled in the society of men who then held the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the sciences. Being already a correspondent of the Academy, to the honours of which he aspired, he found <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> patrons in Lavoisier, Condorcet, La Rocheleoucaud, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">President</a> Bochart de Sarson; and, through the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of D'Alembert, he was received into the Academy of Sciences in 1780. The same year he was associated with Bossut, who had been appointed to deliver the course of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol10.html#article-HYDRODYNAMICS">hydrodynamics</a> established at the Louvre by Turgot. To perform these <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> functions, he was obliged to be alternately at Paris and at Mézières; but the situation of examiner of the pupils of the naval school, to which he was appointed after the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Bezout in 1783, withdrew him from Mézières, where he had laid the foundation of his fame, and initiated in the sciences such men as Meusnier, Tinsseau, Carnot, Coulomb, and others scarcely inferior to them. For the benefit of the naval school he composed a treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STATICS">statics</a>, in which he proceeded synthetically, in order to get rid of equations, and rendered the principles more accessible by relaxing the rigour of demonstration. His next appointment was that of professor of physics in the Lyceum of Paris; an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> which had for its object to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> instruction under agreeable forms, and present it in an attractive shape to a number of indolent amateurs. To interest such frivolous auditors he would have required the peculiar talents of Fontenelle; but <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he failed to impart that fascination to science which formed the distinguishing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> of the illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> named, he knew how to render his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> attractive by piquant views and ingenious illustrations, independently of the graces of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Like many others, he was at first led away by the promises and hopes of the revolution. Adopting those notions of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> perfectibility, which then filled all heads, he conceived that the barriers which arrested generous emulation were for ever removed, and that talents would henceforth command that distinction which of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> belonged to them; but the terrible events that followed in such rapid succession in some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> dissipate this illusion, which he shared in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with so many others. Called to the ministry of marine after the 10th of August 1792, he accepted the appointment, being determined, he said, by the presence of the Prussians on the French <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>; he was thus a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, which then formed the ministers into one body, under the denomination of the Executive <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a>; and it was in this capacity that he concurred with his colleagues in causing the judgment which condemned <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XVI. to death to be carried into execution. But he soon discovered that, amidst the exasperation of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>, his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was not tenable, and ac- Monge accordingly, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of April 1793, he tendered his resignation, which was accepted. Some time afterwards, the committee of public safety made an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the savans to assist in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the French territory. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> hundred thousand men were ready to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">march</a> to the frontier to repulse the European crusade which menaced the republic; but the existing manufactories were insufficient to produce the tenth <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the matériel requisite for so mighty preparations. It was necessary to multiply <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, to describe and simplify their processes, to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the operations of the workshops, to decompose innumerable metallic alloys for the wants of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, to extract <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, to prepare <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, and to draw from the resources of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> alone a prodigious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of powder. The progress of the enemy required extraordinary celerity. Monge applied himself wholly to these operations, and distinguished himself by his indefatigable <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. He directed his attention to the manufacture of arms, the founderies, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BORING">boring</a> of cannon, and the powder-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, superintending and simplifying the various processes; he gave instructions for the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, and composed, at intervals, his Art de fabriquer les Canons, which was soon followed by his Aris aux Ouvriers en Fer, sur la Fabrication de l'Acier, containing an exposition of the means of obtaining steel by combining <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> with a little <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>. Services so important having raised in public estimation men of science, against whom the axe of proscription was soon whetted, they obtained, after the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of Robespierre, a tardy protection for public instruction. The Normal School was created, and a pure light diffused on the exposition of scientific truths. At length Monge published his Géométrie Descriptive, which he had so <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> kept secret, and which unquestionably forms his highest title of distinction. In explaining this collection of ingenious methods, where the modifications of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> are developed and combined by the aid of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and where, from a sort of imitative language, are deduced, by an exact <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, the truths which result from the forms of bodies and their respective positions, he dilated with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> on the advantages which might be derived from his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> for rectifying the judgment and improving the dexterity of workmen, as well as for simplifying <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, and adding to the comforts of society. Of all the applications of which his geometry was susceptible, he has only treated of five, viz., carpentry, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, deployment, linear and aerial <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a>, and the distribution of light and shadow. To him also France was, in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> measure, indebted for the establishment of the Polytechnic School; for, although Berthollet and Guyton-Morveau were associated with him in this undertaking, it was he who arranged the system of studies ultimately adopted, and which remained unaffected by the rapid mobility of the revolutionary creations. This was not only a central school, where aspirants might imbibe the general principles that connect all the branches of the public <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and establish a fraternal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> and free transmission of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> between different classes; it was also open to all those whose scientific conceptions were calculated to improve the useful arts, to economise labour, and to enlighten industry; and although the system of instruction was perhaps too extensive and profound, there can be no doubt that it proved of immense benefit to France. From these labours Monge was called to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, with the sculptor Moïse, the painter Barthélémy, and Berthollet, Thouin, and La-billardière, his colleagues in the Institute, to collect those masterpieces of art, the cession of which had been stipulated by the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Tolentino. This mission lasted more than a year, and Monge, by his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> processes, ably seconded the zeal of his associates for the conservation and removal of the conquered monuments. Having completed his labours in this department, he was <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a>, along with General Berthier, to lay before the Directory the treaty of Campo Formio; and, not long afterwards, he was sent to Rome, along with Daunou, there to organize a republic; an undertaking which had scarcely been completed when Bonaparte sailed for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. Monge, having been ordered to join the expedition, embarked at Civita-Vecchia, along with Desaix, and, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1798, overtook the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>. In Egypt his labours were incessant. He examined the pyramids; visited the obelisk and walls of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HELIOPOLIS">Heliopolis</a>; explored the antiquities scattered round <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>; described the state of the Mekias, or <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> constructed in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Raou-dah by the Kalif Almamoun, to measure the rise of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>; superintended the geodesical and monumental description of Egypt; and was at length appointed president of the Institute formed at Cairo upon the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of that of France. In this last capacity his exertions were prodigious. When the naval defeat of Aboukir had cut off all communication with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, the savans assembled at Cairo had to provide for wants still more numerous than those of France in the year 1793; as, independently of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> resources, they had in fact to create the utensils necessary for the usages of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and the operations of the arts. The members of the Institute, however, divided these labours amongst them, and the attempts of individuals were guided and facilitated by the inquiries and researches of commissions formed out of the same learned body. On this trying occasion Monge and Berthollet were equally distinguished; and when a revolt broke out at Cairo, they proved that their courage and presence of mind, in the midst of danger, were not surpassed by their zeal for the advancement of science. In a journey to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a>, undertaken by <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">Napoleon</a>, Monge recognised the traces of the canal which by the Nile established a communication between the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> and the Mediterranean; he visited the ruins of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PELUSIUM">Pelusium</a>, and, at the opening of the valley through which it is believed that the Hebrews proceeded towards Mount <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a>, he observed the fountain of Moses. He also accompanied Bonaparte to <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, and was seized with a dangerous illness at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACRE">Acre</a>, where, in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a>, he had the affliction to receive the last sighs of his pupil, General Caffarelli. On his return to Europe with Bonaparte, Monge became president of the Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">Commission</a>, and was again placed at the head of the Polytechnic School, where he resumed his place amongst the professors, and often defended, against the prejudices of Bonaparte, the generous youth, whom the despotic <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> of that military <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> had led him to dislike. On the formation of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, he was appointed a member of that body, with an ample provision, and the title of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> of Pelusium. The grief occasioned by the fall of Napoleon was augmented by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the Polytechnic School, and the banishment of the surviving members of the Convention who had sent Louis XVI. to the scaffold; a measure which inferred the expatriation of M. Eschasseraux, one of his sons-in-<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. The erasure of his name from the roll of the Institute, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the expurgations of 1816, gave the last blow to his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a>. Repeated attacks of apoplexy had already shaken his naturally robust frame, whilst the obliteration of his ideas, and all the symptoms of a rapid decline, announced his approaching dissolution. He died on the 28th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1818, in the seventy-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> year of his age. The separate publications of Monge are, 1. Traité Élémentaire de Statique, Paris, 1786, in 8vo; 2. Description expatiée de l'Art de fabriquer les Canons, Paris, 1795, in 4to; 3. Leçons de Géométrie Descriptive, Paris, 1813, in 8vo; 4. Application de l'Analyse à la Géométrie des Surfaces du Premier et du Deuxième Degré, Paris, 1809, in 4to. In this last work he presents the equations of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, planes,

MONGHIR

Pages 424-425

a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> district of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAHAR">Bahar</a>, situated between the twenty-sixth and twenty-eighth degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. The town and fortress of Monghir is situated on the southern <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Ganges. It was the residence of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> Sujah during his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> province, and was strengthened by him during his rebellion against his father, Shah Jehan. The fortifications have been for many years quite neglected, and the only <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> which remains is a small citadel, containing an arsenal and store-rooms. It is still surrounded by a wall and deep ditch, and is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of considerable antiquity. It was an object of contention between the kings of Bahar and Bengal in the early part of the sixteenth century. In 1762 it was the residence of Cossim Aly Khan, and was taken by the British the following year. The travelling distance from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a> is 300 miles. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 86. 38. E. Lat. 25. 23. N.

MONGOLIA

Pages 425-425

an extensive tract of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in Central <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and north-west of Asia. This vast country is not separated from the adjacent countries by any definite line of demarcation. The limits are vague, and the whole space is traversed by the nomadic tribes which, under the name of Mongols <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Tartars, have had so deep a share in all the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> revolutions of Asia. The various pastoral tribes which from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> immemorial have been scattered over the plains of that continent, being united under Zengis Khan, extended their ravages from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to sea, and were at one time possessed not only of the finest regions of the continent, but a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In later times the conquests of Timour were achieved by the same union of these tribes. The Mongol tribes are at present split into a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of petty states, dependent on the great empires of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a> and Russia. They still retain their roaming and pastoral habits, but since the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of firearms they are no longer formidable in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Mongolia, as far as its limits can be defined, is bounded on the east by the country of the Mancheous, on the west by a chain of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> northwards from the Beloor, and on the south by China. The whole of this country is one vast <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> plain, which borders on the Altai, and other mountain chains bounding Asiatic Russia on the north. This includes a considerable portion of the great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of Shamo or Cobi, which is composed entirely of pastureage. In this country are the heads of some of the greatest <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> the Russian and Chinese empires, the Hoangho, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMOUR">Amour</a>, and even the Irtisch. The great disadvantage under which it labours is a scarcity of water. The Mongols, the inhabitants of this region, are of the middle size, being muscular and strongly built; they have <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and flat faces, with low and flat noses; and small oblique <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> eyes, thick lips, a short chin, with very little <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, complete their physiognomy. Their habits are pastoral; and, like all the Tartars, they are addicted to intemperance. They are nominally subject to the empire of China; but their internal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is regulated by their native princes. The Kalkas, the Eluths, and the Buriats, Monishwar with other nations of Asiatic Russia, derive their origin from the Mongols.

MONISHWAR

Pages 425-425

a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bejaipoor, with a good market. It is thirty miles south-west from Poonah. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 74. 25. E. Lat. 18. 16. N.

MONJOUS

Pages 425-426

a people inhabiting the interior of Eastern <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-easterly <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOZAMBIQUE">Mozambique</a>. They occupy a portion of that space which, in our early maps, is allotted to the empire of Monumugi. They are <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> of the ugliest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, of a deep shining <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> cheek-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, thick lips, and small knots of woolly <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> on their heads. Their only weapons are bows and arrows, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of which they are dexterous. With regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> over which they are spread, no correct estimate can be formed. MONK anciently denoted a person who had retired from the world to give himself up wholly to God, and to live in solitude and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a>. The word is derived from the Latin monachus, and that from the Greek μοναχός, solitary. The origin of monks seems pretty well ascertained. The persecutions which attended the first ages of the Gospel forced some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> to retire from the world, and live in deserts and places the most private and unfrequented, in hopes of finding that peace and comfort amongst beasts which were denied them amongst men; and this being the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> of some very extraordinary persons, their example gave so much reputation to retirement, that the practice was <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> when the reason for its commencement had ceased. After the empire became Christian, instances of this kind were numerous; and those whose security had obliged them to live separately and apart, became afterwards united into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>. We may also add, that the mystic <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, which gained ground towards the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the third century, contributed to produce the same effect, and to drive men into solitude for the purposes of enthusiastic <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. The monks, at least the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ones, were distinguished into solitaries, cenobites, and sarabaites. The solitary were those who lived alone, in places remote from all <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and habitations of men. The cenobites were those who lived in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> with several others in the same <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and under the same superiors. The sarabaites were strolling monks, who had no fixed rule nor residence. The houses of monks were of two kinds, viz. monasteries and laurae. Those whom we call monks now-a-days are cenobites, who live together in a convent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, make vows of living according to a certain rule established by the founder, and wear a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> which distinguishes their order. Those who are endowed, or have a fixed revenue, are most properly called monks, monachi; as the Chartreux, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a>, Bernardines, and others. The Mendicants, or those who beg, as the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAPUCINS">Capucins</a> and Franciscans, are more properly called <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> and friars; though the names are frequently confounded. The first monks were those of St Anthony, who, towards the close of the fourth century, formed them into a regular body, engaged them to live in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> with each other, and prescribed to them fixed rules for the direction of their conduct. These regulations, which St Anthony had framed in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, were soon introduced into <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> by his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> Hilarion. About the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, Aones and Eugenius, with their companions Gaddamas and Azyzas, instituted the monastic order in Mesopotamia and the adjacent countries; and their example was followed with such rapid success, that in a short time the whole of the East was filled with men, who, abandoning all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> connections, advantages, pleasures, and concerns, wore out their lives amidst the hardships of want, and various kinds of suffering, in order to arrive at a more close and rapturous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with God and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>. From the East this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> passed into the West, and first into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and its neighbouring <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; though it is uncertain who transplanted it thither. St Martin, the celebrated bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOURS">Tours</a>, erected the first monasteries in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, and recommended religious solitude with such power and efficacy, both by his instructions and his example, that his funeral is said to have been attended by no less than two thousand monks. From Gaul the monastic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> extended itself gradually throughout the other provinces and countries of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Besides the monks of St <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> and those of St Jerome, there were the hermits of St Augustine, and afterwards those of St Benedict and St Bernard, and at length came those of St Francis and St Dominic, with a legion of others. Towards the close of the fifth century, the monks, who had formerly lived only for themselves in solitary retreats, and had never thought of assuming any <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> amongst the sacerdotal order, were now gradually distinguished from the populace, and endowed with such <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> privileges that they found themselves in a condition to claim an eminent station amongst the supporters and pillars of the Christian community. The fame of their piety and sanctity was so <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and presbyters were often chosen out of their order; and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for erecting edifices and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, in which the monks and holy virgins might serve God in the most commodious manner, was at this time carried beyond all bounds. The monastic orders were at first under the immediate jurisdiction of the bishops, from which they were exempted by the Roman pontiff about the end of the seventh century; and the monks, in return, devoted themselves wholly to advance the interests and to maintain the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of the Bishop of Rome. This immunity which they obtained was a fruitful source of licentiousness and disorder, and occasioned the greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the vices with which they were afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a>. In the eighth century the monastic discipline was extremely relaxed both in the eastern and western provinces, and all efforts to restore it were ineffectual. Nevertheless, this kind of institution was in the highest esteem, and nothing could equal the veneration which was paid about the close of the ninth century to such as devoted themselves to the monastic or conventual <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. This veneration induced several kings and emperors to call them to their courts, and to employ them in civil affairs of the greatest moment. Their reformation was attempted by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> the Meek, but the effect was of short <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. In the eleventh century they were exempted by the popes from the authority of their sovereigns, and new orders of monks were continually established; insomuch that in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a> of Lateran which was held in the year 1215, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> was passed, by the advice of Innocent III., to prevent the establishment of any new monastic institutions; and several were entirely suppressed. In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, it appears, from the testimonies of Protestant writers, that the monks were generally indolent, illiterate, profligate, and licentious epicures, whose views in life were confined to opulence, idleness, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. However, the Reformation had a manifest influence in restraining their excesses, and rendering them more circumspect and cautious in their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> conduct. Monks are distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of their habits, into black, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, gray, &c. Amongst the monks, some are called monks of the choir, others professed monks, and others lay monks, the last being destined for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the convent, and having neither clericate nor literature. Cloistered Monks are those who actually reside in the house, in opposition to extra-monks, who possess benefices depending on the monastery. Monks are also distinguished into reformed, whom the civil and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> authority have made masters of ancient convents, and put it in their power to retrieve the ancient discipline, which had been relaxed; and ancient, who remain in the convent, to live in it according to its establishment at the time when they made their vows, without obliging themselves to submit to any new <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REFORM">reform</a>. Anciently the monks were all laymen, and were only distinguished from the rest of the people by a particular habit and an extraordinary devotion. Not only were the monks excluded from the priesthood, but even priests were expressly prohibited from becoming monks, as appears from the letters of St Gregory. Pope Syriacus was the first who called them to the clericate, on occasion of the great scarcity of priests under which the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> was then supposed to labour; and since that time the priesthood has been usually united to the monastical profession. Monk, George, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALBEMARLE">Albemarle</a>, a personage memorable for having been the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in restoring <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, was descended from an ancient family, and born in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a> in 1608. Being an unprovided younger son, he dedicated himself to arms from his youth, and obtained a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of colours in the expedition to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Rhé; he afterwards served with reputation in the Low Countries, as well as in both <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">King</a> Charles's northern expeditions, and did such service in quelling the Irish rebellion, that he was appointed governor of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, but was superseded by parliamentary authority. Being appointed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>-general of the Irish brigade employed in the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NANTWICH">Nantwich</a> in Cheshire, he was taken prisoner by Sir Thomas Fairfax, and remained confined in the Tower of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> until the year 1646, when, as the means of obtaining <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, he took the covenant, and accepted a command in the Irish service under the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. He obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> command of all the parliamentary forces in the north of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, where he did signal services, until he was called to account for a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> made with the Irish rebels; a circumstance which was only obliterated by his future <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>. He served in Scotland under Oliver Cromwell, with such success, that he was left there as commander-in-chief; and he was one of the commissioners for uniting that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> with the newly-erected commonwealth. He also served at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> against the Dutch, and was treated so kindly on his return that Oliver is said to have grown jealous of him. He was, however, again sent to Scotland as commander-in-chief, and continued there five years; when he dissembled so well, and improved circumstances so dexterously, that he restored the king without any disturbance. For this service he was immediately rewarded with both honours and profit. He was created Duke of Albemarle, with an estate worth L7000 a year, besides other emoluments; and he enjoyed the confidence of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> as a compensation for having forfeited that of the people. After his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in 1670, there was published a treatise composed by him whilst he remained prisoner in the Tower, entitled Observations on <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">Military</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">Political</a> Affairs, in small folio.

MONKWEARMOUTH

Pages 426-427

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARD">ward</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, 275 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is divided from Bishopswearmouth by the river Wear, over which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> made wholly of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, except the pins binding the parts together, which are of wrought iron. It is sufficiently <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> to admit of ships passing under it without <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOWERING">lowering</a> their topmasts. An <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> stood here, from which its name is in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> derived. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounted in 1801 to 1103, in 1811 to 1091, in 1821 to 1278, and in 1831 to 1498. Adjoining to it is the populous district <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> suburb, but comprised in the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, Monkwearmouth <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>. It is chiefly inhabited by sailors, and by a numerous class called keelmen, who are employed in conveying coals in barges, provincially called keels, from the interior of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the larger vessels. The population of this district amounted in 1801 to 4239, in 1811 to 4264, in 1821 to 4924, and in 1831 to 6051.

MONMOUTH

Pages 427-429

JAMES <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of, son of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. by Mrs Lucy Walters, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a> in 1649. Upon the Restoration, he was called over to England, where the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> received him with all imaginable joy, and created him <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Orkney, which was changed into that of Monmouth; and he took his seat in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEERS">Peers</a> in the ensuing session of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. He married <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, the heiress of Francis earl of Buccleuch; and hence it came to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> that he had also the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Buccleuch, and took the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Scott, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of Scotland. In 1668 his father made him <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; and in 1672 he attended the French king in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, and gave proofs of bravery and conduct. In 1673 the king of France appointed him <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> with which he appeared before Maestricht; and he behaved with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> gallantry in the attack of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, being the first who entered it in the assault. He returned to England, and having been received with all possible respect, was appointed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. After this he went to assist the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> to raise the siege of Mons, and contributed not a little towards the success of the enterprise. He again returned to England, and was sent, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of general, to quell an insurrection in Scotland, which he effected; but soon afterwards he fell into disgrace; for, being a Protestant, he was deluded into ambitious schemes, upon the hopes of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the Duke of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORK">York</a>. He conspired against his father and the duke; and when the latter came to the throne by the title of James II. he openly appeared in arms, encouraged by the discontent that prevailed; but coming to a decisive <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> before he had sufficient force to oppose the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> army, he was defeated, made prisoner, tried for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, condemned, and beheaded, in 1685, at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of thirty-six. Monmouth, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name, 132 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is situated at the junction of the river Mumnow with the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>, and there are bridges over both streams. It is indifferently well built, has a town-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in the market-place, built on pillars, which form a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLONNADE">colonnade</a>, ornamented with a statue of King Henry V., who was born in this town. At the extremity of the town is the county gaol and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>-house, commodiously arranged, and the former well regulated. It is incorporated, and governed by a mayor, recorder, two bailiffs, and fifteen <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> councilmen. It has <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> returned one member to the House of Commons, and continues to do so under the recent <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. As the river Wye is navigable from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHEPSTOW">Chepstow</a>, some trade arises from that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> around, but especially on the banks of the Wye, is highly picturesque and beautiful. Near it are several objects of antiquity, which are much visited. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounted in 1801 to 3345, in 1811 to 3503, in 1821 to 4164, and in 1831 to 4916. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">MONMOUTHSHIRE</a>. This county was, before 1585, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, but has since been a part of England, although the greater part of the inhabitants still speak one of the three dialects of the Welsh <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; so that in some of the churches divine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> is conducted in that tongue, and in others alternately in that and in English. Monmouthshire is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a>, on the east by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, on the south by the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, and on the west by the Welsh counties of Brecon and Glamorgan. Its greatest length is thirty-three miles, its greatest breadth twenty-six, and its circumference 110 miles. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> is 516 miles, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> 330,240 acres. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the country is highly diversified, exhibiting every gradation from lofty and bleak <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> to highly verdant and beautiful sequestered valleys. Some of the mountains, as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a>-loaf, of 1850 feet, the Blorenge, of 1720, and the Skydyawr of 1498 feet, with several others, display their summits for many months covered with snow, whilst their sides, near the bottom, are cultivated with the different <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of grain, and terminate in meadows of the most luxuriant fertility. Mr Fox, in his Agricultural Survey of this county, divides it into three districts. The first, comprising the southern <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>, consists in part of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tracts of moor or marsh <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, exhibiting in some parts of it a great depth of unctuous loamy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and in others a vast body of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> peaty <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. In certain parts of this district the soil is of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> loamy consistence, highly favourable to the growth of various trees. Another portion is a mixture of clay and loam, forming fertile meadows; and above them is an excellent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> soil, in which turnips, potatoes, and grain, liberally repay the cultivator. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> division comprehends the eastern part of the county, extending to a considerable but varying distance on both sides of the river <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-USK">Usk</a>. The soil is of a faint red <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, highly grateful; and being carefully cultivated, the whole displays the appearance of great fertility. The third division comprises the western and most mountainous parts of the county. The soil on the hills is generally of a thin peaty <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, covering <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, underneath which are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of coal and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> ore, of almost unbounded productiveness. The low lands in this division are chiefly in the state of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> and pasture, whilst the middle lands are occupied partly by pasture and partly by arable husbandry. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> of this county have been generally celebrated for the picturesque scenery which their banks display, and which, added to the many remains of antiquity that are to be seen near them, invite the visits of numerous parties in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> months, and afford the highest gratification to travellers of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The most eminent of these rivers, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> as well as utility, is the Wye. It rises on the southern side of Plinlimmon, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a>, and, forming the line of division between the counties of Brecon and Radnor, passes through a part of Herefordshire, and, entering this county at Dizon, becomes navigable for boats at Monmouth, and empties itself into the Severn at Chepstow. The beauties of this stream are derived from the sinuosities of its course, the uniformity of its breadth, the picturesque country through which it flows, and, amongst many other striking objects on its banks, from the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a> of Tintern, and the mansion and grounds of Piercefield. The tide in this river rises at Chepstow to a greater height than in any other English river; at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of that town the elevation varies, on some occasions, from fifty to sixty feet, and it takes place with most unusual celerity. The Usk rises in the black mountains of Brecknockshire, and, when it enters this county, passes between lofty hills, which gives its borders every variety of beauty that landscape can display. It is navigable for a short distance, but only for barges. It abounds with salmon, some of which are frequently caught in it of a most unusual size. The other rivers are the Rumney, the Mumnow, and the Ebwy, each of which has peculiar and characteristic beauties. The heavy productions of this county, iron, coal, and <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, have given rise to the establishment of various <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> for their conveyance. The Monmouthshire Canal begins at Newport, and, dividing into two branches, connects that town, by the one with Pontypool and Pontnewyd, and by the other with Crumlin Bridge. The Brecknockshire Canal unites with this, and passes, in its course, under a hill, by means of a tunnel 360 feet in length. The county is most abundantly supplied with railroads leading from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> mining districts to the canals; and many private mines have small <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RAILWAYS">railways</a>, provincially called tram-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, leading to the principal iron railroads, by which a facility is afforded for the conveyance of productions through a country the roads of which are eminently bad. The agricultural productions are wheat, barley, and oats; with a few peas and beans. They are sufficient for the supply of the inhabitants, and the small surplus, as well as much fruit, is sent to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>. On the arable lands the system of summer fallowing is pretty generally pursued. The principal manure is lime, the stone from which it is burned being most abundant. The oxen of this county are highly esteemed, both for draught and for fattening. They are usually of a deep-red colour, short in the legs, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> in the carcass, being a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> between the breeds of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a> and Glamorgan. They are very docile in harness, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> fatten so as to weigh from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> hundredweight. They are much sought after by the English graziers, who purchase them when young, and, after employing them in labour, fatten them for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>. The sheep are remarkably small, and the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> is short and coarse; but the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is fine in the grain, and of a most delicate flavour. Of late years much improvement has been made in the flocks by judicious crosses with the Cotswold, Southdown, and Dorset sheep. The horses of the county are generally of a very meagre, light, and uncompact breed. In this county and Brecknockshire the breeding and rearing of mules is carried to a greater extent than in any other part of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. They are found very beneficial in the hilly districts, where the mines are worked. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MALE">Male</a> asses are imported from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and the south of France, to propagate, and the mules are frequently of a size and strength equal to the natives of those countries. The landed <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of this county is in few <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, but divided generally into small farms, varying in rent from £70 to £200. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a> are generally for twenty-one years, and the conduct of the landlords to their tenants is liberal, and somewhat parental." Many farms are held by copy of the court-roll. The greatest <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of Monmouthshire are derived from its mines. Coal and iron ore abound in all the hills. The facilities for interior conveyance have already been noticed. The coals of this county have, under the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament for constructing the canal, the peculiar privilege of being carried to the opposite shore, including the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Bristol and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, as far as Bridgewater, without paying the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>-borne duty. This gives to them a monopoly of those large markets, to the exclusion of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COLLIERIES">collieries</a> in the Forest of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a>, and of Glamorgan and Carmarthenshire. The proprietors of these last-mentioned mines have petitioned parliament to be placed on a similar footing; but, after a most patient <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of all the circumstances in a committee, the peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the coals brought by the Monmouthshire Canal were confirmed. The iron mines were worked as early as the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, and made a rapid progress; but, owing to the great consumption of wood, which soon caused a scarcity of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, they had sunk very low, till about fifty years ago, when the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of making iron from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COKE">coke</a> was introduced. This discovery, with the improvements in machinery, has given a vast impulse to the working of the iron mines. Fifteen or sixteen works, on the largest <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, and many smaller ones, have been established. At one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the weekly delivery of pig iron and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAR">bar</a> iron from these different works is stated to have amounted to one thousand tons. The abundance of iron, and the facility of intercourse with Cornwall, have led to the establishment of some very extensive manufactories of tin plates. The manufactory of a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a> was first practised in England by Thomas Allgood of Pontypool, in the reign of Charles II.; and though the skill of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BIRMINGHAM">Birmingham</a> has been successfully exerted to rival the town whence that ware derived its name, the business is still <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> there, but upon a limited scale. The manufactory of caps, for which Monmouth was celebrated at the period when Shakspeare wrote, has long been abandoned. At Newport and Chepstow there are some considerable establishments for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> ships. Few parts of the island contain more numerous or better preserved remains of Roman and Saxon antiquity than this county. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAERLEON">Caerleon</a> was long the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the British dominions, and the residence of King <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a>. The ruins of the wall, about 530 yards by 480, may still be traced; and the vast masses of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which now appear in a confused state, show that it was formerly a place of great importance. There are many Roman encampments still visible. The remains of the abbeys of Gracedieu, Llantarnam, Llanthony, and Tintern, and of the priories of Goldcliff, Thynemarke, Monmouth, and Usk, invite the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of antiquaries. The castles of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABERGAVENNY">Abergavenny</a>, Caerleon, Caldecot, Castell-Glas, Chepstow, Dinham, Grossmont, Llanfair, Senfrith, Strigul, Usk, and Llandeilo, are the most remarkable amongst numerous other similar buildings. The character of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> of the churches of Abergavenny, Caerleon, Caldecot, Chepstow, Newport, and others, discovers a very <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> origin. The antiquities of Monmouthshire would, indeed, require a volume for their delineation. The county gives the title of Earl of Abergavenny to the family of Neville, not by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> or writ, but as possessors of the castle of that town. The Irish Marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a> derives from it the title of Baron <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTLER">Butler</a>; and the Duke of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUFORT">Beaufort</a> is Baron Herbert of Chepstow and Rogland, and Baron Beaufort of Caldecot Castle. The members returned to the House of Commons are two for the county, and one for the united boroughs of Monmouth, Newport, and Usk. The whole county is within the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LLANDAFF">Llandaff</a>, except three parishes, which are in St <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s, and three others in that of Hereford. The population of this county at the periods of the four decennial enumerations has been as follows: In 1801 it amounted to 45,582, in 1811 to 62,127, in 1821 to 71,833, and in 1831 to 98,200, thus having more than doubled itself in thirty years. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of baptisms in the year 1830 was 840 males and 796 females; the burials were 617 males and 577 females; the marriages were 677; and the illegitimate children 71 males and 71 females.
