The number of families in the same year was 19,911, of whom 5614 were chiefly employed in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, 8626 were chiefly employed in trade, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and handicraft, and the remainder, 5671, were not comprised in either of the preceding classes. The males under twenty years of age were 26,910. The occupiers of land employing labourers were 1648, those not employing labourers were 1143, and the number of labourers in agriculture was 8485. The persons employed in manufacture or making manufacturing machinery was 3203; those employed in retail trade or handicraft, as masters or as workmen, were 6640; the capitalists, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>, professional and other educated men, amounted to 805; the labourers employed in labour not agricultural were 7173; other males twenty years of age, excepting servants, 1011; male servants under twenty years of age 122, and above twenty years 343. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> servants of all ages were 3741. The annual value of the whole real property of the county, as assessed for the income tax in 1815, was £295,097. There are but seven towns having markets, but some others are more populous than these. Those of more than 1000 inhabitants are as follows: | Town | Population | |-----------------------|------------| | Trevethin | 10,280 | | Newport | 7,064 | | Aberystwyth | 5,992 | | Uskawreed | 5,359 | | Monmouth | 4,916 | | Abergavenny | 4,230 | | Chepstow | 3,524 | | Mamhole | 3,208 | | Penmaen | 2,175 | | Lanover | 2,124 | | Llanwenarth | 1,956 | | Mynydd-maen | 1,918 | | Pantegue | 1,884 | | Machen | 1,173 | | Usk | 1,160 | | Caerleon | 1,070 | The seats of noblemen and gentlemen within the county are very numerous. The most remarkable are, Troyhouse, Duke of Beaufort; Bix Weir, General Rooke; Courthfield, William Vaughan, Esq.; Coldbrook, J. H. Williams, Esq.; Dynastow Court, Samuel Bosanquet, Esq.; Kesneyshouse, L. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, Esq.; Llanarth Court, John Jones, Esq.; Llanover, Benjamin Waddington, Esq.; Llanvitsangle, Earl of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; Mamheled, W. Morgan, Esq.; Mayndec, Sir Robert Kemeys; <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PEN">Pen</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PARK">Park</a>, — Williams, Esq.; Piercefield, late Nathaniel <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, Esq.; Pontypool, C. H. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEIGH">Leigh</a>, Esq.; Tregear, Sir Charles Morgan, Bart.; Trewyn, J. Rosier, Esq.; Wynnstow Court, Thomas Swinerton, Esq.

MONOCEROS

Pages 429-429

UNICORN, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a southern constellation, formed by Hevelius, and consisting, in his catalogue, of nineteen stars, but in the Britannic catalogue, of thirty-one stars.

MONOCHORD

Pages 429-429

an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> by which the several proportions of musical sounds and intervals, as well in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> as in the tempered scales, are tried. Originally it had, as its name implies, only one string; but it is better constructed with two; for, by means of the additional string, an opportunity is afforded of judging of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of two tempered notes in every possible variety of temperaments.

MONODY

Pages 429-429

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a mournful kind of song, sung by a person all alone, to give vent to his grief. The word is derived from μονος, alone, and στιχος, I sing.

MONOGAMY

Pages 429-429

compounded of μονος, alone, and γαμος, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, the state <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> condition of those who have only married once, or who are restrained to a single wife. See POLYGAMY.

MONOGRAM

Pages 429-429

a character <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> cipher, composed of one, two, or more letters interwoven, being a kind of abbreviation of a name, anciently used as a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, badge, arms, &c. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MONOMOTAPA">MONOMOTAPA</a>. See Motapa.

MONOPHYSITES

Pages 429-429

a general name given to all those sectaries in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a> who only own one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, and who maintain that the divine and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> natures of Christ were so united as to form only one nature, yet without any change, confusion, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> mixture of the two natures. The Monophysites, however, properly so called, are the followers of Severus, a learned monk of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> (who was created <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of Antioch in 518), and of Petrus Fulgens. The Monophysites were encouraged by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Anastasius, but depressed by Justin and succeeding emperors. However, this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> was restored by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> Baradeus, an obscure monk, insomuch that when he died bishop of Edessa, in the year 588, he left it in a most flourishing state in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, Mesopotamia, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUBIA">Nubia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, and other countries. The laborious efforts of Jacob were seconded in Egypt and the adjacent countries by Theodosius bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and he became so famous that all the Monophysites of the East considered him as their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> and founder, and were called Jacobites, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of their new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. The Monophysites are divided into two sects or parties; the one African, the other Asiatic. At the head of the latter is the patriarch of Antioch, who resides for the most <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of St Ananias, near the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MERDIN">Merdin</a>; the former are under the jurisdiction of the patriarch of Alexandria, who generally resides at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, and are subdivided into Copts and Abyssinians. From the fifteenth century downwards, all the patriarchs of the Monophysites have taken the name of Ignatius, in order to show that they are the lineal successors of Ignatius, who was bishop of Antioch in the first century, and consequently the lawful patriarchs of Antioch. In the seventeenth century a small body of the Monophysites in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> abandoned for some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> the doctrine and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, and embraced the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of Rome. But the African Monophysites, notwithstanding that poverty and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> which exposed them to the seductions of sophistry and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a>, remained firm in their principles, and made an obstinate resistance to the promises, presents, and attempts employed by the papal missionaries to bring them under the Roman yoke; and in the eighteenth century, those of Asia and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> have persisted in their refusal to enter into the communion of the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> entreaties and alluring offers which have from time to time been made by the pope's legates to conquer their inflexible <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>. The Monophysites propagate their doctrine in Asia with zeal and assiduity, and have at length gained over to their communion a part of the Nestorians, who inhabit the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>.

MONOPOLI

Pages 429-429

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, on the spot where formerly stood the Roman city of Equitania. It is situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore, between three hills, and has a small harbour, whence extensive <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a> are carried on. It suffers much at times from a scarcity of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, as there are neither brooks nor <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, the only supply being from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>. It is the seat of a bishop, and, besides the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, contains fourteen churches, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> of which appertain to as many <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> and monasteries. It contains 15,500 inhabitants. MONOPOLY. See on this head <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">COMMERCE</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">POLITICAL</a> ECONOMY.

MONOSYLLABLE

Pages 429-429

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, a word which consists only of one <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a>, and is composed either of one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> more letters pronounced at the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>.

MONOTHELITES

Pages 429-429

an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, which sprung out of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EUTYCHIANS">Eutychians</a>, and were so called from allowing only one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the Monothelites took its rise in 630, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Heraclius for an adherent; it was the same with that of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACEPHALOUS">Acephalous</a> Severians. They allowed of two wills in Christ, considered with regard to the two natures, but reduced them to one, by reason of the union of these natures, thinking it absurd that there should be two free wills in one and the same person. They were condemned by the sixth general <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> in 680, as being supposed to destroy the perfection of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> of Jesus Christ, by depriving it of will and operation. Their sentiments were afterwards embraced by the Maronites.

MONOTONY

Pages 429-429

an uniformity of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> a fault in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>, when a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of words is delivered in one unvaried tone.

MONREALE

Pages 429-429

a parliamentary <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Mazzara, situated on the side of a hill, at the foot of which the river Ammiglo flows, four <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> miles from Palermo. It is the seat of an archbishop, is both healthy and fertile, and has a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, several monasteries, with 12,770 inhabitants, who depend chiefly on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, and whose most valuable product is abundance of almonds.

MONRO

Pages 429-431

Dr Alexander, senior, a celebrated physician and anatomist, was the son of Mr John Monro, who was for some years a surgeon in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> under <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">King</a> William in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, and who afterwards settled in that capacity in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. The subject of this biographical sketch was born in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1697. He showed an early inclination to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic; and his father, after giving him the best <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> which Edinburgh then afforded, sent him successively to London, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, to improve himself further in his profession. At London he attended the lectures of Hawksbee and Whiston on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental <a class="</a>xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and the anatomical demonstrations of Mr Cheselden. At Paris he frequented the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, and the lectures on the different branches of physic and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a>; and, towards the end of autumn 1718, he went to Leyden, and studied under the celebrated Boerhaave. On his return to Edinburgh in the autumn of 1719, Drummond and Macgill, who were then conjunct nominal professors and demonstrators of anatomy to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> of Surgeons, having resigned in his favour, his father prevailed on him to read some public lectures on anatomy, and to illustrate them by showing the curious anatomical preparations which he had made and sent home when abroad. He at the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> persuaded Dr Alston, then a young <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>, to give some public lectures on <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. Accordingly, in the beginning of the winter 1720, these two young professors began to give regular courses of lectures, the one on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">materia medica</a> and botany, the other on anatomy and surgery; and these were the first regular courses of lectures on any of the branches of medicine which had ever been read at Edinburgh, and may be looked upon as the opening of that medical school which has since acquired so <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation all over <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In the summers of 1721 and 1722, Dr Monro, by the persuasion of his father, read some lectures on chirurgical subjects, particularly on wounds and tumours, which he never would publish, having written them in a hurry, and before he had much <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; but he inserted from time to time the improvements which he thought might be made in surgery, in the volumes of Medical Essays and Observations, to be hereafter mentioned. About the year 1720, his father communicated to the physicians and surgeons at Edinburgh a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> which he had <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> formed in his own mind, of having the different branches of physic and surgery regularly taught at Edinburgh. This was highly approved of by them; and through their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> regular professorships of anatomy and medicine were instituted in the university. Such was the foundation of the Medical <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACULTY">Faculty</a> of Edinburgh. His son, Dr Monro, was first made university professor of anatomy; and, two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> three years afterwards, Drs Sinclair, Rutherford, Innes, and Plummer, were made professors of medicine; the professorship of materia medica and botany, which Dr Alston then held, having been added to the university many years before. Immediately after these gentlemen were elected professors, they began to deliver regular courses of lectures on the different branches of medicine; and they and their successors have uniformly <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to do so every winter since that time. But the plan for a medical education at Edinburgh was still incomplete without an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, where students could see the practice of physic and surgery, as well as hear the lectures of the professors. A scheme was therefore proposed by Dr Monro's father, and others, particularly the members of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of Physicians and Board of Surgeons, for raising by subscription a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and supporting an hospital for the reception of diseased <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; and Dr Monro published a pamphlet setting forth the advantages which would attend such an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>. In a short time a very considerable sum of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was raised; a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was fitted up; and patients were admitted into it, and regularly attended by many of the physicians and surgeons in town. As the fund for this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> had considerably increased, owing in a great <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and influence of Mr George Drummond, the foundation was laid of the present <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, commodious, and useful hospital, the Royal Infirmary, in the planning of which Dr Monro suggested many useful hints; and, in particular, the elegant room for chirurgical operations was designed and executed under his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. Provost Drummond and he were nominated the building committee, and the fabric was completed in a short space of time. It has since been so largely endowed, as to be capable of receiving a great <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of diseased poor, whose various <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the students of physic and surgery have an opportunity of seeing daily treated with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and care by physicians and surgeons eminent in their profession; and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of the particulars of all the cases which have been received into the house since it was first opened has been kept, in books appropriated to that purpose, for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the students. In order to render the hospital of still further use to the students, Dr Monro frequently, whilst he continued professor of anatomy, gave lectures on the chirurgical cases; and Dr Rutherford, then professor of the practice of physic, began, in the year 1748, to deliver clinical lectures, to be continued every winter, on the most remarkable cases which occurred in the hospital. Dr Monro, though he was elected professor of anatomy in the year 1721, was not received into the university till the year 1725, when he was inducted along with Mr Colin MacLaurin, the celebrated mathematician, with whom he ever lived in the strictest friendship. From this time he regularly every winter gave a course of lectures on anatomy and surgery, from October to May, upon a most judicious and comprehensive plan; a task in which he persevered with the greatest assiduity, and without the least interruption, for nearly forty years; and so great was the reputation he had acquired, that students flocked to him from the most distant corners of his majesty's dominions. In 1759 the professor entirely relinquished the business of the anatomical <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> to his son Dr Alexander Monro, who had returned from abroad, and had assisted him in the course of lectures the preceding year. But after this resignation, he still endeavoured to render his labours useful to mankind, by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-READING">reading</a> clinical lectures at the hospital for the improvement of the students. Of these, Dr Duncan, who was one of his pupils, has given an interesting account. "There I had myself the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of being a pupil, who profited by the judicious conduct of his practice, and was improved by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and acuteness of his remarks. I have indeed to regret that I attended only the last course of lectures in which he had ever a share, and at a time when he was subjected to a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> which proved at length fatal. Still, however, from what I <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> and from what I heard, I can venture to assert, that it is hardly possible to conceive a physician more attentive to practice, or a preceptor more anxious to communicate instructions. His <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> in the former of these <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> led him to bestow the most anxious care on his patients while they were alive; and his zeal in the latter induced him to make them the subject of useful <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> when they happened to die. In the different stations of physician, of lecturer, and of manager in the hospital, he took every measure for inquiring into the causes of diseases, by dissection. He personally attended the opening of every body; and he not only dictated to the students an accurate report of the dissection, but with nice discrimination contrasted the diseased and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> state of every organ. Thus, in his own person he afforded to the students a conspicuous example of the advantages of early anatomical pursuits, as the happiest foundation for a medical superstructure. His being at once engaged in two departments, the anatomical theatre and clinical <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, furnished him with opportunities both on the dead and living body, and placed him in the most favourable situation for the improvement of medicine; and from these opportunities he derived every possible advantage which they could afford." His father, Mr Monro, lived to an advanced <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and enjoyed the unspeakable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of beholding a son, esteemed and regarded by mankind, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> in the execution of his favourite plan, which formed the great object of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, that of founding a seminary of medical education in his native <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The son, who survived him nearly thirty years, had the satisfaction to behold this seminary of medical education frequented yearly by three or four hundred students, many of whom came from the most distant corners of his majesty's dominions, and to see it arrive at a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of reputation far beyond his most sanguine hopes. Dr Monro died on the 10th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1767, in the 70th year of his age. Of his works, the first in order is his Osteology, which was written for the use of students, but is capable also of affording instruction to the oldest and most experienced practitioner; as, besides a minute <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the parts copied from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, it everywhere abounds with new and important observations immediately applicable to practice. It has been translated into many different languages; has passed through numerous editions; and has been reprinted in foreign countries in the most superb manner, accompanied with elegant and masterly engravings. His description of the Lacteal Sac and Thoracic Duct contains the most accurate account of that important <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body which has yet been published; and his Anatomy of the Nerves <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> transmit to posterity an excellent example of accurate dissection, faithful description, and ingenious reasoning. The six volumes of Medical Essays and Observations, published by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> in Edinburgh, are universally known and esteemed. To that society he was appointed secretary; but, after the publication of the first volume, to which he had largely contributed, the members growing remiss in their attendance, he became the sole collector and publisher of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. To him we are therefore in a great measure indebted for those numerous and important discoveries with which this publication has enriched every department of medical knowledge. In the two first volumes of the Physical and Literary Essays, published by the Physical Society of Edinburgh, in which he had the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of one of the presidents, we find several papers written by him, which are not the least ornaments of that collection. His account of the Success of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INOCULATION">Inoculation</a> in Scotland may be considered as his last publication. It demonstrates his extensive correspondence and indefatigable industry, and has had great influence in promoting that salutary practice. Besides these, he was also the author of several other elegant and masterly productions, which were either never published, or were published without his knowledge and from incorrect copies. A collection of his works, properly arranged, corrected, and illustrated with copperplates, was published by Dr Alexander Monro, his son and successor in the anatomical chair, in a splendid quarto volume, printed at Edinburgh in 1781; and to this was prefixed a life of the author, by another of his sons, Dr Donald, physician in London.

MONS

Pages 431-431

an arrondissement in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Hennegau, in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, comprehending <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> cantons, divided into 141 communes, with 151,500 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> both of the province and the arrondissement. It is situated on the river Trouille, and is strongly fortified; it is well built, and its environs are adorned with tasteful walks. It contains 4600 houses, and about 20,000 inhabitants. Near to it are found <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a>, and abundance of coal. The trade is considerable, consisting of cotton and woollen goods, ironmongery, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">china</a>, and refined <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 52' E. Lat. 50° 27' N.

MONSEIGNEUR

Pages 431-431

in the plural Messeigneurs, a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and respect used by the French in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> to persons of superior <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Dukes, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a>, archbishops, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, and presidents à mortier, were complimented with the title of Monseigneur. In the petitions presented to the sovereign courts, they used the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> Messeigneurs. Monseigneur, absolutely used, was a title applied to the dauphin of France. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was unknown till the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV, before which the dauphin was styled Monseigneur le Dauphin. Monsieur, in the plural Messieurs, a term or title of civility, used by the French in speaking to their equals, or those a little below them. Monsieur, absolutely used, was a title appropriated to Monsieur the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of France, or the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>. The king was also called Monseigneur, but that only by the children of France.

MONSOON

Pages 431-431

a regular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> periodical <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, in the East Indies, blowing constantly in the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> during six months of the year, and contrariwise during the remaining six. In the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> Ocean, the winds are partly general, blowing all the year round the same way, as in the Ethiopic Ocean; and partly periodical, that is, blowing half the year one way, and the other half year on the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; and those points and times of shifting differ in different parts of this ocean. These latter are what have been called monsoons. The shifting of these monsoons does not take <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> all at once. In some places the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the change is attended with calms, but in others with variable winds; and those of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, when they cease to be westerly, are liable to become tempestuous; indeed such is their violence, that they seem to be of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the West <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> hurricanes, and render the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of those seas very unsafe at the time of the year when they prevail. These tempests the seamen call the breaking up of the monsoons. Monsoons, then, are a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of what we otherwise <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> trade winds. They take the denomination of monsoon from an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> pilot, who first crossed the Indian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> by means of them; though others derive the name from a Portuguese word signifying <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> or change of wind and sea.

MONSTER

Pages 431-432

a birth <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> production of a living being, degenerating from the proper and usual disposition of parts in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> to which it belongs; as, when there are too many members, or too few, or some of them are extravagantly out of proportion, either on the side of excess or defect. The word comes from the Latin monstrum, a derivative of monstrando, showing; and hence also the box in which relics were anciently kept to be shown was called monstrum. Dugdale mentions an inventory of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORK">York</a> with this article, Item unum monstrum cum ossibus sancti Petri in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BERYL">beryl</a>, et crucifixo in summato. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> defines a monster to be a defect of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, when, acting towards an end, she cannot attain to it, from some of the principles being corrupted. Monsters do not propagate their kind, for which reason some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> males amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of monsters, as also hermaphrodites. Females which bring forth twins are found most liable to produce monsters. The reason probably is, that although the twins are covered with one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> chorion, yet they have each their separate amnios, which by their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTIGUITY">contiguity</a> may chance to grow together, and so occasion a confusion or blending of the parts. Various theories have been proposed by philosophers and physiologists to account for the production of monsters. But after all, it must be confessed, that we are very little acquainted with those deviations from the ordinary course of nature. With respect to structure, monsters are of various kinds. Some have an excess or defect in certain parts, such as those which are called acephalons, or want the head; those which have two heads, two arms, two legs, and one body, or which have two bodies and one head, or which have three legs; and those which want the arms or the legs. Others err through an extraordinary and deformed conformation, through an unnatural union of certain parts or viscera, through a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> derangement in one or more of their members, and through the extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> which these often occupy in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this derangement or transposition. The monster described by Dr Eller of the Academy of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> was of this kind. It was a fetus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> months, twenty-eight inches <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>, with an enormous head and frightful countenance; and in the middle Monster of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and vast forehead it had a reddish eye, without either eyebrows or eyelids, and sunk deep into a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> hole. Immediately below this eye was an excrescence which strongly resembled a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PENIS">penis</a> with a glans, a prepuce, and an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a>; the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> covered with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> was likewise below the nape of the neck. In other monsters we meet with the unnatural union of some parts, which, from their destination and functions, ought always to be separate; and the separation of other parts, which, for the same reasons, ought constantly to be united. The reader may see the different ways in which the formation of monsters takes place, in four <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> by M. Lemery, inserted in L'Histoire de l'Académie des Sciences, 1738 and 1739. In the volume published by the Academy of Sciences in the year 1724, mention is made by M. Geoffroy of a monster born in Barrois, 1722. This monstrous production consisted of two children without the inferior extremities, and joined together by a common navel. Each of them had a nurse, sucked, and eat pap; and the one sucked whilst the other slept. The reader may likewise consult the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part of Winslow's Memoirs on Monsters, inserted in the volume published by the Academy of Sciences in 1734, where he <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> find the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the two very extraordinary twin monsters, who exhibited during their lives a great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in their moral and physical qualities. We are obliged to refer simply to these memoirs, as they are too long for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a>. It is observed by Haller, that in some monsters the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> structure has been changed by some shock or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, whilst in others the structure, independently of any accident, appears to have been originally monstrous; such as when all the members are reversed from left to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, when the person has six fingers, and in many other instances. M. de Maupertuis mentions that there was at Berlin a family who for several generations had six fingers on each <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. M. de Riville <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> an instance of this at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, of which he has given a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. M. Renou, surgeon at Pommeraye, in Anjou, published an account of some families with six fingers, who were to be found in several parishes of the Lower Anjou, and which had existed there from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> immemorial. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> was perpetuated in these families even when they intermarried with persons who were free from it. Whether the propagation of these supernumerary organs, which are not only useless, but inconvenient and even disagreeable, be owing to the father or mother, the children of both sexes are subject to it indiscriminately. A father and mother with six fingers frequently have a part, and sometimes the whole of their children, free from this deformity; but it again makes its appearance, and in a very great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, in the third <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. From this it appears that such a fault in the conformation is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>. M. Reaumur likewise published the history of a family in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Malta, the children of which were born with six fingers and six toes. But it deserves to be inquired, whether these supernumerary fingers were real fingers. (The reader may here consult the Journal de Physique for November 1774, p. 372.) This variety of sexadigtery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet is not comprehended in the Recherches sur quelques Conformations Monstrueuses des Doigts dans l'Homme, which is inserted in the Memoirs of the Academy of Sciences for 1771. In the Journal de Physique for August 1776, we find a description of a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> uterus and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-VAGINA">vagina</a> observed in a woman who died in childbirth, by Dr Purcell of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>; and in that for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1788, we have an account, by Baron Dietrich, of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> fingers on each hand. Monsters are more common and more extraordinary in the vegetable than in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, because the different juices are more easily deranged and confounded together. Leaves are often seen, from the internal parts of which other leaves <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> forth; and it is not uncommon to see <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of the ranunculus from the middle of which issues a stalk <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> another flower. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BONNET">Bonnet</a> informs us, that in certain warm and rainy years he has frequently met with monsters of this kind in rose-trees. This observer saw a rose, from the centre of which issued a square stalk of a whitish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, tender and without prickles, which at its top bore two flower-buds opposite to each other, and totally destitute of a calyx; and a little above the buds issued a petal of a very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> shape. Upon the prickly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> which supported this rose, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> was observed which had the shape of a trefoil, together with a broad flat pedicel. In the Memoirs of the Academy of Sciences for 1707, mention is made of a rose, from the centre of the leaves of which issued a rose branch two or three inches long, and furnished with leaves. In the Memoirs for 1775, a singular instance is mentioned of a monstrosity observed by Duhamel, in an apple-tree grafted with clay. At the place of the insertion there appeared a bud which produced a stalk and some leaves; the stalk and the pedicle of the leaves were of a pulpy substance, and had the most perfect resemblance both in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and smell to the pulp of a green apple. An extraordinary chamomile is mentioned in the Acta Helvetica. Bonnet, in his Recherches sur l'Usage des Feuilles, mentions likewise some monstrous productions which have been found in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> with kernels, analogous in their nature to those which occur in the flowers of the ranunculus and of the rose-tree. He observed a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, from the eye of which issued a stalk of thirteen or fourteen leaves, very well shaped, and many of them of the natural size. He noticed a second pear which gave rise to a ligneous and knotty stalk, on which grew another pear somewhat larger than the first. The stalk had probably flourished, and the fruit had formed. Reynter has mentioned some individuals monstrous with respect to the flower, in the Journal de Physique et d'Histoire Naturelle for November 1785. These vegetable productions, which are so extraordinary, and so contrary to the common course of things, do nevertheless present deviations subject to particular laws, and reducible to certain principles, by distinguishing such as are perpetuated either by seed or by transplanting, from those which seem to be only accidental. Monstrosities which are perpetuated exist in the original organization of the seed of the plant, such as marked or curled leaves, &c. The word monster is more properly applied to those irregularities in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which arise from frequent transplantation, and from a particular culture, such as double flowers; but those monstrosities which are not perpetuated, and which arise from accidental and transient causes disturbing the primitive organization of the plant when it comes to be unfolded, being the effect of diseases, of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, of a superfluity or scarcity of juices, of a deprivation of the vessels contributing to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUTRITION">nutrition</a>, of the sting of insects, and of contusions and natural grafts, retain also the name of monsters. Of this kind are knobs or swellings, stunting, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GALL">gall</a>-nuts, certain streaks, and other similar defects.

MONTACUTE

Pages 432-432

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, in the hundred of Tintinhull, 123 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It has near it a singular mound <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> sharp hill, covering twenty acres at the base, on which a castle was built by Moreton, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of William the Conqueror, who named it from his friend Drogo de Montacute. It was afterwards converted into a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> and a borough. The inhabitants, who are chiefly occupied in making gloves and sail-cloth, amounted in 1801 to 827, in 1811 to 857, in 1821 to 973 and in 1831 to 1028.

MONTAGNANO

Pages 432-432

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the Austrian delegation of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>. It is situated on the Fiumecello, and is surrounded with walls. It contains a conventual and several other churches, with 8275 inhabitants, who are

MONTAGU

Pages 432-436

Lady <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Wortley, an English lady of distinguished talents, but of eccentric character, was the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Evelyn Pierrepont <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a>, and Lady Mary Fielding, daughter of William <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Denbigh, and was born at Thoresby, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAMSHIRE">Nottinghamshire</a>, in the year 1690. Both on the father's and the mother's side Lady Mary came of a stirring <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>, the Pierreponts and Fieldings having taken <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> parts in the civil <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, though under painful circumstances of family <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>. But there was genius as well as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> in her blood; for the mother of Beaumont the dramatist was a Pierrepont, and Lady Mary had a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> ancestor with Villiers duke of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>, who was her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> uncle. The Fieldings, however, were not thought very bright, until Henry, who was her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>, came to enhance their reputation; and Lady Mary says that they were all called "fair and foolish." At the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of four she lost her mother; but her grandmother, a sensible woman, appears to have done something towards supplying the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of her deceased <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. By Lady Mary's own account of her <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, it was "one of the worst in the world;" but this is to be taken with very considerable qualification. She was indeed left to a superstitious nurse and a weak governess; but her understanding being naturally much superior to that of her instructress, she was induced to profit by her <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>'s advantages, and, under the tuition of his preceptors, acquired some knowledge of Latin, a smattering of Greek, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the French <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. At the age of eight she had made considerable proficiency in her studies, and began to read all the books she could lay her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and romances, particularly those of the old French school, of which she became exceedingly enamoured. Her first known poetical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> was an Epistle from Julia to Ovid, which she wrote at the age of twelve, and which, besides the complimentary cant of gallantry, exhibits a nice <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, being exactly in the style which Dryden would have employed in addressing Lady Castlemain, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Garth, in inscribing upon drinking glasses verses on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of his mistress. At fifteen she formed a project of establishing an English nummery; and had she then been mistress of an independent fortune, she would certainly (she says) have executed it, and elected herself lady-abbess. At twenty, she translated Epictetus, most probably from the Latin version, under the eye of her friend Bishop Burnet. Amongst the early <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> friends of Lady Mary was Mrs <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Wortley, sister of Mr Edward Wortley Montagu, whose father, Sidney, a son of the well-known Earl of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a>, had added the name of Wortley to that of Montagu, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with an heiress. Edward Wortley was not a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> of gallantry, and had taken little pains to cultivate the acquaintance of his sister's friends; but happening one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to meet with Lady Mary Pierrepont in her apartments, he was so much struck with her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and beauty, as well as charmed with the unusual <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> for the classics, that, in a few days, he made her a present of Quintus Curtius, an author she had mentioned as never having read, accompanied with some verses, indifferent enough in themselves, but, from a person of his character, amounting to a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of love. His sister fanned the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> with all her might; and a correspondence ensued, which, after a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of hesitation, doubt, and indecision on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the lady, ended in the marriage of the parties. Mr Wortley has been represented as a dull phlegmatic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, of a tame genius and moderate capacity, or as a man of parts more <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> than brilliant, which is only a civil way of saying the same thing; nor does there seem to be any good ground for questioning the accuracy of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, although his attainments as a scholar, and his distinction as a politician, were both considerable. But however this may be, the marriage seems to have been ill assorted, and certainly proved unfortunate. There was probably no real affection upon either side; and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be true that Lady Mary's temper was not good, Mr Wortley was scarcely the man to supply any defects on her part, or to bear <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> with such infirmities. That she possessed <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> is evident; but her sarcasms and her self-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a>, united with a sense of superiority, and perhaps also some resentment of the coldness evinced towards her by her husband, sufficiently indicate the radical disparity, or rather incongruity, of character which existed between them. In 1714, Mr Wortley obtained a place in the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, and, in consequence, took his lady to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, where her wit, spirit, and beauty attracted general admiration, and made a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, afterwards George II. In 1716, Mr Wortley, who had made no great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> at home, was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to Constantinople, where his success was not more remarkable. But he took his wife with him to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Turkish empire, and thus afforded her an opportunity, in her Letters from the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>, of charming the world with the most luxurious pictures ever yet given of a voluptuous people; and of bringing away with her, in the shape of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INOCULATION">inoculation</a> for small-pox, a talisman for the preservation of beauty. From these, and indeed from all her future letters, it is clear that her good sense was <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and uncompromising, with an ever-increasing tendency towards universal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; and that her husband, excepting as holder of the purse, and a person entitled to certain conventional consideration, had already become an individual of no mark or likelihood in her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. Nobody seems to think of him as he travels, except out of delicacy towards his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>. Gallants at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a> and elsewhere do not see him, nor notice him. Pope makes flagrant love to her in his letters, as if no such person existed; or adds his compliments to the husband, as if the love-making was an affair of perfect indifference to him. Besides Constantinople, Lady Mary and her husband, whilst abroad, visited several parts of Germany; and on their return sailed through the Archipelago, touched on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and, crossing the Mediterranean to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, reached home through Lyons and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in October 1718. From all these places we have letters of the liveliest, and, considering the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> at which she wrote, of the most original description; a traveller so shrewd and observant was till then unknown, and her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> gave to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> an additional <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a>. The manners of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> she found peculiarly congenial to her disposition; and accordingly, when, in 1739, she resolved to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the remainder of her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> on the Continent, she betook herself to that country, and remained there until within less than a year of her <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. On her return from the East, Pope prevailed on her to come and live near him at Twickenham. Both were then in the zenith of their reputation, and mutual admiration seemed to give assurance of the stability of their friendship. But a short time sufficed to prove that this anticipation was ill founded. Jealousy of her talents, and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> sentiments, have been gravely assigned as the primary causes of that dislike on the part of Pope, which soon manifested itself with such exasperated and vindictive animosity. But neither of these causes can have had the least share in producing the rupture. To ascribe it to jealousy of her wit is ridiculous, because on this score there neither was nor could be rivalry or competition; and as to difference of political sentiments, Lady Mary's predilections and attachments were the same before as after the quarrel, and hence Pope's hatred of the Whigs could not have had any such influence as has been ascribed to it. The real cause appears to have been altogether different. Lady Mary's own statement, the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of which seems to be borne out by other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, was this; that at some ill-chosen time, when she least expected what romances call a "declaration," Pope made such passionate love to her, as, in spite of her utmost endeavours to be angry and look <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, provoked an immediate burst of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a>, from which moment he became her implacable enemy. Now, if "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HELL">hell</a> has no fury like a woman scorned," it may, by a parity of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>, be imagined with how deep and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> a sense of mortification the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, misshapen, applauded poet must have felt himself smitten, and all his future recollections degraded, by an ever-present sense of scorn and contempt. To say that he had no <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> thus to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> her, is to say the truth; yet to believe that her manners and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of character, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the times, and of the circles in which she moved, had given no license, no encouragement, no hope of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> to the presumptuous declaration, is impossible; and to trample in this way upon the whole miserable body of his vanity and humility, upon all which the consciousness of acceptability and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> amongst his fellow-creatures had given him to sustain himself, and all which, in so weak, fragile, and dwarfish a shape, required so much to be sustained, was not very humane in her ladyship, and assuredly beyond the reach of forgiveness in Pope. On her part, a little pity might have divided the moment with contempt; it was scarcely necessary to be quite so cruel to one who was really so insignificant. On his, the contemptuous laughter which greeted his proposals must have carried a poisonous blight to his heart, and changed into the venom of deadly malice the blood by which it had been momentarily warmed into love. Yet nothing can palliate, far less excuse, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> and indecent manner in which he indulged his resentment, or the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> prevarication with which he evaded every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of ungrateful behaviour towards those whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> he had once servilely solicited. But it is a relief to turn from the sight of Lady Mary as a beauty and a wit, to consider her in the character of a mother, and, what is more, in that of a public benefactress. On her return from Constantinople, she introduced inoculation for the small-pox into England, through the medium of the medical attendant of the embassy. She had lost her only brother by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, which had also destroyed her own beautiful eye-lashes; and she was resolved to give to her family and the world the benefit of a practice which promised to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the lives and to preserve the beauty of millions. With courageous love, she began upon her own offspring, and lived to see her innovation triumphant, though not until it had encountered such an opposition that she almost repented of her philanthropy. But this only enhanced the merit of her perseverance, and the many sacrifices of time and spirit which she consented to make; for she submitted to be hawked about as a sort of nurse and directress, in families which required comfort under the experiment. Her descendant informs us, that when four great physicians were deputed by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to watch the progress of her daughter's inoculation, they "betrayed not only such incredulity as to its success, but such an unwillingness to have it succeed, such an evident spirit of rancour and malignity, that she never cared to leave the child alone with them one second, lest it should in some secret way suffer from their interference." But these must surely have been only a mother's terrors, aggravated perhaps by a little of her own sarcasm and vehemence. At the same time, professional persons seldom evince much favour for discoveries or improvements in their own art originating with others, whom they regard as interlopers; and it is probable enough that, whilst she contrived, by her ready wit, to make the physicians appear very small in their own eyes, they, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, were fain to assert their own <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> by trying to look big and contemptuous. Lady Mary preserved her supremacy in the world of fashion, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to give fresh proofs of her talents, until the year 1739, when, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, she left England with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to pass the remainder of her life on the Continent. She proceeded at once to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>; and having determined to establish herself in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Italy, she took possession of a deserted <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> on the banks of Lake Isco, in the Venetian territory, where she planned a garden, applied herself to the business of a country life, and solaced herself with books sent by her daughter Lady Bute, which in some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> supplied the want of society. It seems probable that one of the causes which drove her from England was the enmity she had kindled up all around her by the license of her tongue and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, and not any flagrant irregularity of conduct, as some have pretty broadly insinuated. She was always <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> scandal. A journal full of it was burned by her family, not without good reason, if, from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of some of her published writings, a conjecture may be formed as to the nature of its contents. Her very panegyrics were sometimes malicious; and even Pope himself, with all the temptations of wit and resentment, would hardly have written of her as he did, had her reputation for satirical strictures been less a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of notoriety. As to her life on the Continent, it seems to have been chiefly passed, as we have already described, amongst books and gardens, not altogether neglecting the cultivation of intelligent society; though evidences occasionally escape her pen of things more in union with what was alleged of her by her enemies. At the same time it is impossible to attach any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to the malicious exaggerations of Horace Walpole, or to regard with any other feeling than disgust his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> of Lady Mary in her old age, painted with all the evil gusto and the coarse plastering of an angry procures. On the death of Mr Wortley, which took place in 1761, she yielded to the solicitations of her daughter, and, after an absence of twenty-two years, returned to England, where she arrived in the October of the same year. But her <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> had suffered much from a cancer she had long concealed, and the fatigues she had undergone in her journey to England tended to exasperate its symptoms; the malady increased rapidly, and, before ten months had elapsed, she expired, on the 21st of August 1762, in the seventy-third year of her age. Notwithstanding this cruel distemper, she bore her sufferings with a spirit the reverse of complaining, and preserved to the last her vivacity of temper and character. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu was unquestionably the most remarkable woman of her time; the presiding female wit in the days of Pope, the benefactress of her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> by the introduction of inoculation, and the keen satirist of the fashionable circles. Her poems are indeed little else than wit in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHYME">rhyme</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> vers de société; but her prose is truly admirable; better than accurate, to which it has seldom much claim, it is idiomatical, off-hand conversation, without effort and without ineligance, fresh, racy, and piquant, sparkling with wit, and often equally remarkable for strong sense and sarcastic bitterness. The conventional shows of things could not deceive her; she <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> beneath the painted <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASKS">masks</a> which are worn in society, detected much that men and women try to conceal, and fearlessly published her detections. Pity that she did not see a little further into the sweets of things which are not conventional; that she had not more <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> in the heart, as well as in the blood and in good sense; more confidence in virtue, higher aspirations, and more ennobling objects of ambition, than those in pursuing which she wasted her fine powers, and embittered the greater part of her life. It is unnecessary to specify her ladyship's various productions in prose and verse, or even to refer to the col- Montagu, Edward Wortley, only son of the preceding Lady Mary, was born in October 1713, and, in the early part of his life, the object of his mother's most tender regard. In 1716, he accompanied his parents to Constantinople, and, on their return to England in 1718, was placed at Westminster School. Here he gave the first indication of his wayward disposition, by running away, and eluding all search, until about a year afterwards, when he was accidentally discovered at Blackwall, with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of fish on his head. In point of fact, he had bound himself, by regular indenture, to a poor fisherman, whom he had served faithfully, making shrewd bargains, and honestly accounting to the fisherman for his gains. Emancipated from this degrading condition, he was again placed at Westminster School; but ere long he absconded a second time, and bound himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a vessel engaged in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OPORTO">Oporto</a> trade, who, supposing him a friendless boy, treated him with great kindness and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. This generous conduct, however, awakened no corresponding feelings of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> upon his part; for he had scarcely landed at Oporto when he ran away up the country, and contrived to get employment for two or three years in tending the vines. Here he was at length discovered, brought home, and, on <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of amendment, pardoned; but unhappily with no better effect than before. He ran away a third time, after which his father procured him a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>, who so far reclaimed him to habits of regularity, that he obtained an appointment in one of the public offices. In 1747, he was elected one of the knights of the shire for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Huntingdon; but he does not appear to have in any way distinguished himself as a member of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, nor did he long retain his seat, his expenses having so far exceeded his income, that, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the year 1751, he found it prudent once more to leave England. He proceeded to Paris, where, in a short time, he was imprisoned in the Château for some fraudulent gambling transaction in which he had been concerned; but he soon escaped, or effected his liberation, though by what means is unknown. He published a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of his conduct, written by himself, in French, against one <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> Payba, a Jew by birth, who assumed the fictitious name of Roberts; and had it translated into English from an authentic copy, which he transmitted to this country for the purpose. In the parliament which assembled in 1754, he was returned for Bossiney; and, besides some dull communications to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Society, he published a book on the Rise and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FALL">Fall</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Republics, the merit of which was afterwards claimed by his tutor, Mr Foster. In a word, he seems to have been the offspring of the perplexity of his father's and mother's first position, the victim of their mistake, and privileged to obtain what excuses and comforts he could get from them; which, to do them justice, they generally afforded, though not always in the best manner, or with the right distribution of blame, and the proper allowance on all sides. His father died in the year 1761, at an advanced age, and, by his will, bequeathed to his son a considerable annuity, at the same time empowering him to make a settlement of £800 a year upon any woman he might marry, and devising to any son of such marriage Montagu an estate in the west riding of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. It was this clause which gave rise to a story that he had advertised for a wife, promising to marry any widow or single lady, of genteel birth and polished manners, who happened to be five, six, or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months advanced in pregnancy. That such an advertisement appeared is certain; but then its publication took place in 1776, within a few months of his death, and at a time when he was abroad, circumstances which render the story somewhat improbable. His mother died in the year 1762, and left him only one <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a>. He had offended her irreconcilably. But as his father's bequest had rendered him independent, he took a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> leave of his native country, passed the remainder of his life in foreign parts, and died at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> in 1776. Before his death he realized a remarkable prediction of his mother, by becoming first a Catholic and then a Mahommedan, in which latter character he ended his days, with a turban on his head, a long <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, and, it is alleged, a harem into the bargain. He travelled into the East, and wrote some observations on Pompey's Pillar, as it is called, as well as an account of a journey from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a> to the Gebel Mokattam, or Written <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a>. He is also said to have published an Explication of the Causes of Earthquakes, though it has not been mentioned at what time, or in what place. His travels in the East occupied several years, during which he underwent his different <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> transformations, and ultimately settled <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MAHOMMEDANISM">Mahommedanism</a>, the ceremonies of which he performed with a punctuality savouring of that peculiar derangement which he more or less exemplified in almost every <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of his life. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MONTAGUE_ISLAND">Montague <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, one of the New <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>, in the South <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, near Sandwich Island. Long. 168.37. E. Lat. 17.26. S. Montaigne, Michel de, a philosophe-moraliste, famous for his book of essays, was born at the castle of Montaigne, in Périgord, on the 28th of February 1533, being descended of an ancient family named Eyghem, originally from England. His father, a brave and loyal squire, who had served in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and Italy, where he had cultivated his mind and improved his <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, bestowed much <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> on his education, and, in particular, initiated him in the knowledge of languages by a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> much less tardy and laborious than that pursued in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>.
