The expedient he adopted was to provide his son with a German master, who, being entirely ignorant of French, but well versed in Latin, spoke to him only in the latter tongue, which he consequently acquired as a vernacular language, and, at the age of six, was able to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> in it with tolerable freedom and fluency. Greek was also taught him as a sort of diversion. "Nous pelotonons nos déclinaisons," says he, "à la manière de ceux qui, par certains jeux de tablier (échiquier), apprennent l'arithmétique et la géométrie." By means equally gentle and attractive, he was insensibly led to acquire some knowledge of science; and, without forcing his inclination, or imposing the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of application, his habits were formed, and his powers agreeably exercised. All this care and attention he repaid by the most tender affection for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of his father; indeed <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> piety is said to have formed a conspicuous trait in his character, though it must be confessed that he sometimes displayed it in a manner sufficiently singular. At an early age he was sent to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Guéenne, at Bordeaux, then the most flourishing in France, and there he had as masters Nicolas Grouchy, William Guérente, George Buchanan, and Muretus, under whom he appears to have made considerable proficiency. Having completed his studies at the age of thirteen, Montaigne resolved to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; and although his mind, naturally averse to all constraint, must have been repulsed by the conflicting and complicated <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of consuetudinary ju- risprudence with which the tribunals were then surcharged, yet, in 1554, he became a counsellor or advocate at Bordeaux, and continued to practise as such until the death of his elder brother, when he abandoned a profession to which he never had any real liking, and which he appeared afterwards to consider as derogatory. On quitting the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, for the business of which he had evidently no aptitude, he applied himself to the study of men and manners, and in prosecution of this object travelled through various parts of France, Germany, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, and Italy, making his observations on every thing curious or interesting in society, and receiving several marks of distinction in the course of his peregrinations. In 1581 he was admitted a citizen of Rome, in which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> he then sojourned; and the same year he was elected mayor of Bordeaux, an office in which he seems to have given much satisfaction to his fellow-citizens. In 1582 he was sent on a special mission to court about some affairs of importance, and on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of his mayoralty he was again elected to the same office. In 1588 he appeared to some advantage at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the states at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLOIS">Blois</a>, and, though not a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, took a share in the proceedings, but on what pretence or in what capacity does not clearly appear. During one of his visits to court he received the cordon of the order of Saint Michel, a distinction which he appears to have greatly coveted, though we afterwards find him complaining of the discredit into which it had fallen. Having retired to his family residence, he devoted himself to study; but his tranquillity was disturbed by the civil wars which desolated Guienne; and being driven from his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, he wandered about during six months seeking for his family, and often with difficulty obtaining an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> amongst those who had shared his hospitality. It appears, from a statement of De Thou, that Montaigne had sought to bring about a reconciliation between the Duke of Guise and the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">King</a> of Navarre, afterwards Henry IV.; and on his return from Paris, where he had completed the impression of his Essays, in 1588, he was with the historian at Blois when the Duke of Guise was there assassinated. In his old age he was very much afflicted with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and nephritic colic, which led him to observe that "la mort le pinçait continuellement à la gorge ou aux reins;" but he never could be prevailed on to take physic, in which he had no faith whatever. He died on the 13th of September 1598, and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the Feuillants at Bordeaux, where a monument was erected to his memory. Notwithstanding his constitutional tendency to scepticism, and certain unguarded expressions which seem to intimate an entire extinction of the sentiment of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, he is said to have died a Christian, probably because he had mass celebrated in his chamber in his last moments, and expired during the elevation of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOST">host</a>. His reputation as a writer is founded solely on his Essays, which were at one time extremely popular, and which are still read with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> by a numerous class of persons, who, pardoning the delusions of self-love and self-deceit, are charmed by the acuteness and originality mingled with good nature and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol17.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> which he displays, and captivated by the inviting frankness and vivacity with which he unbosoms himself about all his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> habits and concerns. As a writer, he imparted to the French language an energy which it did not possess before, and which has not become antiquated, because it resides in the thoughts and sentiments rather than in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>. As a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, his object was to describe man as he is, without reserve and without exaggeration; he studied himself more than any other subject, and recorded his observations with an acuteness and fidelity which have rendered his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> an authentic record of many interesting facts relative to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> nature. He united in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> the powers of observation and reflection, without which the study of man can never be successfully prosecuted; and although there is no doubt much truth in the acute but severe strictures on his character contained in a masterly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a> of the Port-royal Logic, where his vanity, his self-love, and the indulgent manner in which he speaks of his vices, to say nothing of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of language indicating a total absence of religious principle and sentiment, are very freely exposed, yet, as Mr Stewart observes, "this consideration, so far from diminishing the value of his Essays, is one of the most instructive <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> they afford to those who, after the example of the author, may undertake the salutary but humiliating task of self-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>." In the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRELIMINARY">Preliminary</a> Dissertation (part i. section ii.), to which the reader is referred, will be found an exposition of the philosophical merits and defects of Montaigne, not less remarkable for ability and discrimination, than for the fair and equable spirit in which both are distinguished and appreciated. Montaigne's life was first written by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">President</a> Bouchier, and prefixed to a supplementary volume of his works in 1740.

MONTANISTS

Pages 436-436

certain Christian heretics, who sprang up about the year 171, in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Marcus Aurelius. They were so called from their leader, the heresiarch Montanus, a Phrygian by birth; and hence they are sometimes styled Phrygians and Cataphyrgians. Montanus, it is said, embraced Christianity in hopes of rising to the dignities of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. He pretended to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, and gave out that the Holy Ghost had instructed him in several <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, which had not been revealed to the apostles. Priscilla and Maximilla, two enthusiastic women of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, presently became his disciples; and in a short <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of followers. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> being assembled together, condemned his prophecies, and excommunicated all those who dispersed them. The Montanists, finding themselves exposed to the censure of the whole church, formed a schism, and set up a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of those who called themselves prophets. Montanus, in conjunction with Priscilla and Maximilla, was at the head of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. These sectaries made no <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the creed. They only held that the Holy Spirit appointed Montanus his organ for delivering a more perfect form of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> than that which had been delivered by the apostles. They refused <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> for ever to those who were guilty of notorious crimes, and believed that the bishops had no authority to reconcile them. They held it unlawful to fly in time of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>. They condemned <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> marriages, allowed the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, and observed three tests. The Montanists afterwards became separated into two branches; one of which consisted of the disciples of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROCLUS">Proclus</a> and the other of those of Æschines. The latter are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with following the heterodoxy of Praxes and Sabellius concerning the Trinity.

MONTARGIS

Pages 436-436

an arrondissement of the department of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LOIRET">Loiret</a>, in France. It is 671 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, is divided into <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> cantons and ninety-five communes, and contains 62,500 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name. It stands on a hill at whose feet is the river Loing and the canal of Briare; adjoining is the forest of Montargis. It contains 1240 houses, and 6500 inhabitants, who are employed in making cloth, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTLERY">cutlery</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 38. 33. E. Lat. 47. 39. 58. N.

MONTAUBAN

Pages 436-441

an arrondissement of the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TARN">Tarn</a> and the Garonne, in France, 632 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. It comprehends eleven cantons, which are divided into eighty-three communes, and contain 105,600 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, of the same name, and the seat of a bishop, stands on both sides of the river Tarn, which is navigable, and receives the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> of another river near it. It is a well-built city, surrounded with walls and ditches, and is the seat of a Protestant university, which Montebellaria, an arrondissement of the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOUBS">Doubs</a>, in France. It extends over 490 square miles, is divided into <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> cantons, and subdivided into 148 communes, containing 48,500 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is a city of the same name, situated on the river Leine. It contains 700 houses, with 3750 inhabitants, who are employed, some in making hosiery, and some as watchmakers. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 55'. E. Lat. 47° 58'. N. Montbrison, an arrondissement of the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, in France, extending over 815 square miles. It comprehends <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> cantons, which are divided into 139 communes, and contain 105,500 inhabitants. The capital of the arrondissement, as well as of the department, is a city of the same name, situated on the river Bizey, a small stream which joins the Loire. It is an ill-built town, with narrow and crooked streets, and contains four churches, 880 houses, and 4800 inhabitants. The chief occupation is making cotton goods and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> hangings. Long. 3° 57'. E. Lat. 45° 32'. N. Montcontour, a town of the arrondissement of Loudon and department of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a>, in France, on the river Dive, containing 150 houses, and 1100 inhabitants. It is remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought at it in 1569, when Henry III. defeated the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a>. Long. 0° 10'. W. Lat. 46° 50'. N. Mont de Marsan, an arrondissement of the department of Les Landes, in France, 2180 square miles in extent. It contains twelve cantons, which are divided into 136 communes, and a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of about 83,000 persons. The capital is a city of the same name, situated at the junction of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Midon and Douze, which, united, run to the Adour. It contains 4200 inhabitants, who subsist by trading in the few productions of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. Long. 0° 49'. W. Lat. 44° 0'. N. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MONTDIDIER">Montdidier</a>, an arrondissement of the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOMME">Somme</a>, in France. It is 386 square miles in extent, and divided into five cantons, which are subdivided into 165 communes, containing 64,500 inhabitants. The capital is a city of the same name, situated on a hill, at the foot of which flows the river Dom. It contains 850 houses, and 4300 inhabitants, many of whom are employed in making <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, caps, and hosiery goods. Long. 2° 28'. 46'. E. Lat. 49° 38'. 57'. N. Montechiaro, a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the Austrian delegation of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>. It is situated on the river Mella, in a fertile district, and contains three churches, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and 5978 inhabitants, who are employed, some in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, and others in manufacturing woollen goods. Montego <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>. See Jamaica. Monteguliano, a parliamentary city of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Mazara. It was the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ERYX">Eryx</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, where formerly stood the temple dedicated to Venus, the most sensual of all the heathen establishments, of which no trace now remains. The city contains 8172 inhabitants, who produce some excellent wine. Monteleone, a city of the province of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> Ulteriore, in the kingdom of Naples, the capital of a district <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a dukedom. It was destroyed by the earthquake of 1783, but has been since re-established, and now contains 6650 inhabitants, who furnish <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and of silk, and weave silk goods. Montelimart, an arrondissement of the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOME">Dome</a>, in France, 510 square miles in extent. Montella It comprehends five cantons, divided into sixty-eight communes, and contains 51,300 inhabitants. The capital is the city of the same name, situated at the junction of the river Abron with the Roubion. It is regularly built, with wide streets, and contains an old castle, about 1000 houses, and 5900 inhabitants, the greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of whom are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, and have been so for a long <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, as in this district the doctrine of John Calvin was first introduced, and thence rapidly spread in France. There are some extensive tanneries, and also several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> for spinning both silk and cotton; and the trade in wine, olives, oil, and raw silk, is extensive. Long. 4° 40'. E. Lat. 44° 33'. 38'. N. Montella, a city of the kingdom of Naples, in the province Principato Ulteriore. It contains eight churches and a large Franciscan convent, and has 5750 inhabitants. Monte Maggiore, a town of the kingdom of Naples, in the island of Sicily, and province of Mazara, thirty-six miles from Palermo. It is situated on the river Torto, on the declivity of a fine mountain, and is moderately healthy. It contains 6100 inhabitants. Monte Peleoso, a city, the seat of a bishop, in the province of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BASILICATA">Basilicata</a>, of the kingdom of Naples, with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, four churches, four monasteries, and 5834 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MONTEPULCIANO">Montepulciano</a>, a city of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, in Italy, the capital of a district of the same name. It contains a cathedral, a Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> seminary, and about 2100 inhabitants, who grow some of the best wine of the duchy. Montesarchio, a city of the kingdom of Naples, in the province of Principato Ulteriore, on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from Puglia. It contains seven churches, and 5573 inhabitants, whose chief trade is in corn. Montesquieu, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> de Secondat, Baron de, the celebrated author of the Esprit des Lois, was descended of an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family of Guienne, and born on the 18th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1689, at the castle of La Brède, near Bordeaux, where he passed his early days, and composed those works which have acquired for their author an imperishable reputation. His father having early discovered in him indications of genius, and a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of future eminence, bestowed the utmost pains on his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, which appears to have been conducted with equal judgment and success; and being destined for the magistracy, he employed the energies of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> mind in studying the immense collection of the different codes, and in endeavouring to detect the motives and unravel the complicated relations of the obscure <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> contradictory laws contained in them. His <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> was insatiable; and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it proved the source of his future <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, it was also that of his greatest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. He has himself stated, that he never had to reproach himself with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-READING">reading</a> wasted or mis-spent. He recruited his mind with books of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and travels when exhausted with his arid labours upon <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a>, and had a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> relish for the productions of the classical ages of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and Rome. Enchanted, as he says, with antiquity, he, at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of twenty, composed a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, in the form of letters, wherein he sought to prove that the idolatry of the pagans did not appear to deserve eternal damnation; but this first production of his genius he wisely abstained from giving to the world. On the 24th of February 1714 he was received as counsellor to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Bordeaux, and, on the 13th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1716, he was, through the influence of his paternal uncle, named <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> a mortier. The same year he was admitted into the academy of Bordeaux, which had been recently founded by a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons possessing a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> taste for music and works of entertainment. Conceiving, however, that its object was too limited, and desirous to extend the sphere of its utility, he undertook to convert this coterie of wits into a learned Montesquieu; and his views in this respect were warmly seconded by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of La Force, who founded a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>, and held out several other inducements to the cultivation of science. Montesquieu thought with D'Alembert, that an experiment well performed was preferable to a feeble discourse or a bad poem; and having succeeded in impressing others with the same conviction, he thus became instrumental in establishing at Bordeaux an academy of sciences. As a member of this learned <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>, he contributed his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINGENT">contingent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> or communications, chiefly on subjects connected with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> history, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of study for which he had a particular taste. But his physical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> disqualified him for that minute observation which is essential to the successful prosecution of this particular science. He was not only short-sighted, but his vision was weak; and this infirmity increased so much with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, that, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he became almost <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol2.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>. It may also be observed, that, at the period when Montesquieu applied himself to natural history, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> principles of that science had not yet been established. In 1719, he circulated, by means of the journals, an Histoire Physique de la Terre ancienne et moderne; and he read successively to the academy of Bordeaux a dissertation Sur la Politique des Romains dans la <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>, an Eloge du Due de La Force, and a Vie du Marechal de Berwick, a production which in several <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> recalls the manner of Tacitus. Montesquieu, however, was by no means in haste to appear before the public in the character of author. He preferred waiting until his faculties were ripened by time and matured by reflection; nor was it until the year 1721 that he entered upon his literary <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a>, by the publication of the Lettres Persanes, the first idea of which seems to have been borrowed from the Siamois of the Amusements Sérieux et Comiques of Dufresny, though, in works of genius, the primary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> is of little moment compared with the execution. The success of the Lettres Persanes, and the influence which they exercised, were unparalleled. This is to be ascribed to two causes; the circumstances of the period at which the book appeared, and the form, adapted to every class of readers, into which it was <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. Disastrous wars, cruel persecutions, and rigorous seasons, followed by famine and misery, the natural attendants of these scourges, had darkened the close of a reign, during the brilliant days of which the French people, intoxicated with the glory and success of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a>, had contemplated their own <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> as reflected in his greatness and splendour; and even when great public misfortunes had produced general discontent, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of obedience and the fear inspired by a monarch whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> neither age nor reverses could <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BEND">bend</a>, preserved a respectful silence around. But no sooner had <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. descended to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> than the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a> appeared to indemnify itself for the constraint which he had so long exercised over it; and in this it was powerfully seconded by the regent, who had assumed the reins of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. Then libertinism succeeded to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, effrontery to hypocrisy, familiarity to respect, audacity to submission. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of saying or <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> anything with impunity led men to examine and to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> all that had been agreed to without opposition, or even assented to with enthusiasm. In the midst of the general effervescence thus produced appeared the book of the Lettres Persanes. From the shape into which it was cast, it had all the attractions of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>; it abounded in voluptuous details, which flattered the taste of the age for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and in irreligious sarcasms, which gratified its tendency to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INFIDELITY">infidelity</a>; and it treated with contempt Louis XIV. and his reign, which people now sought to depreciate. But it must nevertheless be admitted, that, with all these faults, the book displays an ardent <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> for the welfare of mankind; a courageous zeal for the triumph of reason and virtue; <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> views upon <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, public <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, criminal jurisprudence, and the dearest interests of nations; a penetrating insight into the vices of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, as well as those of governments; and, generally, strong <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of profound reflection, which takes the reader more by surprise that it seems to be the constant object of the author to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> it under the mask of frivolity. Its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a>, however, and that which won the suffrages of all, consisted in the keen, animated, sprightly satire of French manners and caprices, and in a style always lively, sparkling, full of happy innuendoes and unexpected contrasts, the pointed <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRONY">irony</a> of which sometimes rose to the most energetic eloquence. Four years after the publication of the Lettres Persanes, Montesquieu caused to be printed separately, in 1725, the Temple de Guide, an ingenious trifle, though <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and without <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, being equally devoid of easy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> or natural <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>, and which Madame du Deffant happily called the Apocalypse of Gallantry. It appears, by a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> written long after the publication of the Temple de Guide, that the author declined to acknowledge this slight production, which he had composed for the amusement of some friends, in whose society he was accustomed to mingle at the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of a lady of his acquaintance. The same year, at the opening of the parliament of Bordeaux, he delivered a discourse on the duties of magistrates, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a>, attorneys, and all those connected with the administration of law; which, though but little noticed, is written in a flowing style and full of unction, different from the ordinary manner of Montesquieu, and in that vein of eloquence which addresses itself more to the sentiments than to the reason of men. In 1728, he sold his office and withdrew from the magistracy, the duties of which he had so well described. The desire to regain his freedom, and apply himself entirely to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and letters, was no doubt one of his motives; but the principal cause of this determination seems to have been a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of inadequacy to fill the situation in which he was placed. That continual presence of mind, that prompt and ready judgment, that attentive <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a> which traces throughout all its details the subterfuges of private interest, and that facility of elocution which displays <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> the instant they are discerned, rendering them at once triumphant; in these qualities, so indispensable in a judge, Montesquieu was, by his own account, entirely deficient. He informs us, indeed, that his whole merit as president consisted in rectitude of purpose, and understanding sufficiently the questions themselves; but that he had never been able to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> the forms of procedure, although he had applied himself to the subject. Being now at liberty to devote himself exclusively to philosophy and letters, he presented himself as a candidate for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the French Academy, vacant by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of M. de Sacy; but <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Fleury wrote to the academy that the king had declared he would not give his approbation to the author of a work containing impious sarcasms against religion. Montesquieu, however, though at once amazed and offended by the refusal of the king and his minister, contrived, by a little <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, to propitiate the cardinal; he asserted his claim with firmness and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, yet disavowed those letters of the book which formed a legitimate ground of objection against him. The king was appeased by the intervention of the minister, and, on the 24th of January 1728, he was received into the academy, on which occasion he delivered an inaugural discourse, which is printed amongst his works. Montesquieu having accomplished this object, resolved to travel, and, in the course of his peregrinations, visited almost all the countries of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He proceeded first to <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, where he often <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Eugene; he then passed into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, whence he journeyed to Italy, and at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> became acquainted with John Law of Lauriston, who, from the height of grandeur, wealth, and celebrity, had fallen into obscurity, neglect, and poverty, and also with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> de Bonneval, who had as yet only gone through part of the cycle of his romantic adventures. From Venice he proceeded to Rome, where he became acquainted with Cardinal Corsini, afterwards Clement XIII., and with Cardinal Polignac, author of the *Anti-Lucrèce*. He next visited <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, but having met with a cold reception there, he soothed his ill humour by writing some satirical stanzas, which, however, he did not think fit to print. From Italy he passed into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, and traversing the different countries watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, stopped some time in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, where he met <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Chesterfield, with whom he had become acquainted at Venice. He then visited England, where he resided about two years, was admitted a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Society, and treated with marked distinction by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Caroline. On his return to his own <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he retired to his castle at La Brède, where he resumed his favourite pursuits. He had either before or during his travels caused to be printed in Holland a little work entitled *Réflexions sur la Monarchie universelle*, which is now but little known, and extremely rare, though it is referred to by the author himself in a passage of the *Esprit des Lois*. The object of this piece was to prove that, in the actual state of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> nations of Europe, it is impossible even for the ablest and most ambitious of sovereigns to establish an universal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>. After two years spent in his retreat at La Brède, Montesquieu published, in 1734, his *Considérations sur les Causes de la Grandeur et de la Décadence des Romains*; a work which, if not the most remarkable, is perhaps the most finished of all his productions, and in which he had to enter into competition with several eminent men, both amongst the ancients and the moderns, particularly Polybius, Machiavelli, Saint-Evremond, and Bossuet. But Polybius, though a learned geographer, a skilful <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>, an adroit negociator, and a profound thinker, was a prolix historian and an indifferent writer. Machiavelli had selected certain facts of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman history</a>, rather as examples than as the principal subject of his reflections on politics. Saint-Evremond, full of ingenious views, but deficient in general information, and not very intimately acquainted with facts, has left his judgments imperfect and his analyses incomplete. Bossuet, having to consider the history of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> merely as a portion of that of the world, has contented himself with an outline embracing only the principal points. Montesquieu is the first writer who has grappled with this great subject in all its details, and who compared all the facts with laborious sagacity. He has overlooked none which can afford <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> for reflection, or warrant any inference of importance, and yet he has managed to compress the whole into a volume of moderate thickness. The *<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIALOGUE">Dialogue</a> de Sylla et d'Euricrate*, which is subjoined to this work, and may be considered as forming part of it, is one of those productions in which Montesquieu has displayed the greatest eloquence; and with this may be classed another piece not less remarkable, namely, *Lysimaque*, in which he has delineated, in a manner altogether sublime, that system of stoicism which raised <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> above the ordinary weaknesses of his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and enabled him to brave with joy, and even with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, the cruelties of tyrants and the iniquities of fortune. The Considerations on the Grandeur and Decline of the Romans make us acquainted with the history of a single people; but Montesquieu had long been engaged in studying that of all other nations, in discovering the causes of those revolutions which had successively changed the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the world, and in investigating those laws and customs which had contributed to their prosperity or decline. The success of the treatise on the Roman people, which in some sort formed only a detached portion of the vast <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> he had conceived, served to increase his ardour in the execution of so great an undertaking, to the completion of which fourteen more years of incessant labour were devoted. Sometimes he thought that he advanced rapidly, and would speedily accomplish his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; at other times he appeared to recede, and to become perplexed by the immensity and complication of the subject. At length, after twenty years of unremitting application, he had the satisfaction to put the last <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to a production upon which he had expended so much anxious labour and meditation, and which he entitled *L'Esprit des Lois*. But before sending this work to the press, he judged it prudent to consult one of his intimate friends, whose talents and knowledge he respected; and with this view he sent his manuscript to Helvetius. The latter, however, was so little satisfied with the production after perusal, and so much alarmed for the danger to which the reputation of Montesquieu would be exposed by the publication of a work which he considered as so defective, that at first he did not venture to express what he thought of it, and solicited the author's permission to communicate the manuscript to a common friend, Saurin, the author of *Spartacus*. The latter coincided in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> with Helvetius, and both agreed that, by the publication of this book, the celebrated author of the *Lettres Persanes* would injure his reputation, and lower himself in the estimation of the world. After some hesitation, this extraordinary judgment was communicated to Montesquieu, accompanied with an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> entreaty on the part of both that he would subject the whole to careful revision, and upon no account publish the work in the crude and imperfect state in which it then appeared. The strange counsels of these friends, however, had so little influence on Montesquieu, that he sent the manuscript to the press without altering a word, prefixing this epigraph, *Prolem sine matre creatam*, to indicate that his work had no <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODEL">model</a>; and, as if to mark still more strongly how little he was moved by their unfavourable judgment, he congratulated himself, in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, on having produced a work which was not altogether destitute of genius. Nor did the result disappoint the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> expectations he had formed. Its success was in fact so great, that in little more than a year and a half after its publication, it had gone through twenty-two editions, and been translated into almost every <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of Europe. The *Esprit des Lois* appeared about the middle of the year 1748, and before the end of the year 1750 its reputation was universal. If the Spirit of Laws, however, was much read, much admired, and much praised, the work, like all those which have produced a great <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, was also much criticised. Madame du Deffant said of it, that it was not *l'esprit des loix*, but *de l'esprit sur les loix*, a saying which had just that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of truth which gives currency to an epigram. Those who penetrated to a greater depth, and understood the difficult questions he had treated, perceived that, although the author had refuted some paradoxes of the Abbé Dubois, he had himself fallen into grave errors; that not having sufficiently examined the foundations of the feudal system, he had conceived too favourable an opinion of that form of government; that in order to establish certain principles, he --- 1 This reference is contained in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOTE">note</a> to book xxi, chap. 22, tom. ii, p. 274, of the edition of Lequien, and is in these terms: "Ceci a paru, il y a plus de vingt ans, dans un petit ouvrage manuscrit de l'auteur, qui a été presque fondé dans celui-ci." The *Esprit des Lois* appeared in 1748; and if the words "il y a plus de vingt ans" be exact, this little work must have been written about the year 1727, or perhaps a little earlier. Montesquieu drew his examples from suspected travellers or discredited authors; that from particular instances he too frequently deduced general conclusions; that a certain degree of neologism and obscurity appeared in his definitions, and an uncommon <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the ordinary words of language in the enunciation of the fundamental principles of his <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>. He was also censured for having attributed to the influence of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> and to physical causes effects which are due solely to moral causes; for having frittered <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> some subjects into small chapters which have often insignificant or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> titles; for having brought together others which have little or no connection with those which precede and follow them; and for being often so deficient in method and arrangement, that his work, as a whole, is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, although many of the parts are exceedingly fine, and that it appears to be in some sort an admirable collection of fragments, made for the purpose of being afterwards arranged and moulded into a regular and systematic form. Lastly, he has been <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with some confusion of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, certain forced turns of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, and a style sometimes strained, and frequently laboured. But although these criticisms appear to be well founded, the reputation of Montesquieu was greatly enhanced by the publication of the Spirit of Laws; and it may be said with truth, that this work alone would have been sufficient to insure him lasting renown, and to constitute a noble monument of his genius, sagacity, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>. For some observations equally liberal, profound, and discriminating, on the work in question, the reader is referred to the first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRELIMINARY">Preliminary</a> Dissertation (part i. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. iii. p. 94, et seq.). Montesquieu had resolved not to reply to any of the criticisms which might be made on the Esprit des Lois; but the attacks of an anonymous author, who, in a journal called Nouvelles Ecclésiastiques, had, amongst other things, represented him as an atheist, induced him to deviate from this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. In the Lettres Persanes he had treated the Christian religion with too much levity; but afterwards, when his mind was fully matured by age, study, and reflection, he had seen cause to alter his views; and hence, in the Esprit des Lois, he recommends Christianity in expressive terms, not only as the most perfect of all <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> systems, but also as the most powerful support of the whole social system. He therefore deemed it of importance to repel the calumnious insinuations of the ecclesiastical journalist; and at the same time he wished to refute by anticipation the theologians of the Sorbonne, who, being dissatisfied with some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the Esprit des Lois, were proceeding to condemn the work. It was with this <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> purpose that he wrote his Defense, which may be considered as a model of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> discussion, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> pleasantry, and contemptuous moderation. "What pleases me in my Defense," said he, "is not seeing the venerable theologians grumbled; it is seeing them laid gently upon their backs." But he took no notice whatever of a crowd of brochures, filled with absurd criticisms or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> abuse, which appeared against the Spirit of Laws. The public, said he, avenge me on the one by their contempt, and on the other by their indignation. The appearance of a book like the Spirit of Laws naturally formed an epoch in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> and literary history; but its effect was different in different countries, being greatest in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, where it obtained a reputation, which has since <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to increase, and least in France, where its influence was and still is but small. This may be accounted for partly from the different circumstances in which these countries were respectively placed, and partly also from the fact that, whilst Montesquieu pointed out the hazards to which the British constitution was exposed from the incessant conflicts of a tyrannical oligarchy and a turbulent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMOCRACY">democracy</a>, he had confined his researches to the dark ages of the French monarchy, in regard to which his efforts were doubtful, and his conclusions disputed. But if his work did not prove as useful to his country as he had hoped, the reputation which he acquired in his lifetime far exceeded that which men of letters can ordinarily aspire to obtain. He was considered throughout all Europe as the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> of nations, and the founder of the philosophy of jurisprudence and politics. But, far from being dazzled by this high reputation, he continued to live like a sage, and to enjoy the society of his friends, dividing his time between his castle of La Brède and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, that is, between study and the world. In the country, he occupied himself with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GARDENING">gardening</a> and agricultural improvements, and, though jealous of his seignorial <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, was much beloved by the peasantry, whose comfort and happiness it was his object to promote. In the capital he was always a welcome guest, although simple and somewhat negligent in his dress, as well as in his conversation. He was always disposed to render justice to talents, and to relieve merit in distress. One <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> he received from Henry Sully, an English <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, who had greatly contributed to improve horology in France, the following letter: "I am tempted to hang myself, but I believe nevertheless that I should not do so if I had an hundred crowns." To this Montesquieu immediately replied: "I send you an hundred crowns, my dear Sully; do not hang yourself, and come to see me." Although in some of his opinions Montesquieu inclined to the sect of the philosophers, like Buffon, and Duclos, and many others, yet he kept aloof from the men, because he loved neither the proselytism of impiety, nor the excesses of the spirit of cabal. Nor was this the only cause of his estrangement from Voltaire. Being in a great <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> insensible to the charms of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, he thought the reputation of that celebrated man usurped, and did not hesitate to express his opinion to that effect; whilst Voltaire, on the other hand, was by no means sparing in malignant reflections and bitter criticisms. In fact, they mutually accused each other of having too much wit, and frequently abusing it in their writings. But Voltaire had an exquisite sense of literary merit, which triumphed over his strongest antipathies; and, under its benign influence, he did justice to the author of the Spirit of Laws, by observing, that when the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a> had lost their titles, Montesquieu found and restored them; a fine thought, notwithstanding the epigrammatic form in which it is expressed. But whatever might be his sentiments in regard to Voltaire and the other men of letters of his time, it was only in conversation, or in the intimacy of familiar intercourse, that he allowed the secret of his opinions to escape; he never wrote against any of his contemporaries, and conducted himself with a dignity and wisdom which were the effect of the moderation of his passions, as well as the result of reflection. At the solicitation of D'Alembert and the Chevalier de Jaucourt, Montesquieu, having completed the Esprit des Lois, consented to write for the Encyclopédie, and composed for that work the Essai sur le Goût, some inedited chapters of which were afterwards published in the Archives Littéraires (tom. ii. p. 301). It appears that soon after the publication of the Esprit des Lois, his physical strength diminished rapidly, and no longer corresponded to his ardour in literary pursuits. He had conceived the design, as he informs us in his journal, of giving greater <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> and depth to several parts of the Spirit of Laws; but he found that he had become incapable of carrying his intention into effect. "Mes lectures," says he, "m'ont affaibli les yeux; et il me semble que qu'il me reste encore de lumière, n'est que l'aurore du jour où ils se fermeront pour jamais." And in fact he died soon afterwards, on the 10th of February 1755, at the age of sixty-six, that is, only seven years after the publication of his great work. He was attacked at Paris with a violent inflammatory fever, which, in spite of every effort to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARREST">arrest</a> Montesquieu has said of Tacitus, that he abridged everything because he saw every thing. This fine eulogium has been applied to Montesquieu himself, and these great men have often been compared. But geniuses of this order have each a particular character of originality, which invalidates such comparisons, and falsifies all the similitudes that are sought to be established between them. Were it necessary to determine the precise degrees of pre-eminence which distinguish Tacitus and Montesquieu, it might be said that the French surpasses the Latin author in the variety and extent of his knowledge, in the grandeur of his conceptions, and in the abundance of his thoughts, but that he yields to the Roman in respect of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> and eloquence; that, in a word, he is greater as a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, but inferior as a writer. Tacitus invariably sustains the dignity of his expressions on a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the importance of his subject; he impairs not the gravity of his style by ingenious antithesis; and he is careful never to enervate his energetic phraseology, nor to enfeeble the vigour of his narrative, by the graces of wit or the artifices of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>. His penetration and sagacity, fortified by the study of severe models, no less than by his own natural character, saved him from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of such faults. But it is not so with Montesquieu, of whose manner as a writer, if we desired to convey an idea by referring to ancient examples, we should say that it consisted of several of the finest qualities of Tacitus, and many of the brilliant defects of Seneca.

MONTE VIDEO

Pages 441-445

CISPLATINO, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">OR</a> BANDA ORIENTAL, a tract of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, which for some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> was the subject of an obstinate <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> and the united provinces of La Plata. It has Brazil on the east and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east; on the west and north-west it is separated from Entre Rios and other provinces of La Plata, as also from Paraguay, by the river Uruguay; and on the south it is washed by the Atlantic and the Rio de la Plata. It is somewhat of a conical form, rounded at the bottom, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> to one side towards the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-APEX">apex</a>, which is situated in latitude 27° 30' south. At the broadest it extends over five degrees of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>; and Monte Video, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, which lies nearly in the centre of the base, is situated in latitude 34° 50' south, and longitude 56° 20' west. It received its name of Banda Oriental from its position with respect to the Uruguay; but this was changed to Monte Video when it was erected into an independent republic. This country, the first which salutes the eye of the European traveller on entering the Rio de la Plata, is equally distinguished for salubrity of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, fertility of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and geographical position. In these respects it is superior to any of the provinces of La Plata, or the republics of Buenos Ayres and Brazil. Fertility is indeed characteristic of the whole of these countries, but the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> is exceedingly flat and monotonous. The surface of Monte Video, on the contrary, is diversified by an endless variety of hills and valleys; and yet scarcely an unproductive spot is to be found. A Spanish traveller thus speaks of it: "The whole country abounds in excellent pastures, and not a single spot of ground is left waste. The pastures are of excellent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, and fertilized in an astonishing manner by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRRIGATION">irrigation</a> of many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, rivulets, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>. At each step the traveller finds himself agreeably surprised by meeting with streams of pure and salubrious <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which tend to enhance the charms of the surrounding scenery, consisting of a constant succession of hills, eminences, meadows, wilds, rugged defiles, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, with which all the territory abounds." The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> river is the Uruguay, which rises amongst the mountains of Brazil, and, after traversing the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Rio Grande, sweeps past the north-western and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the western limits of Monte Video. It is celebrated for its volume of water, but is only navigable for the space of sixty leagues, on account of a slight <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, which, however, might be easily avoided by a regular canal along one of its sides, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of little difficulty. The most considerable tributary of the Uruguay is the Negro, which is likewise the largest river in the province. It originates in a ridge of hills, which runs northward from Maldonado and Monte Video, and is navigable for some leagues above its junction with the principal stream. The scenery of the Rio Negro is celebrated for its beauty, its banks being delightfully fringed with various <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, particularly the sarsaparilla plant, which is reputed at certain seasons to impart medicinal properties to the water. A <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BEND">bend</a> of the river before its junction surrounds a fertile, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOZENGE">lozenge</a>-shaped piece of ground, so as nearly to isolate it. This is called Rincón de Gallinas, and it was found extremely useful during the war as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of refuge for the cattle, a dike having been run across the narrow isthmus. The Gualeguay is a river of nearly the same size as the Negro. The other streams of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOTE">note</a> are the Ybicuí, Cibollati, Yi, St Lucia, Gueguasay, Diaman, Arapéi, Guarey, Olimar, Pardo, Tacuarí, Yguarón, and Tacuarembo. The immense currents of these rivers are formed by a multitude of rivulets, many of them very considerable, which run in all directions, excepting an elevated ridge of land which crosses the whole country, and is called Cuchilla Grande. Almost all these rivers might be rendered navigable with little trouble throughout the greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their courses. Those that are easily navigated, besides the two already mentioned, are the Cebollati and St Lucia. For ten or fifteen leagues from the banks of all the principal rivers, the country has been occupied by grazing farms; but the centre and northward portion of the province is wild, and covered with wood; and northward, beyond latitude 30°, the trees acquire considerable magnitude, and are suitable for all purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and ship <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. These are floated down the Uruguay, and, when the river is full, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over the falls of Salto Grande and Salto Chico without difficulty. As the grazing business produces such immense profit to those who possess capitals laid out in estates, of which there are some of immense size, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> as a speculation has occupied but little <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. The soil, however, is capable of producing abundantly, and almost without labour, all kinds of grain, fruit, and vegetables. A traveller thus speaks of the climate and the productions of Monte Video: "The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, peaches, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, figs, oranges, apples, &c., are exceedingly fine. In this enchanting climate, with the exception of a few of the tropical fruits, all the fruits most esteemed <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> perfection in the open <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a>. In fact, I believe that the climate is surpassed by none in the world, not even by that of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> or the south of France. It experiences neither the sultry <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> nor the chilling blast of winter." The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Monte Video, the capital of the republic, is situated on the northern <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Rio de la Plata, near its mouth, 120 miles north-east from Buenos Ayres, in latitude 34° 50' south, and longitude 56° 20' west. It is built on a small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, which projects forwards, and constitutes the eastern boundary of the harbour. On the opposite isthmus a strong fort is erected, and the town is still further secured by a wall and ditch, and several <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> forts. On the opposite side of the harbour rises the hill of Monte Video, also surmounted by a fort, which, along with those already mentioned, commands the harbour. The town rises gradually from the harbour, and presents a handsome appearance as it is approached from the shore. Like Buenos Ayres and other places built by the Spaniards, Monte Video is disposed in regular squares all nearly of a uniform size. The streets are wide, well paved, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> each other at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>. There is a plaza about 150 yards <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> at the upper end of the town, the west side of which is occupied by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and handsome brick edifice, surmounted by a cupola, covered with glazed tiles; and on the east side is the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>. The houses are chiefly one story in height, and are built of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or brick, with flat roofs without <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHIMNEYS">chimneys</a>. The better sort of houses are generally built round a square <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, the sitting rooms being on the side next the street, the lodging rooms in the two wings, and the inferior apartments at the back. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">Provisions</a> here are cheap and in great abundance. Monte Video is a most excellent position for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. It is central for collecting and exporting the produce of the province, and for distributing the goods imported in return. It is also very superior to Buenos Ayres as an intermediate port for the transhipment of goods from the larger vessels which arrive from distant countries into smaller vessels fitted to navigate the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARANA">Parana</a> and Uruguay, because the channel of deep water runs along the north side of the Rio de la Plata. Indeed, from various circumstances, this port is the best on the Plata. The exports consist of tallow, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a> beef; and the imports are manufactured goods, coffee, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and the like. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> at this place is humid; storms are not unfrequent in summer; and in the winter months, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, and August, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a> is sometimes severe. The climate of the capital, therefore, is not equal to that of the interior parts of the country. Monte Video was built by a Spanish colony from Buenos Ayres, and for a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> formed an object of ambition to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. When the former shook off the Spanish yoke, the Brazilian court seized the opportunity of taking possession of it; but it was recovered, after a long siege, in 1814, and retaken by the Brazilians in 1821. By the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of 1828 it became the capital of the republic, which was called by the same name. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> cannot be estimated with any exactness; it may be from 15,000 to 20,000. The place next in importance to Monte Video is Maldonado, which is situated upon a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the same name, lying more immediately at the mouth of the river than the capital. By some writers it is considered as preferable to Monte Video for a place of anchorage and shelter. It stands on the brow of a hill, rising gently to the height of 250 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Immediately off the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, Lobos and Gorrete. Under cover of the latter, which stands in the mouth of the harbour, and is noticed for the growth of stick-liquorice, a small <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ships may ride in safety in all weathers. The principal buildings form a quadrangle, on the north side of which is a considerable inn, and on the south side a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; whilst the rest of the square is occupied by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> habitations. The houses in the streets issuing from the square, or running <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to its sides, are chiefly low, and constructed of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The whole number is about 250, and the inhabitants amount to about 1000. A place <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the same name is situated about <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles from this town towards the north-east, and is said to have been formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> place in the district. Northward of Maldonado the coast continues low to the Rio Grande, in lat. 32° 15', in which parallel the Brazilian territory commences. The soil is extremely rich, and, in a ridge of hills which runs northward from the neighbourhood of Maldonado, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver were formerly worked. Proceeding to the westward of Monte Video we meet with several bays and rivers well adapted for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, to which they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> no doubt be applied as the country advances in population. At Colonia, opposite to Buenos Ayres, there is a tolerably commodious --- 1 Brackenbridge's Voyage to South America. harbour for large ships, which is well fortified. At Las Vacas, a few leagues farther, at the mouth of the Uruguay, there are good anchorage and shelter for small vessels; and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Martin Garcia, which is near to it, is the rendezvous of ships of war. There are several other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages besides those mentioned, but none of sufficient moment to require particular notice. Monte Video, having been originally settled by a Spanish colony from Buenos Ayres, fell naturally under Spanish domination, but came at length to be a bone of contention between <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and Portugal. From its peculiar position it was a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> of no common value to either <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. To Spain it gave the control of both sides of the Rio de la Plata, whilst to the sister-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> it was necessary to the free and secure navigation of the vast interior expanse of Brazil. During the devastating wars between these two powers, relative to the various boundaries of their immense South American possessions, Monte Video, then the Banda Oriental, was overrun and wasted, sometimes by one party, sometimes by the other; and their respective pretensions were differently regulated by successive treaties. At the commencement of the revolution, the Orientalists, as the inhabitants of Monte Video were then called, naturally joined the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Buenos Ayres; but in what capacity, whether as a dependent or independent power, has not been made apparent. At all events, when the British were expelled from the Plata, hostilities commenced between the rival cities of Monte Video and Buenos Ayres, during the continuance of which the former suffered severely. For some time the party in the Spanish <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> maintained the ascendancy, notwithstanding an effort of the Creoles to follow the example of Buenos Ayres, in throwing off the Spanish yoke. In 1810 the government of Buenos Ayres laid siege to Monte Video, which was carried on at intervals, being alternately abandoned and resumed as they were successful or otherwise against the Spanish royalists in the upper provinces, till the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the year 1814, when the republicans succeeded in capturing the place. During this protracted struggle, all intercourse between the city and the interior was necessarily cut off; and the ruinous effects of this on trade may easily be conceived. But its calamities did not terminate here. Not many months after the establishment of a republican government in Monte Video (the first acts of which were to set up a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> press, and to open <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> and colleges), the troops of Buenos Ayres were called off to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> the enemy in the upper provinces; and the city soon afterwards fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Artigas, a notorious brigand, and his lawless banditti. Under the guidance of this individual, whose authority was <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and without the slightest control, the Orientalists gained a victory over the Buenos-Ayreans in 1815, at Gaubijou, and thus made themselves independent of that republic. But the Brazilians soon found a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> for occupying the country. Pretending an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> that Artigas would spread the revolutionary contagion over Brazil, they attacked him, scattered his forces, and compelled him to seek refuge in Paraguay. The Brazilians maintained possession of the Banda Oriental till 1822, when the republic, nominally at least, attached itself to Brazil under the name of the Cisplatine province. That same year Brazil separated itself from the mother country, to which for a time the Orientalists remained true; but on the submission of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> troops they called upon the Buenos-Ayreans for aid. This was granted, and ultimately the Banda Oriental was formally declared to be united to Buenos Ayres. But the standard of independence having been raised in 1826, war was declared towards the close of that year by Dom Pedro, who entered into an elaborate exposition of the alleged <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of Brazil. Both parties wasted Monte Video, which, whilst it was the cause of quarrel, became likewise the arena where either party attempted to decide it. But their resources were inadequate for enabling them to strike a decisive blow; and the solicitations of Great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, which, like other neutral nations, suffered by the war, at length procured a peace, which was signed at Rio in August 1828. By this pacification it was in substance provided that the Banda Oriental should become an independent state, under the mutual guarantee of the two contracting parties. Thus the war, after having drained the resources of both Brazil and Buenos Ayres, ended in a drawn <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> as to the subject of the contest. From time to time since that period, hostilities have broken out in the various provinces situated in this part of the South American continent; and it will require many years of tranquillity before the great resources of Monte Video are properly developed. According to the official returns of 1835, the number of British and foreign vessels employed in the import trade amounted in that year to 893; tonnage, 89,238; the value of their cargoes amounted to $3,095,398 dollars currency; whilst the exports, as far as the returns have been given, are of the value of $2,765,401 dollars.
