The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> misfortunes with which it has been overwhelmed have greatly retarded the increase of the population, which at present amounts to about 100,000 souls. Montezuma, or Moctezuma, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> when Cortes invaded that country in the year 1518. See Mexico. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONTFORT">Montfort</a>, an arrondissement of the department of Ille Vihaine, in France, extending over 390 square miles, and containing a population of 56,800 persons. It is divided into five cantons and forty-six communes. The capital, of the same name, stands on the river Meu, near its junction with the Chaillon. Its walls are dilapidated, and it contains only 1250 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONTGOMERY">Montgomery</a>, a borough and market-town, the capital of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of that name, in North <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, 169 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is situated on an elevation on the right bank of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>. In <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times it was fortified, and had a castle, the remains of which show it to have been an extensive pile of building, though but a small portion of it is now entire. It is an ancient corporation, and sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, in conjunction with five other towns, viz. Llanidloes, Welshpool, Machynlleth, Newtown, and Llanfyllin. There is a market on Tuesday, and six annual <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> are held. The population amounted in 1801 to 972, in 1811 to 932, in 1821 to 1062, and in 1831 to 1188. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERYSHIRE">Montgomeryshire</a>, an inland county of North Wales. It is bounded on the east by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, on the north by Denbighshire and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MERIONETHSHIRE">Merionethshire</a>, on the west by Cardiganshire and Merionethshire, and on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RADNORSHIRE">Radnorshire</a>. It is of an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> form, its greatest length from north to south being thirty-six miles, and its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> breadth from east to west about thirty-two miles. Its area is estimated at 982 square miles, or 620,720 statute acres; but it is probably overrated. It is a county of very irregular surface, composed in the centre of a ridge of lofty mountains, which nearly divide it, and whence various branches project, which, though not equal in height to the main ridge, attain a considerable elevation. The loftiest of the mountains, Plinlimmon, or Pumlumon, is <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> through Montgomeryshire, and enters Merionethshire; from its centre various streams run, some to the east and some to the west, the former into the Severn, and the latter to the sea at Cardigan Bay. Plinlimmon is, at the highest point, 2463 feet above the level of the sea; the other mountains which branch from it are, Llandinam, 1898 feet, the Long Mountain, 1330, and that on which a pillar to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Rodney is erected, 1204. From the irregularity of the surface, and the great elevations, the chief part of the county is bare, raw, Montgomeryshire; but in the valleys between the mountains there are some most delightful and fertile spots, watered by translucent rivulets, and bordered with the richest forest scenery. The rivers which run westerly from the mountain ridges are, the Traeth-bach, the Maw, and the Dovey. The <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>, the Severn, the Vyrnwy, and the Tanat, which receive smaller mountain torrents, run to the eastward; the two first, which receive the others, keep nearly a parallel course to the plains of Salop. The Severn, though at first a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> mountain rill, and soon afterwards a rapid <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>, speedily assumes a tranquil character, and glides through deep vales till it enters Shropshire, and becomes the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of our English rivers. It is the only stream navigable in this county, but it is not passable by boats except at periods of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and frequently ship <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> lies on its banks a long time, waiting for sufficient water to float it down the stream. A canal has been constructed, connected with the Ellesmere Canal in Shropshire; but though completed, it is found to be a very unproductive undertaking. There are some picturesque waterfalls, which invite the inspection of travellers in this romantic county. The most remarkable of these is Pystyll-Rhaeadr. The brook, or rather the river Rhaeadr (for, after rains, it deserves the latter name), runs down a gentle declivity for a short distance, and then suddenly precipitates itself over a perpendicular ledge, whence it falls, rather in the form of spray than in that of a torrent, to the depth of two hundred feet, whilst the projecting rocks which intercept its fall produce a spectacle and sounds that are highly terrific. This cataract appears in its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> only after a wet season, for in very dry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> it is an insignificant rill. The agriculture of Montgomeryshire is in a very backward state; not one eighth of the land is under the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>; about three eighths of it is devoted to pasture, but the food it produces is small for the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> on which it grows. Nearly half the county is in an uncultivated state, or covered with wood. Some few good cultivators have latterly, in some spots, introduced the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> four-course system of turnips, barley, clover, and wheat; but it prevails to a very limited extent, owing to the deficiency of capital amongst the occupiers. The greater part of the arable land is destined to produce corn without intermission till it becomes exhausted, when it returns of itself to a very imperfect and unproductive kind of pasture. Though these remarks refer to the greater part of the county, yet a portion of it adjoining to Shropshire forms an agreeable exception, as it is well cultivated, and very prolific, especially on the banks of the Severn. In almost every part of the county <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> is cultivated for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, in small patches; and the making of it into cloth forms the employment of itinerant weavers. The cows of this county somewhat resemble the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a> breed, and are said to have been originally brought from that county. When removed to better pasture, and fattened, they are highly valued by the butchers, because they yield less offal, and collect a greater <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> on the more valuable parts of the body. The sheep are of small size, but their mutton is exquisite. The <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> is of a very fine quality, and the best Welsh flannels are made from it. There is a very numerous breed of small horses in the mountainous parts of Montgomeryshire, which are nearly in a state of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. They are known by the name of Merlins, and range during the whole year through the most elevated parts of the country. By their exposure, and the ease with which they are subsisted, they acquire a very hardy frame, and are capable of performing labour far beyond what their size and apparent strength indicate. They are driven, when required, into an enclosure, where the best are selected from those which have attained their third year, and the remainder are turned out to range at large as before. Notwithstanding their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> size, the greater part of the commodities furnished by the county are conveyed on their backs from one place to another. The valleys in this county have been long celebrated for a breed of excellent horses, introduced originally from the south of Spain, by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Shrewsbury, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. These, by various crosses, have been much improved, and they now furnish some of the best hunters in the kingdom, from uniting strength with speed. <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">Limestone</a> is not generally found in this county, and rarely unmixed with argillaceous earth; so that the lime required for building is brought from one extremity to the other by the canal. Coal is only found in an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the county, on the borders of Salop; but the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is small, and its combustive quality causes it to burn so rapidly as to make it a much more expensive <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, except in the vicinity of the pits, than either wood or turf. The mineral which abounds most in the mountains of Montgomeryshire is <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, which is extracted in many parts of them. The ore known by the name of galena, provincialy called potters' ore, was formerly discovered in a prodigious vein at Llangynog; but, after much profitable excavation, the miners reached a fault in the vein, and its continuance has not yet been ascertained. At Llanymnach are the vestiges of mines worked in very remote periods, which exhibit intricate recesses, and form a kind of subterraneous <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a>. Both <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and lead ore are still found in these ancient mines, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> with sulphuric and carbonic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, known by the common appellations of calamine and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-jack. A very rich lead mine at Talless was formerly worked, and yielded large profits to its owner, Sir Watkins Williams Wynne; but, owing to a great increase of water, the working has been discontinued. The ranges of mountains are partly composed of schistus, from which are drawn large quantities of slates, applied to the covering of houses, or sent to London and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> to be fitted for <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. This was formerly one of the best wooded counties of North Wales, and it has, for the last seventy years, contributed to supply a great part of the best oak timber to the royal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCK">dock</a>-yards. The size of the Montgomeryshire oaks has made them much prized for naval purposes; some have been felled which have contained more than 600 cubic feet. This oak is of a remarkably good quality; but the difficulty of conveyance has rendered the price very low on the spots where it is grown, and formerly much of even the most valuable quality was used for fuel. The only <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are those of woollens, made from the fleeces of their native sheep, and mostly confined to flannels known through England, and highly prized, under the denomination of Welsh flannels. They have been imitated both in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, but have not been equalled in fineness of texture, combined with softness. The farmers, and even the cottagers, make these flannels; and they are collected by a kind of middle-men, who bring them to the market of Welshpool, whence they are sold to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of Shrewsbury, who distribute them over the kingdom. The annual value of those sold at the market is about £50,000, and the cost of the wool is estimated at about half that amount. One member is returned to parliament by the freeholders for the county, and one for the towns of Montgomery, Llandudnoes, Machynlleth, Llanfyllin, Newtown, and Welshpool. The population of this county amounted in the year 1801 to 47,970, in 1811 to 51,931, in 1821 to 66,482, and in 1831 to 65,700. The baptisms in the year 1830 were of males 656, and of females 644. The burials of males were 498, and of females 506. The marriages were 425. The families were 13,407, of which those chiefly employed in agriculture were 6610; those chiefly employed in trade, manufactures, and handicraft, were 4198; and the remaining 2599 were not comprised in the two preceding classes. The males under twenty years of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> were 16,723. The occupiers of land employing labourers were 1938, those not employing labourers were 1610, and agricultural labourers were 5749. Those employed in manufactures, or in making manufacturing machinery, were 1630; those employed in retail trade or handicraft as masters were 3370; the capitalists, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>, professional and other educated men, were 418; the labourers employed in other than agricultural labour were 976; and the other males twenty years of age, except servants, were 851. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> servants were 311; and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> 3695. The annual value of the real <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, as assessed in 1815, amounted to L207,286. The most remarkable seats of noblemen and gentlemen are, Powis Castle, Lord Powis; Lydiarth <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>, Sir W. W. Wynne, Bart.; Llangedwen, Mr Wynne; Towyn, E. Corbet, Esq.; Llandinam, M. Stephens, Esq.; Vayner, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Windus; Newton <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PARK">Park</a>, Richard Shaw, Esq.

MONTH

Pages 445-445

the twelfth <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a year. See <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-CALENDAR">Calendar</a>.

MONTI

Pages 445-446

VICENZO, the greatest poet which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> has produced since the bright days of its literary <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, was born in Romagna, on the 19th of February 1754. His father was one of those small Italian landholders whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is peculiarly primitive and patriarchal, and the farmhouse, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> villa, as it is called, which he occupied, was situated amongst the vineyards and agricultural <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which lies between Fusignano and the Alfonsina, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>. In this rural retirement Monti passed several years of his boyhood, without receiving any instructions except from his parents; but the family having removed to Majano, he was sent to the seminary of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FAENZA">Faenza</a>, and there he acquired an extensive knowledge of the Latin <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. His first attempt in Latin <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> was singularly unhappy; but his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the Roman poets amounted to a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> effort of his muse was regarded by his masters as a miraculous effort of precocious genius. By his father he was destined to follow the profession of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>; but yielding a reluctant compliance with the wishes of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, and continuing to evince a predilection for literature which was subversive of all <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> application, the elder Monti sent the youthful poet to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the legal or medical profession. Yet even these pursuits were found too <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> for a mind so highly imaginative and ardent, and ultimately Monti resigned himself wholly to the cultivation of literature and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. His first Italian poem was entitled The Prophecy of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>; and, although an unequal production, it contains some vigorous and even sublime <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>. About this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the perusal of Dante opened up to him new and splendid views of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and beautiful in the poetry of his native <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and henceforth the bard of the Divina Commedia became his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODEL">model</a> and his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. His admiration of Dante bordered on idolatry, and catching a portion of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a> of his favourite, he wrote the Vision of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a>, in which he displayed that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of imagery and command of language which distinguish his compositions. Monti was at this time scarcely eighteen years of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His genius attracted the notice of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Borghese, who took him under his protection, and conducted him to Rome. Here he extended his knowledge of the classics, and his acquaintance with the learned, whose favour he secured by various efforts of his muse. But it was not until he attained his twenty-sixth year that public <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was directed to him, on the occasion of the celebration of the quinquennali of Pius VI. in 1780. The compositions which he recited drew forth such general applause that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Braschi, the pope's nephew, made him his private secretary. Under this nobleman he <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> several years at Rome, producing at intervals such occasional poems as kept alive rather than extended his poetic reputation. At last the fame of Alfieri inspired him with emulation; and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> with a desire to rival <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, which he had heard read by the poet in a circle of the most distinguished literati of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, he composed his tragedy of Aristodemo. It was acted with the greatest success at Rome in 1787, and Monti was induced to write another drama, Galeotto Manfredi, which proved an entire failure. His genius was not dramatic, but lyrical; and highly-wrought imaginative rhapsodies were more in accordance with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> bias of his mind than the concatenation of plots, and the delineation of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> passion. About this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> Monti married. The French revolution had now begun to shake, as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> by an earthquake, the time-worn and decayed governments of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; and the French, eager to extend the moral convulsion, and regenerate the whole world, despatched numbers of individuals to different countries, there to spread revolutionary tenets. Amongst those who had crossed the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a> for this purpose was Hugh Basseville, a person of considerable talents and some literary acquirements. He had been appointed secretary to the French embassy at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>; and whilst thus employed he visited Rome, for the purpose of propagating revolutionary doctrines. This imprudence cost him his life. He was stabbed on the night of the 13th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1793, and died soon afterwards, overwhelmed with remorse, it is said, for having attempted to raise sedition against the pope. Monti being attached to the papal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, laid hold of this circumstance, and celebrated at once the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a> of Basseville, and the unfortunate tragedy acted in France almost at the same moment, in a poem entitled the Basvilliana. This production is entirely supernatural in its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of the murdered <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>, like the body of Moses, is contended for by the angel of God and the enemy of mankind; and although the former is triumphant, yet the disembodied spirit of the republican is doomed for a certain period to hover about the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, and to witness all the atrocities which are there perpetrated. The subject is treated in a powerful and happy manner, the imagery with which the poem is adorned being in the highest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> original and majestic. As a whole, it approached more nearly to the grandeur and sublime daring of Dante than any thing which had been produced for centuries; and the fame of Monti rose above all rivalry. But the tide of French republicanism, having now rushed through the passes of the Alps, and overflowed the fertile plains of Italy, entirely changed the aspect of affairs in that country, and brought Monti into <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> contact with some of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">Napoleon</a>'s generals. To this circumstance we must <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the admiration which the poet began to entertain for the French <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, and the lively anticipations of good to be derived by his country from the new order of things which were awakened in his mind. But the Italian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> eyed with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> suspicion the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASQUERADE">masquerade</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> in which they were invited to play a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>; and many of them, seceding from the offices of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, left these open to the ambition of meaner or less scrupulous aspirants. The enthusiasm of Monti hurried him away with the general current in which so many warm young hearts were borne along. In one of his letters, the poet observes, "I grew insane with the rest, and my conversion procured me <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>;" but it did not procure him either peace or --- <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XVI. was beheaded on the 19th of January 1793. Monti respect. By many of his own countrymen he was viewed with envy and aversion, whilst the republicans denounced, in the author of Basvilliania, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> enemy of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEMOCRACY">democracy</a>, and Monti was ultimately dismissed from his office. In a mythological poem entitled Musogonia, he paid court to Napoleon; and in a still finer production, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROMETHEUS">Prometheus</a>, he enthusiastically celebrates the triumphs of the Gallic <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>; at the same time pouring out the vials of his wrath upon England. This must doubtless have greatly delighted Bonaparte, and the poet was soon afterwards named <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMISSARY">commissary</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the Rubicon; but in a short time he was obliged to resign his office. During the absence of the conqueror in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, the Italian republics melted away like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> before the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; and their partisans, amongst whom was Monti, were compelled to seek refuge beyond the Alps. The poet fell into a state of the most deplorable destitution; but the return of Napoleon, and his new victories in Italy, afforded Monti an opportunity of partially retrieving his fortunes. He returned to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, and there published his poem, the Mascheroniana, the chief object of which is to bind new wreaths of victory around the brow of Napoleon, already encumbered with laurels. Shortly afterwards, Monti produced a third tragedy, entitled <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Gracchus; and, in 1802, an ode, in which he calls upon his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> idol to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> himself at the head of the Italian people, which, as is well known, Bonaparte did not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> hesitate to do. The rewards of the poet were, first, a professorship at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, and, a few years subsequently, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of offices and honours at Milan. In 1805, when Napoleon was crowned <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> of Italy, the event was celebrated by Monti in a poem called Il Benificio. Indeed, every fresh victory and new conquest of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> of France afforded a theme for the courtly muse of the Italian poet. The triumph of Jena resounded in his ode entitled the Spada di Federico; the attempted usurpation of the Spanish throne was sung in the Palingenesi; and various other conquests were celebrated in numerous odes and hymns. Besides these works, he finished, in less than two years, a translation of the Iliad, which, without possessing much spirit, is considered as elegant and faithful. The overthrow of Napoleon in 1814 deprived Monti of all his public employments; and after this period, although he composed an occasional poem, his labours were chiefly confined to prose. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of these are, considerations on the difficulty of properly translating the poetry of the Iliad, and several dialogues on the Italian language, full of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and acute criticism. By an order of government to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the national <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, his attention was still more entirely engrossed with the subject of language. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> question in Italy was, and still is, whether the pure and classical language, the only one not wholly barbarous and vulgar, is Italian or Tuscan. The academy Della Crusca espoused the latter view of the question, whilst Monti undertook a crusade against them, attacking their decisions with the utmost vigour, and no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> success. He continued to reside at Milan, corresponding with various members of his family, and with the distinguished men of the day. In 1823 his imagination awoke again, and he once more turned his thoughts to poetry. He restored the true <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-READING">reading</a> of the Convito of Dante, wrote an idyl on the nuptials of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a>, and then contemplated the completion of the Feroniade, a poem which he had begun many years before. In this production he celebrates the praise of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Braschi, for having, by a magnificent work, drained the insalubrious Pontine Marches. He had nearly completed his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, when <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> put a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> period to his labours. In 1826 an apoplectic attack gave a severe shock to his frame; but he lingered more than two years, and expired on the 13th of October 1828, in the seventy-fourth year of his age. It has been said of Dryden, that if all the great chiefs of poetry surpassed him, each in his own peculiar vein, yet his native fire and originality gave him a place close beside them. It is much the same with Monti. He has neither the sublimity of Dante, nor the tenderness of Petrarch, nor the inventive flow of Ariosto, nor the epic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> and voluptuous grace of Tasso; but he has a fervour of feeling, a power of imagery, and an overflowing redundancy of ideal thought, which mark the genuine poet, and entitle him to a place immediately after these great masters of the lyre. His genius was not that of a tragedian; lyrical and imaginative rhapsodies, rather than the concatenation of a plot and the representation of human passion, were adapted to the natural bent of his mind, and in these he chiefly excelled. It is more difficult to justify his character and conduct as a man than to vindicate his claims to the laurel. In times of less public excitement, he would have quietly cultivated letters and poetry in retirement, and his faults would never have been dragged into notice. But, to atone for his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> tergiversation and servile worship of power, he possessed the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> virtues in the highest degree. He had great warmth of heart, was zealously attached to his friends, and grateful for benefits; generous, kind, and true in all the ordinary intercourse of life. A friend thus speaks of him: "In person he was tall and handsome; his forehead ample; the shape of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> regular; and his eyes, gleaming from beneath his arched and full brows, shone at once with lively yet softened <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, which commanded both affection and respect. An <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> of melancholy was diffused over his countenance, to which the habits of reflection would have given a severe and even disdainful <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, had not the sweetest smile illuminated it with the gracious light of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. His carriage was dignified, his mien serious, and his whole aspect that of a man of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, and of one warmed and softened by the benevolence and affection of his disposition." (R. R.)

MONTILLIA

Pages 446-446

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Cordova, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>. It is situated near the river Xeñil, and produces a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wine of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> excellence, and which is most highly prized by the connoisseurs in the southern cities. The city stands on the Castro and Biofrio, and contains 6300 inhabitants.

MONTJOIE

Pages 446-446

a town, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the circle of the same name, in the Prussian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle. It is situated in a narrow valley between lofty hills, and contains 380 houses, with 3280 inhabitants. The finest cloths and cassimeres are made here, and the best machinery for the purpose is extensively applied.

MONTLUCON

Pages 446-446

an arrondissement of the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALLIER">Allier</a>, in France, 457 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. It is divided into five cantons and 79 communes, and contains 61,500 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river Cher. It is surrounded with walls, and defended by a castle upon an elevation which commands the town. The inhabitants are 4800, employed in woollen <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2.31. E. Lat. 46. 22. N.

MONTMEDY

Pages 446-446

an arrondissement of the department of the Meuse, in France, extending over 522 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It is divided into six cantons, and these again into 132 communes, containing 60,000 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, situated on the river Ebiers. It is strongly fortified, and defended by a citadel in the upper town, built on a rocky eminence. It contains only 1800 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 20. E. Lat. 49. 36. N.

MONTMORENCY

Pages 446-446

a town of the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a> and Oise, and arrondissement of Ponloise, in France. It is finely situated, and near it is the valley of the same name, which was <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> the residence of the celebrated Rousseau. It contains 250 houses, and 1950 inhabitants.

MONTMORILLON

Pages 446-447

an arrondissement of the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNE">Vienne</a>, in France, extending over 797 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It contains six cantons, divided into 65 communes, inhabited by 49,500 persons. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, situated on the river Garonne, by which it is divided into two parts. It contains 460 houses, and 3250 inhabitants.

MONTPELLIER

Pages 447-447

an arrondissement of the department of the Hérault, in France, 838 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. It comprehends 14 cantons, which are divided into 117 communes, and contains 103,500 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, which gives its name to the arrondissement, is in a fine district, surrounded with walls, and stands on the declivity of a hill between the river Mardanson and the Lez. The higher <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> consists of narrow and crooked streets, with very few good buildings; but the lower part <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> suburb has good, well-built, regular streets. The city has some beautiful promenades around it; and from an elevated public walk near it, called the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">Place</a> du Peyron, there is one of the finest prospects in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The city contains a university of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> celebrity, with a library of 42,000 volumes, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a>. It contains 8000 houses, with 3500 inhabitants, of whom about 6000 are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, who, besides cloths of cotton and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, produce many chemical preparations, particularly cream of tartar, vitriol, aquafortis, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ETHER">ether</a>, glauber salts, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and much perfumery. The trade is facilitated by a canal, which connects the city with the Mediterranean. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 47. E. Lat. 43. 36. N.

MONTREAL

Pages 447-448

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a>, the first in size and commercial importance, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, in that district. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> and signory, on the south side of which the city stands, is about thirty miles in length by from five to ten in breadth, and contains 197 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It is situated on the St Lawrence, at the head of ship <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, 180 miles above Quebec, and 200 below Lake <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ONTARIO">Ontario</a>. On the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> a small stream divides it from the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>, which is also a signory, and about twenty miles <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>; and from Isle Bizare, which is four miles in length. Montreal is situated <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the river, upon a belt of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> about two miles in breadth, and at the back of which is the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Mountain. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river upon which it is built has a gradual elevation from twenty to thirty feet, sloping again at the back of the town, where there is a canal to carry off any accumulated <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Including the suburbs, it is much more extensive and somewhat more populous than Quebec, but it wants the sublime scenery which characterizes that city. The whole of the lower town has a gloomy and uncomfortable appearance, the streets being narrow and incommodious. It consists of one <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> street for shops and trade, which runs <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the river, with others which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> it at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, and also intersect another street running parallel to it, and dividing the old from the more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> town. This <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Montreal contains several spacious public buildings, with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fashionable dwelling-houses, built of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and the villas in the neighbourhood have an imposing appearance. It has a respectable esplanade called the Champ de <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, where the troops are reviewed. To the east extends the Quebec suburb, and to the north and west the suburbs of St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANTOINE">Antoine</a>, St Lawrence, and St Recollet. Amongst the public buildings, the first which requires to be mentioned is the new Catholic <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, said to be the most splendid temple in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, not excepting that of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, which, however, is nearly equal to it. The foundation-stone was laid in 1824, and it was opened for public worship in 1829. This magnificent structure is thus described by Mr McGregor in his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> on British America. "It is dedicated to the Virgin <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>. Its length is 255 feet, breadth 234, and the height of the walls 112 feet." The style of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> is taken from the rich Gothic of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. It has six <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> towers; between these, along the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, is a promenade twenty-five feet wide, elevated 112 feet above the ground. It has one superior altar, and six of less <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>. It has five public and three private entrances; and from 10,000 to 12,000 people, which it <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> accommodate, may disperse in five <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> six minutes. The eastern window, behind the altar, is thirty-three feet <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and seventy high; the other windows are ten feet by thirty-six feet. It is surrounded by a fine terrace. The chime of bells, clocks, altars, and all the interior arrangements, correspond with the magnificence of the exterior. From 7000 to 8000 persons frequently congregate within this edifice." There are several other Catholic churches besides the cathedral; one of these, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but plain in appearance, was built in the suburbs, upon the arrival of a bishop from France, after the termination of the late <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and for whom a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> was built near it. The bells of the Catholic churches are kept constantly ringing, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> annoyance, especially to strangers. The whole island of Montreal is comprised in one signory, and is claimed by the seminary of St Sulpice, which consists of twenty members and four assistants. They discharge the whole parochial duties for the Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the town and suburbs; and they maintain, in whole or in part, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, at which 204 young men are educated in the classics and sciences. They also educate, at various <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> which they have established, more than 1300 scholars, besides making extensive distributions in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. In addition to these various duties, the whole management of the farms, and other temporal concerns, is carried on by the members. The revenues of the seminary may be taken at an <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> of L3277 currency a year, equal to L6700 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. In exacting the lods et ventes due to them on the transference of land, they are very liberal, and usually <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> for these fines. The improvement of Montreal has been much retarded by signorial and feudal exactions. The feelings of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> have been much mortified in being compelled to submit to demands for the support of institutions contrary to their principles; whilst no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was paid by the British <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to the establishment of scholastic institutions for the benefit of the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. The adjustment, therefore, of the claims of the seminary of St Sulpice is the most important subject in which the inhabitants are interested. The principal English <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a handsome and spacious edifice. The Scotch kirk is a plain unadorned <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, but the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a> have a very fine chapel. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, prison, and government-house, are substantial buildings, but without any pretensions to architectural <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. There are three numeraries in the city, belonging to which are some beautiful islets, as well as lands on the largest of these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. There is an English university, where the various branches of a polite and learned <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> are taught. There is a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, which has been of great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in illustrating the natural history and unfolding the vast resources of America. There are also a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>' <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, a general <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and a well-conducted news-room; and twelve newspapers, as well as some other periodicals, are published in Montreal. It enjoys considerable trade, and possesses several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. There is a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> foundry; and machinery for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> engines, stoves, and the like, is made in the town. There are likewise distilleries, breweries, and other manufactures of necessary <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>; and also several ship-building establishments. A bank was established in 1817, and there is now a branch of it at Quebec. There is likewise a committee of trade, which regulates various commercial matters and charges. There are no wharfs at Montreal, and the ships and steamers <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> quietly in pretty deep water, close to the clayey and generally filthy bank in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the city. From its position, Montreal will always <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONTREUIL">Montreuil</a> constitute one of the greatest commercial emporiums of America; and it must increase in magnitude and importance, along with the rapid improvement and increasing population of the upper and surrounding countries. The trade is not suspended in winter, as at Quebec. During that season, thousands of sledges come in from all directions laden with agricultural produce, frozen carcasses of beef and pork, firewood, and other articles. In return these traffickers receive manufactured goods of all kinds, the warehouses and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> being always well supplied. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> vast rafts of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> Montreal for Quebec; and boats of a rude <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> bring <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the productions of the upper <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. This was the headquarters of the fur trade before the North-west and Hudson Companies joined their interests; and there is still a warehouse there. More than three fourths of the population are French; the rest are Britons and Americans. The population in 1825 amounted to 22,357, and in 1831 to 27,297; at present (1837) it is nearly 37,000. The city of Montreal is represented in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> legislature by four members; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> by two. The imports and exports, as well as other statistical information, are included in those of Quebec, and will be found under that article. Montreal is situated in long. 73° 25' W., and lat. 45° 30' N.

MONTREUIL

Pages 448-448

an arrondissement of the department of the Pas de <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>, in France. It extends over 490 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, and is divided into six cantons, which are subdivided into 142 communes, having a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of 72,800 persons. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is of the same name, and stands on the left <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river Canche, eight miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It contains 840 houses, and 3560 inhabitants, who subsist in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> from trading in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and refining <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> and tunnery, and in part from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of travellers passing through it in the way between Calais and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>.

MONTRON

Pages 448-448

an arrondissement of the department of the Gironde, in France, 624 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. It is divided into eight cantons, and these into 90 communes, containing 69,500 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of that name, is built on two hills, at the bases of which flows the river Baudial. It contains 450 houses, and 3160 inhabitants; and is celebrated for the excellent tanned and curried <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> it produces.

MONTROSE

Pages 448-451

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> burgh and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of Scotland, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Forfar, distant seventy miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, thirty north-east from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUNDEE">Dundee</a>, and about forty south from Aberdeen, in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> 2° 10' west, and latitude 56° 34' north. It is pleasantly situated on the west side of a narrow <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, formed by the German Ocean on the east, the South Esk river on the south, and on the west by a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> basin, into which the tide, flowing up the South Esk, spreads itself after passing the town. It is a burgh of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> antiquity, and received its first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> I., although, from the tenor of that charter, it seems to have been a burgh even before that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The petty-customs, weigh-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-market dues, &c. are levied in virtue of a charter granted by David II. James IV. also granted a charter, dated 1493, by which the magistrates are still empowered to levy shore-dues, anchorage, and plankage, at the harbour, for the purpose of upholding piers, buoys, and moorings. The magistrates likewise hold a writ of privy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> from James VI. dated 1600, authorizing them to hold a weekly grain-market on the High Street. Owing to an informality in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of its magistracy in 1816, the burgh was disfranchised by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">Court</a> of Session; and in 1817 a new charter was granted by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, by which the old practice of self-election was abolished, and every year ten of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> were renewed by the suffrages of the guildry and trades. But the municipal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> improved on this charter, and now the magistrates and councillors are elected by the parliamentary voters. The town-council consists of nineteen members, including the provost, three bailies, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of guild, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>. Their jurisdiction extends over the royalty of the burgh. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTABLE">Constable</a> Hill, which the town acquired by purchase, is beyond their jurisdiction, although included in the parliamentary boundaries. The name of the town is connected with some important events in Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. It was here that in 1296 John Baliol surrendered his crown to Edward I. of England; and it was from the port of Montrose that the celebrated Sir James Douglas embarked in 1330, with a numerous retinue, on a pilgrimage to the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">Land</a>, to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURY">bury</a> the heart of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">King</a> Robert Bruce in the Holy Sepulchre. It is distinguished as the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in Scotland where the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> was taught, and as having sent forth from its seminary the learned scholar and divine, Andrew Melville. It is likewise the birth-place of the celebrated Marquis of Montrose. This was the only town in Scotland, so late as the commencement of the eighteenth century, where an individual could be found who understood the management of pumps in coal-works. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1715, James, the first pretender, landed here from the French fleet, which had passed the Frith of Forth, the place of its destination; and here also, in February of the ensuing year, he and his suite again embarked for France. The town is in general well built, and has of late years been considerably enlarged by the erection of several new streets. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> street extends, under various denominations, the whole length of the town; and the centre <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, named the High Street, is spacious, and contains many elegant buildings. From the east side of this main street run several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> streets, which connect it with the different smaller streets and buildings lying in that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. The town-house, which stands in the High Street, is a handsome edifice of two stories, with an arcade below, and contains the council-room, guild-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, courtroom, news-room, and public library. The old <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, which is collegiate, is a large, plain <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, measuring 98 feet in length by 65 in breadth. It has two tiers of galleries, and is seated for 2500, but contains nearly 3000. A new steeple was attached to it in 1835, consisting of an elegant and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> Gothic tower, upwards of a hundred feet high, surmounted by a spire nearly of the same height. This is said to be the highest steeple in Scotland. St John's Church, formerly a chapel of ease to the old parish church, but to which a parish was annexed in 1835, is a handsome edifice, seated for about 1500 individuals. There are also two congregations belonging to the United Associate <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SYNOD">Synod</a>, two of Episcopalians, one of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">Independents</a>, one of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>, two of Baptists, and one of Glasites. St <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s Chapel, belonging to the Episcopalians not connected with the Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, was founded in 1722, and is a neat and commodious place of worship. The Academy, erected in the year 1814, is a fine edifice. It is under the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the town-council, and is conducted by a rector, who teaches <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> languages; and it has, besides, two teachers of English, two for <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>; and two for Latin and Greek. In 1832 a spacious seminary was erected by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> incorporated trades, for affording <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> on cheaper terms than those of the Academy. There is a free school, founded by Mr David <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WHITE">White</a>, in which a hundred boys are taught; and another supported by Miss <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STRATON">Straton</a>'s endowment, in which forty-two boys and thirty-five girls are educated. Besides these, there are numerous private <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> throughout the town. The Lunatic <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ASYLUM">Asylum</a>, situated in the Links, is a plain and commodious edifice. It was erected in 1780, but has since then been considerably enlarged, and is now capable of containing eighty patients. It is considered as being one of the best institutions of the kind in Scotland. A portion of the Montrose is a town possessed of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. It is a port of the customhouse, and, as such, includes the havens and creeks from Bervie Brow to the Tay. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> receipts for the year ending 5th <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1835 amounted to L7369. 2s. 9d.; for the year ending same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> 1836, to L6827. 3s. 2d. Nett receipts, after deducting all expenses, for 1835, L2135. 9s. 6d.; for 1836, L1672. 7s. 8d. The vessels belonging to the port amounted, in 1837, to 105, registering about 11,050 tons. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> proportion of these are engaged in the importation of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> from the different ports on the Baltic. A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> are also employed in bringing coals from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> and Sunderland for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the town and neighbourhood; and there are two large vessels engaged in the whale-fishery. A very large <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>-vessel, and two regular traders, are now employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> trade. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of cured herrings and salmon is considerable. Ship-building is carried on to a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; and there is a commodious patent slip for repairing ships. The principal business of the town consists in making sail-cloth, sheeting, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>; and there are now several extensive flax <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> connected with this trade, besides two rope and sail manufactories. There are here very extensive links <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWNS">downs</a> between the town and the sea, which afford one of the best golfing grounds in Scotland, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> practised by all ranks. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>-ground on the links is admirably fitted for the purpose, but for several years it has not been used. The inhabitants of Montrose have availed themselves of the general <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> act for burghs, passed a few years ago; and the town is now properly protected by an efficient body of police. Very great improvements have also been made in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PAVING">paving</a> and cleaning of the streets. The town is well lighted with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAS">gas</a>, and abundantly supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> conducted by <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> from a distance of three miles. Montrose unites with Forfar, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BRECHIN">Brechin</a>, Arbroath, and Bervie, in sending a member to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The number of voters in the parliamentary burgh is about 400. In September 1836, the burgh funds were estimated at L54,344. 2s. 7d. and the debts and obligations at L29,609. 11s., leaving a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> in favour of the town of L24,734. 11s. 7d. The revenue of the town, arising from land, feu-duties, and shore-dues, is nearly L3000 a year. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the town in 1811 amounted to 8955; in 1821, to 10,338; and in 1831, to 12,055. The number of inhabited houses in the latter year was 1190. The population is now (1837) estimated at 15,000. Montserrat, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It is about <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> leagues to the north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>, being situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river Llobregat, on an insulated mountain nearly eight leagues in circumference, and raising its head above the surrounding hills till it reaches the height of 3300 feet. It appears, from the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to it, like a huge pile of most enormous bowls, the bitumen which joined the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a> having been decomposed. As the traveller ascends, he observes vegetation gradually decreasing, till towards the top, when it entirely ceases, and nothing is presented to the view but naked rocks, separated like pillars, forming various pyramids, varying in height from 20 to 150 feet. The ascent, though steep and fatiguing, is not dangerous, as far as the church, which is large and richly ornamented; but the constant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of upwards of eighty lamps lighted with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a> has sullied the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and pictures, and dimmed the brilliancy of the silver. The number of monks and lay-brothers residing here amounts to upwards of one hundred; besides which, there are twenty-five boys who officiate in the choir, with a physician, surgeon, and servants. Besides those who reside in the convent, there are several of the monks who live in a kind of hermitage or oratory on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-PINNACLE">pinnacle</a> of several of the insulated rocks. These hermits are supplied with food twice in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, and their gardens yield some Montserrat. They are not permitted to eat meat, or to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> with each other, but live a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of perfect solitude, possibly of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, during the whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, excepting when they descend to the general <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, which is performed in the church of the convent. The <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> of the noviciate for the ordinary monks is six months; but those who wish to live in one of the hermitages must <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> six years of very severe probation before they can be allowed to reside in them. Although the romantic situation, the extensive and varied prospects, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> curiosities of the place, draw to it many travellers who are not infected with any devotional feeling, yet the number of real votaries is very great. These come to say prayers, to pass a few days in devotion and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>, to kiss with reverence the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of a miraculous image of the holy Virgin; and, what is of most importance to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, to deposit votive offerings, which are eagerly accepted by the recluse inhabitants. By the rules of the order, they are bound to maintain for three days every pilgrim who comes to pay his devotions to the sacred image. The devotees are allowed <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> in the morning, broth at noon, and bread again at night. Although this parsimonious kind of hospitality is not very expensive for each individual who arrives, yet the number is so great that the annual cost is considerable; and although the presents from the rich far exceed the cost of their maintenance, yet these presents are preserved carefully till they are quite spoiled by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Their original endowment was only the mountain; but by rigid economy they have, in the course of ages, been enabled to purchase considerable estates in the vicinity. Some of these, indeed, have been appropriated by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to its own use, and probably at no distant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> the remainder may share the same fate. It is singular that there should be always a number of candidates, both for the cells of the monks and for the hermitages of the recluses. They make a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VOW">vow</a> never to quit the mountain, and they are not allowed to enter into holy orders. This may perhaps account for the continuance of those who are once admitted; but it is not easy for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> to understand that state of mind which induces men in the full vigour of their bodily and mental faculties to withdraw from the world, and abandon every pursuit but that of inactive devotion and the tiresome repetition of prayers, with no variety to amuse and no excitement to animate them. Montserrat, one of the West <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, belonging to Great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, is situated in 16° 47' north latitude, and 92° 18' 25" west longitude. It is about twelve miles in length by seven and a half in breadth, and contains a superficies of 30,000 acres. Like the islands in its vicinity, it runs from south-east to north-west, and presents an equally broken and mountainous surface; an arrangement and physical structure which has led to the conclusion that these islands owe their origin to volcanic eruption. The extremity of the mountain chain terminates on the north in a bold headland <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, where there is no landing-place and little anchorage. The land slopes to the sea in a succession of conglomerate eminences, which extend to the base of the mountain. On the south there is no approach for vessels of any size until they get to the westward, the sea for a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> or two being studded with huge rocks and shelving banks of coral. The <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> then suddenly shoots up to the height of 1500 feet, and continues to rise pile above pile, throwing out lateral branches, until they attain the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> of 2500 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the Atlantic. This chain stretches across to the northern extremity of Montserrat, where it terminates, as we have mentioned. Many of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are inaccessible, and are separated from each other by immense perpendicular chasms several hundred feet in depth. These gullies, however, as well as the mountains, are covered to the very summits with lofty woods, and all the beautiful variety of vegetation which a mountainous region within the tropics presents. On the south-west side of the chain is a small souffrière, situated 1000 feet above the sea, in a dell formed by the approximation of three conical hills, the scenery around which has been described by Mr Coleridge as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and beautiful in the highest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. The road from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Montserrat, to this place, after stretching along the margin of the sea, winds inwards by a gentle declivity towards the mountains. The path becomes strewed with the snowy amaryllis (pancratia Caribbea), and the scarlet hibiscus; and on either side lime and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> trees form a verdant hedge. The whole of the valley in which the souffrière lies is broken into vast and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> masses of clay and <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, which are scattered about in the utmost confusion. The surface of the ground is everywhere hot, indeed so much so near the streams of water which run between the fragments, that it is difficult for the foot to support it more than half a minute. The water at its source boils up violently, and a cloud of vapour constantly settles over it. The sides of the mounds of clay are encrusted with pure <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>; but, notwithstanding this, the vegetation of bushes and creepers all round is green and luxuriant, whilst the rampart of mountains in which the solitary valley is embosomed is clothed with woods whose feathery grass-like plumage <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> devotedly to the setting <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> under the unceasing breath of the trade-<a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. There are no marshes, but there is a small lake on the top of a hill about two miles west from Plymouth, which remains constantly full. Plymouth, the capital, is small, but substantially built, of a fine gray <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and has a comfortable appearance. The geological features of this island are similar to those of the islands in the neighbourhood. Many of the rocks have been termed only vast masses of clay of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> hues; but in the conical hills carbonate of lime, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> pyrites, and aluminous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> abound. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is in general dry, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, thin, gravelly, and thickly covered with blocks of clay and sandstone, excepting in the valleys where the loamy earth is deposited by rains. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Montserrat is remarkable for its salubrity, a characteristic which has obtained for it the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONTPELLIER">Montpellier</a> of the West Indies. The temperature of course varies according to the locality and the elevation above the sea. It is subject to hurricanes, but these are neither frequent nor severe. To enumerate the staple products of Montserrat, would be merely to recapitulate what is said of them under the heads of Jamaica, St Lucia, and other West <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> islands. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIGO">Indigo</a> was formerly raised in great quantities, but this branch of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> is now abandoned. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> and rum produced are highly esteemed. Of the former there were exported in 1832, 2,322,208 pounds, valued at L16,549; and of the latter, 74,064 gallons, valued at L3307. The total amount of exports for the same year was L21,517, and of imports L11,067. In 1830 the shipping inwards was 5824 tons, and outwards 6576 tons.
