Mercy was to be shown to every Jew, as to a brother, and whether he were a friend or a foe; and all oppression was forbidden towards strangers, for, says the divine lawgiver, "ye were strangers in the land of Egypt, and know the heart of a stranger," and towards the widow and fatherless, for "if thou afflict them in any wise, and they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry; and your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless." The Mosaic punishments were not very various. Reparation was sometimes enjoined, by restitution, by compensation, and by fines. The principle of retaliation was frequent, "eye for eye, tooth for tooth, and beast for beast;" but the most common award was death, "to cut off the offender from among the people," and preserve the community from the moral contagion of his example. Striking, cursing, or continuing obstinately disobedient to a parent, was punished in this way; as were also man-stealing, with intent to sell or reduce to slavery, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, blasphemy, idolatry and false worship, sabbath breaking, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">witchcraft</a> and sorcery, sodomy and bestiality, <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-INCEST">incest</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, fornication, and lewdness, all of which crimes were punished with death. Nor was there any provision in the law for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> of offenders, or any power lodged anywhere for that purpose. The law was imperative and inexorable, excepting only in the case of casual <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOMICIDE">homicide</a>, for which six cities of refuge were provided throughout the land, that the manslayer might flee thither and be safe. The last branch of the code is the Ceremonial Law, or ordinances of divine service. The situation of the Jewish in relation to the Deity was singular. They were, in a pre- eminent sense, "a peculiar people, above all the nations of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>;" and as the nation and the land of Israel were denominated holy, so other nations were called polluted and unclean; "aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>." But though this was the case nationally considered, there were certain things which defiled a Jew, and rendered him unclean. The first notice which we have of this is in the judicial law, where it is said, "ye shall be a holy people unto me; neither shall ye eat any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> torn of beasts in the field; ye shall <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> it to the dogs." But the several occasions of defilement are stated at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in that branch of the code which we are now considering; where we find that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a> in the person, in garments, or in a house, rendered these respectively unclean, and that, amongst other things, certain animals, beasts, fishes, fowls, and reptiles, were unclean. The defilement contracted was sometimes but temporary, and ceased with the morning's ablution; at other times it could be removed only in the way prescribed by the law. There were also certain persons, places, and times, which were accounted peculiarly holy. The holy place par excellence was the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a>, the outer <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of which occupied a space of one hundred cubits in length by fifty in breadth, or about one hundred and eighty feet by ninety. The only entrance to this court was from the east by a hanging rail of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine-twined <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>. Here, under the open sky, stood a laver of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> for the priests to wash in, and the altar of burnt-offering. Into this court every clean Hebrew or proselyte of the covenant might enter with his offerings. At the west end of this court stood a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a> about fifty-four feet in length by eighteen in breadth, which was properly called the tabernacle, and divided into two apartments. The first, which St Paul calls the first tabernacle, was about thirty-six feet in length, and contained the shew-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CANDLESTICK">candlestick</a> of pure <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, &c.; and into this, which was denominated the holy place, only the priests durst enter or look. Beyond this apartment was another about eighteen feet <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, called the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> tabernacle, most holy place, or Holy of Holies, which was separated from the first tabernacle by a veil of embroidered linen hung upon pillars of wood overlaid with gold. Here stood the ark of the covenant. It was made of wood overlaid with gold, and contained the book of the testimony. Upon the ark, and of like dimensions with it, was the mercy-seat, of pure gold, with a cherub of beaten gold on either side, stretching its wings over the mercy-seat, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the cherubim being towards each other. It was from above the mercy-seat, and between the cherubim, that God met and communed with Moses and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> priest; none else was permitted to enter the sacred precincts, and even the high priest could only do so once a year, and this not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the errors of the people. The priesthood was in the family of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a>. The priests served at the altar, prepared the victims, and offered the sacrifices; they kept up the fire upon the altar of burnt-offerings, and in the lamps of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> candlesticks; they kneaded, baked, and offered the shew-bread; they publicly blessed the people, and were consulted by them as the interpreters of the law, and judges of controversies; and, in time of war, they carried the ark and sounded the trumpets. Their garments, which were specially prescribed in the law, were a tiara, a girdle, a linen tunic, and linen drawers. The high priest had a plate or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of gold on his tiara, with the inscription, "<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLINESS">Holiness</a> to the Lord." He had also the square <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BREASTPLATE">breastplate</a> of judgment, with its twelve <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a> containing the names of the twelve tribes, and the Urim and Thummim fixed in the breastplate; the ephod having on the shoulders two onyx stones, whereon were also engraved the names of the children of Israel; the blue robe of the ephod with golden bells hung to the skirt to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> when the high priest walked in and out from the holy place; and, lastly, the high priest's coat. The Levites, who were consecrated to God, instead of the first-born of the nation, were assigned to the priests, to wait upon them, to serve the tabernacle, to carry it, to encamp round it, and to minister in relation to it. They were divided into three classes, from the three sons of Levi, Gershom, Kohath, and Merari, each of which had its own particular <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. The charge of one class was the tabernacle, and its coverings and hangings; that of another was the boards of the tabernacle, its bars, pillars, and sockets; and that of the third was to bear "the most holy things," that is to say, the sanctuary or most holy place, and all the vessels and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> appertaining to it. But these were not to be touched by them; they were to be taken <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and put up by the priests, and simply carried under cover by the bearers, and this upon their shoulders; whereas the other two classes of the Levites had, the one two waggons and four oxen, and the other four waggons and eight oxen, for their service. And as the Levites were appointed to assist the priests, so Moses was allowed seventy elders of Israel "to bear Israel the burden of the people with him." The holy Festivals were the weekly Sabbath and the Sacred season of Unleavened Bread; 2: the feast of Weeks, or of the first <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the ground; and, 3: the feast of Tabernacles, or the gathering in of the corn and wine. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PASSOVER">Passover</a> was observed on the fourteenth day of the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Jewish year, which began in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a>; and the feast of Unleavened Bread lasted the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> following days. The feast of Weeks was a moveable feast. The feast of Tabernacles was in the seventh month, or in our September. On the first day of the month, which was observed as a Sabbath, the trumpets were sounded, whence that day was called the feast of Trumpets. The tenth day, which was likewise Sabbatical, was the great day of Atonement, when every one was required to afflict his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>; and on the fifteenth day the feast of Tabernacles began, and lasted seven days. It was on the great day of Atonement also that the Jubilee was proclaimed every fiftieth year, and then every one returned to his family and possessions, and the land lay fallow for a year. All these feasts and times were specially ordered in the law; and the matter and manner of the sacrifices and offerings then to be made were therein also specially prescribed. There were other sacred seasons, such as the times of new moons; and every day the Temple was open for worship, and sacrifices and offerings were made every morning and evening. Besides the stated sacrifices and offerings, free-will offerings were allowed; and to meet particular vows, persons were valued in the law according to their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> and age; but it was specially provided that no devoted thing should be redeemed,—"every devoted thing is most holy unto the Lord." A few words may now be added on the history of this remarkable code. It was promulgated before the Israelites began their journey to Canaan; and they had not proceeded far on their way thither when the authority of Moses was signalized, particularly on two occasions; first, when Miriam the sister of Moses was struck with leprosy for envying and speaking against Moses; and next, when Korah, grandson of Kohath, whose <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> was to carry "the most holy things," ambitious of a higher charge, headed a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, who would have put down all subordination and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, on the pretence that "all the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> were holy, every one of them." But Moses, after remonstrating with them on their rebellion, invoked on them the divine vengeance, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which they all perished. In the time of Joshua, the successor of Moses in the captaincy of Israel, the people were settled in the promised land. From Joshua's death they had no regular succession of leaders down to the time of Samuel, when they sought a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a>, and obtained one, first, in the person of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>, and then of David; in whose reign, that is to say, nearly five hundred years after the departure out of Egypt, a permanent Temple was erected at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, instead of the former Tabernacle. In their internal arrangements the Temple and Tabernacle were alike, the house of God at Moriah consisting, like the Mosaic Tabernacle, of a porch or court, the temple or sanctuary, and the most holy place, or place of the oracle; but the change of the Tabernacle, which was ambulatory, to a fixed and permanent temple, occasioned the alteration on the Mosaic code to which we alluded in the beginning of this article. There was now no need for the Levites in their capacity of bearers of the tabernacle. King David, therefore, distributed the priests and the Levites into new classes, and appointed treasurers, singers, porters, and other officers. His son <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, also, ordered for the temple an immense molten <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and caldrons for <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> for the sacrifices; and for himself a throne of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> overlaid with gold. This was the First Temple; for, at the captivity of the last remaining tribes, it was finally destroyed; and, upon the return of the Jews under <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a>, a new temple on the same site was erected, of which it was predicted that its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> should exceed the glory of the former. This was accomplished in the appearance there of the Messiah, the king and priest of a spiritual Israel, who has abolished the distinction between Jew and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENTILE">Gentile</a>, and, having offered up himself as a sacrifice for sin, is gone into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for his people, till they also be introduced into the same presence as "kings and priests." Mosaic, or Mosaic <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">Work</a>, an assemblage of little pieces of glass, marble, precious stones, and other substances, of various colours, cut square, and cemented on a ground of stucco, in such a manner as to imitate the colours and gradations of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. The critics are divided as to the origin and reason of the name. Some derive it from mosaium, a corruption of musaeum, as that is of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>. Scaliger derives it from the Greek μοσας, and imagines that the name was given to this sort of works, as being very fine and ingenious. Nibricensis is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it was so called because ex illis picturis ornabatur <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MUSCA">musca</a>.

MOSALSK

Pages 578-578

a circle of the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KALUGA">Kaluga</a>, extending in east <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> from 36° 18' to 37° 3', and in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude from 53° 58' to 54° 48'. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is generally <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>; and though the circle comprehends 2310 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, the inhabitants are only 170,500. It contains several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, some of them extensive. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, of the same name, 614 miles distant from St Petersburg, is situated on the river Mosalka, and has 343 houses, and 1640 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 34° 45' E. Lat. 53° 35' N.

MOSCHUS

Pages 578-578

a Grecian poet of antiquity, usually coupled with Bion, and both of them contemporaries with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a>. In later times, all the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> idyllia were collected and attributed to Theocritus; but the claims of Moschus and Bion to some few little pieces have been admitted, and this is sufficient to make us inquisitive about their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> and story; yet all that can now be known about them must be collected from their own remains. Moschus, by composing his delicate elegy on Bion, has given the best memorials of Bion's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Moschus and Theocritus have by some critics been supposed to be the same person; but there are irrefragable evidences against such an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>. Others, proceeding upon the authority of Suidas, maintain that he as well as Bion lived later than Theocritus, whilst others again suppose him to have been the scholar of Bion, and probably his successor in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the poetical school; which, from the elegy of Moschus, does not seem unlikely. Their remains are to be found in all the editions of the Poetae Minores. Of the separate editions, some are very valuable, particularly the rare and curious one of Mekerchus, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a>, 1565, in 4to; and those of Schwebelius, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, 1746, in 4to, of Heskin, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, 1748, in 8vo, and of Gilbert <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAKEFIELD">Wakefield</a>, 1795, in 8vo.

MOSCOW

Pages 578-579

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of European Russia, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the circle and of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of that name, and one of the two capitals of the vast Russian empire. It was <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> the only capital, and is still the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the splendid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of the coronation of each <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> is performed. It was first founded by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> George L in 1147, and vastly extended by Prince Daniel in 1300. It <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to increase till the year 1383, when it was captured by the Tartars, and nearly destroyed. It was, however, again rebuilt, and had attained some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of prosperity, when, in 1571, it was again taken and destroyed by the same people. It soon arose from this disaster with more than its former splendour, when, in 1611, it was seized by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>, and almost wholly burned <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; the houses being then, as at the former <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, almost exclusively built of wood. It recovered from this disaster, and again became a city of vast <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, and wealth, all of which had made <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress under the reign of the Empress Catherine. In 1812, when Bonaparte invaded Russia, at the head of an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> composed of men of nearly all the European nations, Moscow, in a circle of twenty-four miles, contained five divisions, viz. 1st, the Kremlin, containing the citadel, the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and many other public and private buildings; 2d, Kitaigorod; 3d, Belegorod; 4th, Semlanosgorod; and 5th, the thirty Slobodes <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> suburbs. The whole contained 288 churches, and 10,000 houses, besides booths of wood, with a population of 350,000 persons. After the French had defeated the Russians at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BORODINO">Borodino</a>, it appeared necessary to the latter to offer up their capital in order to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> that empire, of which it formed but an inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>. Whether the fires which broke out after the French had entered the city were kindled by that people or by the Russians themselves, has been a subject of animated contest. The fact is notorious that the Russian governor had, two days before the entrance of the enemy, removed all the fire engines, and withdrawn the firemen; and it is no less certain that a whole street, filled with magazines of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> of all kinds, was fired by the owners of them the night after all the carriages had been put in requisition by the commissaries of the French army. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, there is the testimony of many eye-witnesses that numerous houses and wooden booths were set on fire by the French troops, from the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of plunder, from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, from negligence, or from not knowing how to cook their food in the intricacy of the stoves and flues of the Russian houses, which induce many fires even amongst those accustomed to their constant <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. But from whichever cause it arose, more than 500 fires were kindled, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> at the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The burning continued from the evening of the 15th till the 20th of September, during which time 7932 houses were laid in ashes. The Kremlin was designed to have been blown up. by the French on their evacuation of Moscow; but the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> adopted succeeded only partially. The loss of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> occasioned by this catastrophe was estimated, by commissioners appointed to value it, at the sum of L14,500,000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>, although many of those whose losses had been the greatest preferred no claims for indemnification. The rapidity with which Moscow has recovered from its calamity is almost as surprising as the extent of the losses it sustained. It has been again rebuilt, and within ten years there were 11,000 houses and 25,000 inhabitants. It has continued to advance since that time, and the population in 1831 was calculated to exceed by 50,000 persons that of the year 1812, when it was destroyed. In 1826, most of the public buildings had been re-constructed. There were then in the city six cathedrals, twenty-one monasteries, 270 Greek churches, and eight for other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> sects. The Kremlin has been repaired and beautified, at an expense of 500,000 roubles; and it is improved in its appearance by the greater regularity it now presents. The university has been re-established, and the collections, especially of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and of anatomy, have been rendered more select and are much better arranged than formerly. The foundling <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> has been again built, and filled with several thousand children. A new and extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> has been erected, and ornaments the city; it is used as a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> for troops in the very severe <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. It exhibits a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of 580 feet, is forty-five feet in height, and 170 feet in breadth, and is sufficiently capacious for 2000 foot and 1000 <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to be reviewed. The foundation of a new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> was laid in 1817, on the anniversary of the retreat of the French, to be dedicated to the Saviour, and which, when finished, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> be the largest place of worship in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The new city being built on a regular plan, has wider and straighter streets than before; and the private buildings of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> bear a greater proportion to the whole, and exhibit more correct <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. Moscow is in winter the residence of all the great and rich noble families, and whatever splendour they may display is exhibited there. Their palaces are <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, surrounded with gardens, in some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> with parks, and have now received more an Asiatic than an European appearance. Abundant amusements are to be found for the higher classes, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>, balls, concerts, clubs, casinos, freemasons' lodges, icebergs, sledge races, and, though last not least, at various gambling tables. There are 163 taverns, and 120 other public houses, for the reception of travellers; and no less than 607 public <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. There are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, woollen, and cotton, and of all the various <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> which are required by the higher classes, when so rich as many are in Russia, and when but one place in a vast extent of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> can supply them. There is a considerable trade carried on, first with the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on the Baltic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>; secondly, there is the intercourse by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> with Germany; thirdly, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> of commodities with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>; fourthly, the trade with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>; fifthly, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a> by land, carried on along the frontiers of that empire; and, sixthly, the trade with Central <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. These branches, when brought to a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> in Moscow, create great mercantile operations, and may account in some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> for the rapidity with which the re-establishment of this capital of Russia has been accomplished. It is in long. 37° 27' 40" E. and lat. 55° 45' 45" N. Moscow, or Moskva, a government in European Russia. It is so called from the river of that name, which is the most considerable stream in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. It extends from <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> 35° 9' to 38° 35' east, and from latitude 54° 40' to 56° 30' <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and occupies 10,436 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. About two fifths of the surface is wood-land, nearly the same proportion is ploughed land, and the remainder consists of marshes, meadows, gardens, and the sites of the cities, towns, and villages. According to the best Russian accounts, there are within the government 15 cities, 3450 parishes, some of which may be denominated towns, 3058 villages, and 1324 noblemen's mansions and estates. The inhabitants were, in the year 1816, 1,289,823; since that period there has been a rapid increase of population, and, on a fair calculation, it amounted in 1832 to 2,600,000 individuals. These persons are almost all adherents of the Greek church, though some exceptions may be made in the capital, where there are Catholics, Lutherans, Calvinists, and Jews, who are all tolerated, and have their several religious <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>. The whole of the province may be denominated a plain, though it is occasionally interspersed with gentle elevations, or with groups of hills, few of which exceed 200 feet in height. It contains abundance of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>; according to Storch there are no less than 190, but none of these is of any considerable extent. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> river, the Moskwa, is navigable for barges and boats. It is usually frozen from the middle of November till the end of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. The greater part of the rivulets, whether issuing from <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> or from the lakes, contribute to form the stream of that river. The <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a> passes through a small part of the north of the province, and the Oka through a portion of the south. Although the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is of moderate fertility, yet as the population, thin as it is, is more dense than in any of the other provinces, it does not produce corn sufficient for the consumption, but must every year draw a supply from the adjoining districts. The same is the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> with animal food, which is brought to the capital in the winter in a frozen state in great quantities. There are no <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> worked in the province. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> natural productions exported are wood and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>, but the manufactured goods are considerable. These are almost exclusively furnished by the capital, and are noticed under that head. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is severely <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a> in winter, which extends through nearly half the year. It is, however, not unhealthy. The government is divided into thirteen circles.

MOSELLE

Pages 579-580

a department in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of France, formed out of the district of Messin, of French Luxembourg, and of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of German Lorraine. It extends in east <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> from 5° 20' to 7° 45', and in north latitude from 48° 55' to 49° 30'. It is bounded on the north by the department of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Luxembourg, on the east by that duchy and the Bavarian circle of the Rhine, on the south by the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEURTHE">Meurthe</a>, and on the west by that of the Meuse. It extends over 2473 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> 609,000 hectares, which are apportioned in the following manner, viz. 278,920 arable, 48,490 meadows and pastures, 151,365 woods and forests, 4940 vineyards, 10,216 gardens, and the remainder consisting of the course of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, the site of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages, and utterly uncultivated <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, which latter constitutes nearly one fourth of the whole department. The subsoil is generally calcareous, often covered with a heavy clay difficult to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, but in some parts mixed with sand or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and its power of production varies from moderate fertility to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> barrenness. It produces some good wheat and rye, but the corn does not equal the consumption, though the culture of potatoes has been much extended of late years. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> river, the Moselle, which begins to be navigable at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METZ">Metz</a>, and falls into the Rhine at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COBLENZ">Coblenz</a>, receives the waters of the smaller streams. It is a rapid river, often causing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> damage by the overflowing of its banks. Besides the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> grain, much <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> and some <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> are grown. The vine is much cultivated, but the wine is not of a good flavour, as most of that known by the name of Moselle wine throughout <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> grows on the banks of that river after it has quitted the French territory. The hills around Metz have their sides covered with vines, but the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a> are more used for the purposes of making <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> and brandy than wine. There are some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> worked, and the material is converted into heavy <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of ships, and for casting cannon. Some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and woollen cloths are made, and there are fabrics of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, glass, and earthenware. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> amounts to 350,000 persons, who are mostly of the Catholic <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, though there are some few Calvinists, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>, and Jews, mostly in Metz. The French <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> spoken only in the cities. In the villages a patois called Lorraine is most prevalent; but in the eastern part a corrupted German prevails, and the inhabitants have the marks of that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a> in their dress, countenances, and manners. The department sends four deputies to the legislative body. It is divided into four arrondissements, 27 cantons, and 834 communes.

MOSES

Pages 580-581

the son of Amram and Jochebed, was born in the year 1571 before Christ. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, perceiving that the Hebrews had become a formidable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, issued an edict commanding all the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> children to be put to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. To avoid this cruel <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>, Jochebed, the mother of Moses, having concealed her son for three months, at length made an ark <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of bulrushes, daubed it with pitch, laid the child in it, and exposed him on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. Thermuthis, the king's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, who happened to be walking by the river's side, perceived the floating cradle, commanded it to be brought to her, and, being struck with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the child, determined to preserve his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In three years afterwards the princess adopted him as her own son, called his name Moses, and caused him to be diligently instructed in all the learning of the Egyptians. But his father and mother, to whom he was restored by a fortunate accident, were at still greater pains to teach him the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of his fathers. Many things have been related by historians concerning the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of Moses's life, which are not to be found in the Old <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>. According to Josephus and Eusebius, he made <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> upon the Ethiopians, and completely defeated them; and they add, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> Saba, in which the enemy had been forced to take refuge, was betrayed into his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> by the king's daughter, who became deeply enamoured of him, when she beheld from the top of the walls his valorous exploits at the head of the Egyptian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. But as the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this expedition is more than doubtful, we shall confine ourselves to the narrative of Sacred Writ, which commences at the fortieth year of Moses's life. He then left the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Pharaoh, and went to visit his countrymen the Hebrews, who groaned under the tyranny and oppression of their unfeeling masters. Having perceived an Egyptian smiting a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, he killed the Egyptian, and buried him in the sand. But he was obliged, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, to fly into the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Midian, where he married Zipporah, daughter of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> Jethro, by whom he had two sons, Gershom and Eliezer. Here he lived forty years, during which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> he employed himself in tending the flocks of his father-in-<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Having one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> led his flock towards Mount Horeb, God appeared to him in the midst of a bush which burned with fire but was not consumed, and commanded him to go and deliver his brethren from their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a>. Moses at first refused to go, but was at length prevailed on by two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, which the Almighty wrought for his conviction. Upon his return to Egypt, he, together with his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a>, went to the court of Pharaoh, and told him that God commanded him to let the Hebrews go to offer sacrifices in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>. But the impious monarch disregarded this command, and caused the labour of the Israelites to be doubled. The messengers of the Almighty again returned to the king, and wrought a miracle in his sight, that they might move his heart, and induce him to let the people depart. Aaron having <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his miraculous rod, it was immediately converted into a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>; but the same thing being performed by the magicians, the king's heart was more and more hardened, and his obstinacy at last drew down the judgments of the Almighty upon his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, which was afflicted with ten dreadful plagues. The first was the changing of the waters of the Nile and of all the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> into blood, so that the Egyptians died of thirst. In consequence of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol14.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, the land was covered with innumerable swarms of frogs, which entered even into Pharaoh's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. By the third plague the dust was converted into <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a>, which cruelly tormented both <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> and beast. The fourth plague consisted of a multitude of destructive flies which spread throughout Egypt, and infested the whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The fifth was a sudden pestilence, which destroyed all the cattle of the Egyptians, without injuring those of the Israelites. The sixth produced numberless ulcers and fiery boils both upon man and upon beast. The seventh was a dreadful storm of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIL">hail</a>, accompanied with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, which destroyed every thing that was in the field, whether man or beast, and spared only the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel dwelt. By the eighth plague swarms of locusts were brought into the country, which devoured every green <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, the fruit of the trees, and the produce of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. By the ninth plague thick darkness covered all the land of Egypt, excepting the dwellings of the children of Israel. The tenth and last plague was the death of the first-born in Egypt, who were all in one night cut off by the destroying angel, from the first-born of the king to the first-born of the slaves and of the cattle. This dreadful calamity moved the heart of the hardened Pharaoh, and he at length consented to allow the people of Israel to depart from his kingdom. Profane authors who have spoken of Moses appear to have been in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> acquainted with these mighty wonders. That he performed miracles, has been allowed by many, by whom he was considered as a famous magician; and he could scarcely appear in any other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to men who did not acknowledge him as the messenger of the Almighty. Both Diodorus and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> mention the distressed state to which Egypt was reduced by these terrible calamities. The Hebrews, amounting to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of six hundred thousand men, without reckoning women and children, left Egypt on the fifteenth day of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> Nisan, which, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of this deliverance, was thenceforth reckoned the first month of their year. Scarcely had they reached the shore of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, when Pharaoh with a powerful army set out in pursuit of them. On this occasion Moses stretched forth his rod upon the sea; and the waters thereof being divided, remained suspended on both sides till the Hebrews passed through dry footed. The Egyptians determined to follow the same course; but God caused a violent <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> to blow, which brought back the waters to their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and the whole army of Pharaoh perished in the waves. After the miraculous passage of the Red Sea, the army proceeded towards Mount <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a>, and arrived at Marah, where the waters were bitter; but Moses, by casting a tree into them, rendered them fit for drinking. Their tenth encampment was at Rephidim, where Moses drew <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> from the rock in Horeb, by smiting it with his rod. Here likewise Amalek attacked Israel. Whilst Joshua fought against the Amalekites, Moses stood upon the top of a hill, and lifted up his hands, in consequence of which the Israelites prevailed, and cut their enemies in pieces. They at length arrived at the foot of Mount Sinai on the third day of the ninth month after their departure from Egypt. Moses having ascended several times into the mount, received the law from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of God himself in the midst of thunders and lightnings, and concluded the famous covenant between the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> and the children of Israel. When he descended from Sinai, he found that the people had fallen into the idolatrous worship of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> calf. The messenger of God, shocked at such ingratitude, broke in pieces the tables of the law which he carried in his hands, and put twenty-three thousand of the transgressors to the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. He afterwards re-ascended the mountain, and there obtained new tables of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, upon which the law was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a>. But when he descended, his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> shone so that the Israelites dared not to come nigh unto him, and he was obliged to cover it with a veil. The Israelites were here employed in constructing the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a>, according to a pattern shown them by God. It was erected and consecrated at the foot of Mount Sinai, on the first day of the first month of the second year after their departure from Egypt; and it served the Israelites instead of a temple till the time of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>, who built a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for the God of his fathers, after a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODEL">model</a> shown him by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>. Moses having dedicated the tabernacle, consecrated Aaron and his sons to be its ministers, and appointed the Levites to its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. He likewise gave various commandments concerning the worship of God and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Jews. This was a theocracy in the fullest <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the word. God himself governed them immediately by means of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> Moses, whom he had chosen to be the interpreter of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> to the people; and he required all the honours belonging to their king to be paid to himself. He dwelt in his tabernacle, which was situated in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, like a monarch in his palace; he gave answers to those who consulted him, and himself denounced <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> against the transgressors of his laws. This was properly the time of the theocracy, taken in its full extent; for God was not only considered as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> who formed the object of their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship, but as the sovereign to whom the honours of supreme majesty were paid. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> was nearly the same under Joshua, who, being filled with the spirit of Moses, undertook nothing without consulting God. Every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, both of the leader and of the people, was regulated by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the Almighty, who rewarded their fidelity and obedience by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of miracles, victories, and successes. After Moses had regulated every thing regarding the civil administration and the marching of the troops, he led the Israelites to the confines of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>, to the foot of Mount Nebo; and here the Lord commanded him to ascend into the mountain, whence he showed him the promised land, into which he was not permitted to enter. He immediately afterwards yielded up the ghost, without sickness or pain, in the one hundred and twentieth year of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and 1451 years before <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ. Moses is incontestably the author of the first five books of the Old Testament, which go by the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, and which are acknowledged to be inspired, by the Jews, and by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of every persuasion. Some, however, have denied that Moses was the author of these books, and have founded their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> on this, that he always speaks of himself in the third person. But this manner of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> is by no means peculiar to Moses; it occurs also in several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> historians, such as Xenophon, Caesar, Josephus, and others, who, possessed of more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> or good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> than some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> historians, whose egotism is altogether disgusting, have not, like them, left to posterity a spectacle of ridiculous vanity and self-conceit. After all, it is proper to observe, that profane authors have related many falsehoods and absurdities concerning Moses, and also concerning the origin and the religion of the Jews, with which they were in fact but little acquainted. Plutarch, in his book concerning Isis and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, says, that Judeus and Hierosolymus were brothers, and descended from Typhon; and that the former gave his name to the country and its inhabitants, and the latter to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city. Others allege that they came from Mount Ida in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>. Strabo is the only author who speaks anything like reason and truth concerning them; although he too says that they were descended from the Egyptians, and considers Moses their <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a> to have been an Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOSHAISK">Moshaisk</a> priest. He acknowledges, however, that they were a people strictly <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> and sincerely religious. Other authors by whom they are mentioned appear not to have had the smallest acquaintance either with their laws or with their worship; and frequently confound them with the Christians, as is the case with Juvenal, Tacitus, and Quintilian.

MOSHAISK

Pages 581-581

a circle of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>, in Russia, extending over 630 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, and comprehending one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, one market-town, and 264 villages, with 56,530 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is the city of the same name, situated on the Moshaiska. It is fortified, and has a strong citadel. It was burned <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the retreat of the French in 1812, but has been since rebuilt and improved. It contains <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> churches, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, 670 houses, and 4240 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 27° 50'. E. Lat. 55° 40'. N.

MOSHEIM

Pages 581-581

John Laurence, an illustrious German divine, was born in 1695. He was descended of a noble family, which might seem to open to his ambition a fair path to civil promotion; but his zeal for the interests of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, his thirst of knowledge, and particularly his <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for sacred literature, induced him to consecrate his talents to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The German <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> loaded him with literary honours; the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> induced him to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a> called him thence to Helmstadt, where he filled the academical <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, was honoured with the character of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> counsellor to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and presided over the seminaries of learning in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Wolfenbuttel and in the principality of Blackenburg. When a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was formed of giving an uncommon <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of lustre to the university of Göttingen, by filling it with men of the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in letters, Dr Mosheim was deemed worthy to appear at the head of it, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>; and here he died, in the year 1755, universally lamented. In depth of judgment, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of learning, in purity of taste, in power of eloquence, and in laborious application to all the various branches of erudition and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, he had certainly few superiors. His Latin translation of Cudworth's Intellectual System, enriched with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> annotations, discovered a profound acquaintance with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> learning and philosophy. His illustrations of the Scriptures, his labours in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Christianity, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> he threw upon religion and philosophy, appear in many volumes of sacred and profane literature; whilst his Ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, from the birth of Christ to the beginning of the eighteenth century, is unquestionably the best that has yet appeared. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, written in Latin, has been translated into English, and accompanied with notes and chronological tables by Dr Archibald Maclean; and from the translator's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition, 1758, in five vols. 8vo, this short account is taken.

MOSQUE

Pages 581-582

a temple <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship amongst the Mahommedans. All mosques are <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> buildings, generally constructed of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. Before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> gate there is a square <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> paved with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, and low galleries round it, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of which is supported by marble pillars. In these galleries the Turks wash themselves before they go into the mosque. In each mosque there is a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of lamps; and between these are suspended many crystal rings, ostrich eggs, and other curiosities, which, when the lamps are lighted, make a fine show. As it is not lawful to enter the mosque with stockings or shoes on, the pavements are covered with pieces of stuff sewed together, each being wide enough to hold a row of men kneeling, sitting, or prostrate. The women are not allowed to enter the mosque, but remain in the porches without. About every mosque there are six <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> towers, called minarets, each of which has three little open galleries, one above another; these towers, as well as the mosques, are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and adorned with gilding and other or- nments; and from them the people are summoned to prayers by certain officers appointed for the purpose, called muezzins. Most of the mosques have a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> belonging to them, in which travellers, of whatsoever <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> they may be, are entertained three days. Each mosque has also a place called tarbe, which is the burying-place of its founders; within it there is a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> six or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>, covered with green velvet or satin; at the ends are two tapers, and round it several seats for those who read the Koran and offer up prayers for the souls of the deceased. MOSQUITO SHORE. See the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> GUATEMALA and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONDURAS">HONDURAS</a>.

MOSS

Pages 582-583

a name given to swampy ground, which is otherwise called a fen <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> bog. In many of these grounds, as well in England and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> as in other parts of the world, there are found vast numbers of trees with their stumps erect, and their roots piercing the ground in a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> posture, as when growing. Many of these trees are broken or cut off near the roots, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> along, for the most <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. Some persons, in attempting to account for this, have resolved it into the effect of the Deluge; but this is a very wild conjecture, and is proved to be groundless by many unanswerable arguments. The waters of this deluge might indeed have washed together a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of trees, and buried them under loads of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; but then they would have lain irregularly and at random, whereas they all lie lengthwise from south-west to north-east, and the roots all stand in their natural perpendicular posture, as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> as the roots of trees in a forest. Besides, these trees are not all in their natural state. Many of them bear evident marks of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> workmanship, some being cut <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with an axe, others split, and the wedges still remaining in them; some burned in different parts, and others bored through with holes. These things are also proved to be of a later <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> than the Deluge, by other matters found amongst them, such as utensils of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> people, and coins of the Roman emperors. It appears from the whole, that all the trees which we find in this fossil state grew originally in the very places where we now find them, and have been only thrown down and buried there, not brought from elsewhere. It may indeed appear an objection to this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that most of these fossil trees are of the fir kind, and that Cæsar says expressly that no firs grew in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but this is easily answered, by observing, that these trees, though of the fir kind, are not of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> usually called the fir, but pitch-tree; and Cæsar has nowhere said that pitch-trees did not grow in England, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> abound with these trees; and there are still forests of them in many parts of Scotland, and a number of them upon a hill in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a> to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. It is also objected by some to the system of the firs having grown where they are found fossil, that these countries are all bogs and moors, whereas such trees grow only in mountainous places. But this is founded on an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>; for although in Norway and Sweden, and some other <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a> countries, the fir kinds all grow upon barren and dry <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROCKY_MOUNTAINS">rocky <a class=</a>"xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, yet in warmer countries they are found to thrive as well upon wet plains. They are found plentifully in Pomerania, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>; and in the western parts of New England there are vast numbers of fine stately trees of this kind in low grounds. The <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> seems to be, that these trees <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, such as is found at the bottoms of all the mosses where they are found fossil. The roots of the fir kind are almost always found fixed in these; and those of oaks, where they are discovered fossil in this manner, are usually found fixed in clay; so that each kind of tree is always found rooted in the places where they stand in their proper soil; and there is no doubt but that they originally grew there. Having thus found that all the fossil trees which we meet with once grew in the places where they are now buried, we may conclude that in these places there were once noble forests, which have, by some accident, been destroyed; and the only question that remains is, how and by whom this was effected. We have reason to believe, from the Roman coins found amongst them, that it was done by the people of that empire, at the time when they were established or establishing themselves here. Their own historians tell us, that when their armies pursued the wild Britons, these people always sheltered themselves in the boggy woods and low watery forests. Cæsar expressly mentions this, observing, that Cassibelannus and his Britons, after their defeat, passed the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, and fled into such low morasses and woods that there was no pursuing them; and we are informed that the Silures secured themselves in the same manner when attacked by Ostorius and Agricola. The same thing is recorded of Venutius <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Brigantes, who, to secure himself, fled into the boggy forests of the midland part of this <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and Herodian expressly states, that in the time when the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were pushing their conquests in these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, it was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the Britons to secure themselves in the thick forests which grew in boggy and wet places, and, when opportunity offered, to issue out thence and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon the invaders. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of all this was the destruction of these forests. The Romans, finding themselves so plagued with parties of the natives issuing out upon them at all times from these forests, gave orders for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> down and destroying all the forests in Britain which grew on boggy and wet grounds. These orders were punctually executed; and to this it is owing that at the present day we can hardly be brought to believe that such forests ever grew in our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> as are now found buried in morasses. The Roman historians all agree, that when Suetonius <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAULINUS">Paulinus</a> conquered <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANGLESEY">Anglesey</a>, he ordered all the woods to be cut down there, in the same manner as the Roman generals had done in England; and Galen tells us, that the Romans, after their conquest in Britain, kept their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> constantly employed in cutting down forests, draining marshes, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PAVING">paving</a> bogs. And not only were the Roman soldiers employed in this manner, but all the native Britons made captives in the wars were obliged to assist in it; and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DION">Dion</a> Cassius informs us, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Severus lost no fewer than fifty thousand men in a short time in cutting down the woods and in draining the bogs of this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. It is not to be wondered at that such numbers executed the immense destruction of which we find <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> in these buried forests. One of the greatest subterranean treasures of wood is that near <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HATFIELD">Hatfield</a>; and it is easy to prove that the people to whom this havoc has been attributed were upon the spot where these trees now lie buried. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-ROAD">road</a> of the Romans from the south to the north proceeded from Lindum or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a> to Segelocum or Little Burrow upon <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, and thence to Danum or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DONCASTER">Doncaster</a>, where they kept a standing garrison of Crispinian <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. A little off on the east and north-east of their road, between the two last-named <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, lay the borders of the great forest, which swarmed with wild Britons, who were continually sallying out, and retreating to it again; intercepting their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, taking and destroying their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>, killing their allies and passengers, and disturbing their garrisons. This at length exasperated the Romans so much, that they determined to destroy it; and to do this safely and effectually, they marched against it with a great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and encamped on a great moor not far from Finningly. This is evident from their fortifications yet remaining. There is a small town in the neighbourhood called Otterfield; and as the termination field seems to have been given only in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of battles fought near the towns whose names have this termination, it is not improbable that a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> was fought here between all the Britons who inhabited this forest and the Roman troops under Ostro-rius. The Romans slew many of the Britons, and drove the rest back into the forest, which at that time over- spread all the low country. On this the conquerors, tak- ing advantage of a strong south-west <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, set fire to the pitch-trees, of which the forest was principally composed; and when the greater part of the trees were thus destroy- ed, the Roman soldiers and captive Britons cut down the re- mainder, excepting a few <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ones, which they left stand- ing as memorials of the destruction of the rest. These single trees, however, could not stand <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> against the winds, but falling into the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> which run through the country, interrupted their currents; and the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> then overspreading the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> country, formed one great lake, and gave origin to the mosses or moory bogs, which were af- terwards formed there by the workings of the waters, the precipitation of earthy <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> from them, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> of rotten boughs and branches of trees, and the vast in- crease of water-moss and other such <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which grow in prodigious abundance in all these sorts of places. Thus were these burned and felled trees buried under a newly- formed spongy and watery earth, and afterwards found on draining and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> through this deposit. Hence it need not appear strange that Roman weapons and Roman coins are found amongst these buried trees; and hence also it is that amongst the buried trees some are found burned, some chopped and hewn; that the bodies of the trees all lie by their proper roots, and with their tops lying north-east, that is, in the direction in which a south-west wind would have blown them down; and that some of the trees are found with their roots lying flat, these being not cut nor burned down, but blown up by the roots afterwards when left single. It is not wonderful, that such trees as these should have <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to grow even after their fall, and to shoot up branches from their sides which might easily grow into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> trees. By this system it is also easily explained why the moor- <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> soil in the country is in some places two or three yards thicker than in others, or higher than it formerly was, since the growing up of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PEAT">peat</a>-earth or bog-ground is well known, and the soil added by the overflowing of waters is by no means inconsiderable. As the Romans destroyed this great and noble forest, so they probably also destroyed several other ancient fo- rests, the ruins of which furnish the bog-wood of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a>- shire, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, and other counties. But as the Romans were not much in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, or in Ireland, it is not to be supposed that forests cut down by these people gave origin to the fossil wood found there; but although they did not cut down these forests, others did, and the origin of the bog-wood is the same with them as it is with us. Holingshed informs us, that Ed- <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARD">ward</a> I. being unable to get at the Welsh because of their hiding in boggy woods, gave orders that these should all be destroyed by fire and by the axe; and doubtless the roots and bodies of trees found in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PEMBROKESHIRE">Pembrokeshire</a> under ground are the remains of the execution of this order. The fossil wood in the bogs of the Isle of Man is doubt- less of the same origin, although we have not any account extant of the time nor the occasion of the forests there being destroyed; but as to the fossil trees of the bogs of Ireland, we are expressly told that Henry II. when he conquered that country, ordered all the woods to be cut down that grew in the low parts of it, in order to secure his conquests, by cutting away the places of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> for rebels.

MOSTRA

Pages 583-583

in the Italian music, a mark at the end of a line <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> space, to show that the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of the next line is in that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> this note be accompanied with a sharp or flat, it is proper to place these <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> along with the mostra.

MOSUL

Pages 583-583

a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Asiatic <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, which, al- though lying almost in the very heart of the pachalik of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, forms of itself, with a small territory, not extending more than two miles on each side of the town, an inde- pendent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, under the order of a pasha of two tails. It is situated on the western <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Tigris, on ground so low that the river, which is nearly 100 yards wide, and flows with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> rapidity, often rises to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the houses. The houses are built partly of brick and partly of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and the roofs and even the ceilings of the apart- ments are vaulted, owing to the scarcity and dearness of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>.
