CAIUS, surnamed Codrus, and afterwards Scævola, was one of the illustrious Roman family of the Mutili, and rendered his name famous in the war between Porsenna king of Tuscany and the Romans. That prince having resolved to restore the family of Tarquin the Proud, went to besiege Rome in the year 507 before Christ; but Mutius determined to sacrifice himself for the safety of his country, and boldly entering the enemy's camp, killed Porsenna's secretary, whom he took for Porsenna himself. Being seized and brought before Porsenna, he told the king boldly, that three hundred young men like himself had sworn to murder him; "but since this hand has missed thee," continued he, "it must be punished;" then putting his right hand on the burning coals, he let it burn with such constancy as astonished the beholders. MUTIUS Scævola, Q. surnamed the Augur, was an excellent civilian, and instructed Cicero in the laws. He was made praetor in Asia, and afterwards became consul, when he performed important services for the republic. He must not be confounded with Quintus Mutius Scævola, another excellent civilian, who was praetor in Asia, tribune of the people, and at length consul, 95 before Christ. He governed Asia with such prudence and equity, that his example was proposed to the governors who were sent into the provinces. Cicero says of him, that he was the most eloquent orator of all the civilians, and the most able civilian of all the orators. He was assassinated in the temple of Vesta during the wars of Marius and Sylla, eighty-two years before Christ.

MUTTON

Pages 660-660

the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of a sheep after the animal has been killed. Mutton has been <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> preferred to the flesh of all <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>; and, indeed, besides being more perfect, it has the advantage of being more generally suited to different climates, whereas beef, for instance, requires a very nice intermediate state, which it seems to attain chiefly in England; for although Scotland supplies what are reckoned the best cattle, it is in the rich English pastures that they are brought to perfection. But the sheep can be brought almost to the same perfection in this northern region as in the southern countries.

MUTUAL

Pages 660-660

a relative <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a>, denoting something that is <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> between two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> more persons. Thus we say, mutual assistance, mutual aversion. There are mutual or reciprocal duties, offices, and the like, between superiors and inferiors, as the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> and his subjects, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and his servants, &c. Vaugelas makes a distinction between mutual and reciprocal; mutual, according to him, being understood of what is between two only; and reciprocal, of what is between more than two. But this distinction is little regarded in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> usage.

MUTULE

Pages 660-660

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> modillion set under the cornice of the Doric order.

MUTUNUS

Pages 660-660
or MUTINUS, in fabulous history, a deity amongst the Romans, similar to the Priapus of the Greeks. MUZZLE of a Gun or Mortar, the extremity at which the powder and ball is put in; and hence the muzzle ring is the metallic circle or moulding which surrounds the mouth of the piece.

MYAGRUS DEUS

Pages 661-661

in the heathen <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, a name sometimes given to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and sometimes to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, on occasion of sacrifices being offered to them for driving away the vast numbers of flies which infested the victims on certain public occasions. The word is usually spelt Myagrus; but this must be an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, as the word does not express the "fly-destroyer," but the "mouse-destroyer," and it is sufficiently testified by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, that flies were the only creatures against whom this deity was invoked. Pliny calls this deity Myiodes, and tells us that the flies which used to pester the Olympic <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> went away in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> on the sacrificing of a bull to this god. We find in Athenæus, also, that this sacrificing to the god of flies at the Olympic games was a constant <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>. Some authors distinguish these two deities, and tell us that the latter, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Myiodes, used to visit the nations in vengeance with a vast multitude of flies, and that, upon paying him the due honours of a sacrifice, they all went away again; and this seems to agree with what Pliny mentions in several places. At the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Olympic games, Jupiter was worshipped under the name of Apomous or Myiogruss Deus, and supplicated to effect the destruction of these troublesome creatures. This happened only once in many years, when the sacrifices were performed there; but the Elians worshipped him continually under this name, deprecating the vengeance of heaven, which usually sent, towards the latter end of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> (as they expressed it) an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of flies and other insects, which infested the whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> with sickness and pestilence.

MYCALE

Pages 660-661

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> and mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, and also a promontory of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, opposite <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAMOS">Samos</a>, celebrated for a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> which was fought there between the Greeks and Persians about the year of Rome 275. The Persians, about 100,000 strong, had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> returned from the unsuccessful expedition of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; and having drawn their ships to the shore, they had fortified themselves strongly, as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> determined to support a siege. They suf- suffered the Greeks to disembark from their fleet without the least molestation, and were soon obliged to give way before the cool and resolute intrepidity of an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men. The Greeks obtained a complete victory, slaughtered some thousands of the enemy, burned their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, and sailed back to Samos with an immense booty, in which were seventy chests of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONEY">money</a>.

MYCENAE

Pages 661-661

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Argolis, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the Argives was divided into two portions by Acrisius and his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Proetus, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> and Mycenae were their capitals. These, as belonging to the same family, and distant only about fifty stadia, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> six miles and a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> from each other, had one tutelary deity, Juno, and they were <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> proprietors of her temple, the Heraeum, which was near Mycenae. It was here that Agamemnon reigned. He enlarged his dominions by his valour and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, and possessed, besides Mycenae, the region about Corinth and Sicyon, and that which was afterwards denominated Achaea. On his return from <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, he was slain with his companions at a banquet. Mycenae then declined, and under the Heraclidae was made subject to Argos. The Mycenaean, having furnished eighty men, partook with the Lacedaemonians in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> acquired at Thermopylae. The jealousy of the Argives produced the destruction of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, which was abandoned after a siege, and laid waste in the first year of the seventy-eighth Olympiad, or 466 years before Christ. Some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the wall remained in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, with a gate, upon which were lions, a fountain, the subterranean edifices where Atreus and his sons had deposited their treasures, and, amongst various sepulchral monuments, one of Agamemnon, and another of his fellow-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> and sufferers.

MYCONDAH

Pages 661-661

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the territories of the rajah of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MYSORE">Mysore</a>. It is of some importance, as it is placed at the entrance of a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-westward into the valley of Chittendroog, which it is intended to defend. It is 188 miles N.N.W. from Seringapatam. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 76. 10. E. Lat. 14. 16. N.

MYCONE

Pages 661-661

an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, situated in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 25. 51. E., lat. 37. 28. N. It is about thirty-six miles in circuit, and has a town of the same name.

MYCONUS

Pages 661-661

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> called Cyclades, near Delos, under which the last of the centaurs slain by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> are feigned to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> buried. Hence the proverb, Omnia sub umum Myconum congerere, applied to an injudicious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> unnatural affiance.

MYDAN

Pages 661-661

a small district in the Afghan <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Kabul, situated between the 33d and 34th degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude.

MYIODES DEUS

Pages 661-661

in the heathen <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, a name sometimes given to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, but more frequently to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, to whom a bull was sacrificed, in order to render him propitious in driving away the flies which infested the Olympic games.

MYLASA

Pages 661-661
or Mylassa, in Ancient Geography, a noble city of Caria, in Asia Minor, situated about three leagues from the Sinus Ceramicus. It was the capital of Hecatomnus, king of Caria, and father of Mausolus. Pliny, speaking of Menander king of Caria, says that the Rhodians preserved with the greatest care his portrait painted by Apelles. But it was not in honour of this Menander that a Corinthian pillar was erected at Mylasa, which still exists, and on which is to be seen the following inscription: "The people erected this pillar in honour of Menander, the son of Uliades, and grandson of Euthydemus, the benefactor of his country, and whose ancestors also rendered it great services." Caria was taken by Mithridates, and afterwards by Labienus, whose father had been one of Caesar's generals. Hybris, whose eloquence and valour deservedly entitled him to a distinguished rank amongst his countrymen, in vain encouraged them to make an obstinate defence whilst it was besieged by the latter. He himself was obliged to yield to necessity, and to take refuge at Rhodes; but scarcely had the conqueror quitted the city, when Hybris returned and restored liberty to his country; and, not content with rendering it this service, he also destroyed the power of a dangerous citizen, whose riches and talents had rendered him a necessary evil. Euthydemus, often banished, and as often recalled, but always too powerful in a state the independence of which he threatened, saw his ambition checked by the zeal and activity of Hybris. The Romans left to Mylasa that liberty of which it rendered itself so worthy by the great efforts it made to preserve it. Pliny calls it Mylasa liberaria; and Strabo informs us that it was one of the most magnificent cities of antiquity, the temples, porticoes, and other public monuments of which were highly admired. This city is now called Melassos. When Pocock visited this place it was perfect and entire; but at present no traces of it remain.

MYLAU

Pages 661-661

a town of the circle of Voigtsland, in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, on the river Golzsch. It contains 240 houses, and 1790 inhabitants, who are chiefly employed in making muslins and cotton goods.

MYMUNSING

Pages 661-662

a district of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, situated between the 24th and 28th degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. The boundaries of this territory are the Garrow <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a> and the district of Rungpoor on the north, Dacca Jelalpoor on the south, Silket and Tipperah on the east, and Ranjeshy and Dinagepoor on the west. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is intersected by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> river Brahmapootra, into which flow innumerable streams from both sides; and, owing to the flatness of the country, it is liable to inundations during the rainy seasons. It produces in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> very abundant crops of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, of a coarse <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, which is its staple produce. Some parts of the country are overrun with wood <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> jungle, and are but thinly inhabited. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town is Bygonbary, which is the residence of the judge and collector, who are subordinate to MYO <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">ISLE</a> the Dacca <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of circuit. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> consists of pretty nearly equal numbers of Hindus and Mahomedans. According to a census taken by orders of the Marquis Wellesley in 1801, the population amounts to 600,000.

MYO ISLE

Pages 662-662

a small <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> situated in the Eastern Seas, in the Molucca passage, which separates <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CELEBES">Celebes</a> and Gilolo. The inhabitants, by whom it was occupied whilst the Portuguese held the Moluccas, were expelled by the Dutch, lest it should become a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for the smuggling of spices. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 126. 15. E. Lat. 1. 23. N.

MYOLOGY

Pages 662-662

in anatomy, signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the muscles, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> the knowledge of what relates to the muscles of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. See ANATOMY.

MYRIAPODA

Pages 662-664

A wingless tribe of insects, formerly so called, of which centipedes (the genus Scolopendra of Linnæus) form the most characteristic example, are now regarded as a separate class of the articulated tribes, in conformity with the views of Dr Leach and other writers who have studied their structure and economy. Under this <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, therefore, as formerly intimated, we shall present the reader with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> notice of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> genera, of which the prevailing forms have been already exhibited (in connection with our representations of insects) on Plate CCXXXIX. of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>. We owe the establishment of the class to Dr Leach, M. Lamarck having viewed the Myriapoda as arachnides, while M. Latreille, except in a single work, regarded them as true insects. As such they were likewise included by Linnæus, and the older systematic writers, in the order Aptera. The Myriapoda are distinguished from true insects by their greater amount of feet (twenty-four and upwards); by the want of any precise <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> appreciable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> into thorax and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>, and by the numerous segments into which their bodies are divided. Each segment, with the exception of the first, is furnished with a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of legs, terminated for the most <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> by a single hook. The stigmata, or openings for respiration, are placed on each <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> segment, a circumstance which has induced some observers to regard the latter as only semi-segments, in as far as in true insects each <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> has its pair of stigmata. But we see no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for the establishment of any strict <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> of form between the subjects of two distinct classes of articulated beings; and indeed, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we do so in regard to the character in question, we produce a greater discordance by the necessity, in that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a>, of assigning to each so-called (<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>) segment, a couple of pair of legs. The mandibles are bi-articulate, and are followed by a piece in the form of a labium, quadrifid, with articulated divisions resembling little feet, and corresponding in position to the lamellae of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CRUSTACEA">Crustacea</a>. Then succeed two pair of small feet, of which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, sometimes hook-shaped, seem to replace the four maxillæ of the last-named order, or the two maxillæ and the lower lip of insects. They may be regarded as maxillary feet. The antennæ are two in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. Their form cannot be easily generalised, because, although they may often be, as Latreille says, "courtes, un peu plus grosses vers le bout, ou presque filiformes;" yet in some (genus Scutigera) they are very <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and become much more slender towards the extremity. The number of the articulations also varies greatly. The organs of vision are usually formed by a union of smooth or simple eyes; but in some these parts are analogous to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> eyes of insects, the facettes, however, being proportionally larger, rounder, and more distinct. All Myriapodes are apterous. The subjects of our present notice differ likewise from insects in this remarkable peculiarity, that the number of their segments, and consequently of the stigmata and legs, increases with the size of the individual. It would even appear, from the observations of Savi the younger, that the genus Julus is born without feet; from which it has been observed, that those Myriapodes are subject, at some early <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of their lives, to a regular metamorphosis. Degeer had long before observed, that the number of their parts increased with the general growth of the body. The organs of respiration consist of two principal tracheæ extending <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> along the body, and receiving <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> from the lateral spiracles. Myriapodes are generally supposed to be longer lived, and of more continuous growth, than insects; and, according to Savi the younger, two years elapse (at least in the genus Julus) before the development of the generative system; but it must be borne in mind, that many insects exist for a length of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the larva state (to which the early condition of the Myriapodes so closely corresponds), and are thus of equal <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONGEVITY">longevity</a> with the many-footed subjects of our present inquiry. The Myriapodes in general shun the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. They conceal themselves under <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, beneath the bark of trees, among old <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, and in various other localities. Some inhabit <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and others are destructive to culinary vegetables. Many are carnivorous, seizing upon animal substances, both dead and living, with their curved jaws. They are said to infuse a poisonous juice into their wounded victims. In our subdivision of the class, as in the preceding generalities, we shall follow the system of Latreille, by whom the Myriapodes are partitioned into two primary groups, which differ from each other both in habits and structure. ORDER I.—CHILOGNATHA. This primary <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GROUP">group</a> corresponds to the genus Julus of Linnæus. The body is for the most part cylindrical, and of a crustaceous consistence. The antennæ are composed of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, of nearly equal size. The mandibles are thick, without palpi, distinctly divided into two portions by a median articulation, and with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> implanted in a concavity of their upper extremity. Beneath is a kind of labium or lower lip, divided at its exterior surface, by --- 1 See the article Entomology of this work, vol. ix. p. 59, foot <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. 2 Linn. Trans. xx. 376. 3 Memorie Scientifique, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>, 1822. notches and longitudinal sections, into four principal areas, tuberculated on the upper margin, and of which the two intermediate are short and narrow, and placed at the upper extremity of another <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>, which serves them as a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> base. The feet are very short, and always terminate in a single hook; four anterior feet placed immediately beneath the labium, resemble the others in form, but are more approximate at their base, with the radical <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> proportionally longer. Most of the other legs are attached by double pairs to a single segment of the body. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> organs are placed beneath the seventh pair of legs, those of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> behind the second pair. The stigmata, as usually described, are very small, and placed on alternate segments outside the origin of the legs. The Myriapodes of this division are slow of movement, and advance, as it were, by a gliding <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. They assume in defense a round or spiral form. The first segment of the body, in some the second, is larger than the others, and presents the form of a corselet or buckler. The double pairs of legs do not occur until we reach the fourth, fifth, or sixth pair; the first three or four pair being free from their origin, or adhering to their respective segments only by a median or sternal line. The two or three terminal segments of the body are usually without feet. On each side of the body there is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of pores, formerly regarded as stigmata, but which, according to M. Savi, merely emit an acid liquor of disagreeable odour, and probably intended as a means of defense; the true stigmata, or respiratory openings, as described by the Italian naturalist, being placed on the sternal piece of each segment, and communicating internally with a double series of pneumatic pouches, disposed en chapelet along the body, and giving out tracheal branches, which ramify over the other organs. These pouches or vesicular tracheae, according to M. Straus, are not connected with each other, as among ordinary insects, by a principal trachea. The form of the newly-hatched bodies of the Iulide, as observed by M. Savi in the vicinity of Pisa, was somewhat kidney-shaped, quite plain, and without appendages. After the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a> of eighteen days they underwent their first moult, and only then assumed the form of the adults; but they were still composed of only twenty-two segments, and the total number of their legs amounted to twenty-six pair. These observations are in some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> inconsistent with the assertion of Degger, who in the young state of these creatures counted only three pair of legs and eight segments: but is it certain, asks M. Latreille, that the moult described by M. Savi was actually the first; or ought we not rather to presume that they do not <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> suddenly from an apodal state to the possession of twenty-six pair of legs? In other words, that they are subject to certain intermediate changes, which may have escaped the observation of M. Savi? After the second moult, however, the last-named naturalist informs us, the genus Iulus exhibits thirty-six pair of legs, and after the third, forty-three, and the body then consists of thirty segments. In the adult state the number is considerably increased. Two years afterwards another moult takes <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and it is only then that the generative system is developed. From the period of birth, which takes place in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, the renewals of the skin were observed by M. Savi to take place almost monthly till November, and the exuviae were seen to contain even the membrane which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> the interior of the alimentary canal and tracheae. The organs of the mouth were the only parts not there observed by M. Savi. The food of these Myriapodes consists both of animal and vegetable substances, generally dead and decomposed. They deposit a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number of eggs. The generic groups are as follows. We shall enter into few details, as we have illustrated so many of the prevailing forms by means of accurate figures. **Genus Glomeris**, Lat. Body convex above, concave below, with a range of small scales along the lower sides. It is composed of twelve segments, exclusive of the head. The male has thirty-two legs, the female thirty-four. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> are not numerous. Although *G. octatus* inhabits the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, the greater proportion are terrestrial, occurring under stones, particularly in mountainous countries. *G. margaritata* (Plate CCXXXIX, fig. 1) is common in most European countries. **Genus Iulus**, Lat. Body cylindrical and extended, without any projecting <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CRESTS">crests</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> margins. The larger species are terrestrial, and live in woods; the smaller attack fruits, roots, and various <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> produce, to some of which they are very destructive. They all assume a spiral position in repose or when alarmed; the head being placed in the centre. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIOR">Prior</a> to the time of Latreille, this entire division was included under the genus *Iulus*, Linn. But the French naturalist restricted the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> to the cylindrical species, and formed of the others his genera *Glomeris*, *Polydesmus*, *Polyzonus*. Various species are described by Dr Leach, in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> which stands in need of revision. We have here figured *I. sabulosus*, a common European species, Plate CCXXXIX, fig. 3. A monstrous Myriapod is mentioned by Ulloa as inhabiting the district of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>. He describes it (if his terms have not been mistranslated) as sometimes extending a yard in length, and measuring five inches across. Here there is no doubt some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> exaggeration. He adds that its bite is mortal, if a timely remedy be not applied. From its cylindrical form it has been regarded as an *Iulus*. **Genus Polydesmus**, Lat. Body linear, the segments compressed on the under surface, with projecting ridges on the upper, somewhat in the form of transverse <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> scales. The species of this genus, of which our *Iulus complanatus*, Linn. may be regarded as the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TYPE">type</a> (Plate CCXXXIX, fig. 2), dwell under stones in dampish places. They assume the spiral form when touched, and feed both on animal and vegetable matters in a state of decomposition. Certain other species, of which the eyes are obvious, form the genus *Craspedosoma* of Dr Leach. **Genus Polyzonus**, Lat. Body soft, membranous, terminated by a tuft of lengthened scales. The only species of which we have any knowledge is the *Pol. legurus*, Lat. (Plate CCXXXIX, fig. 5), regarded as a scolopendra by the generality of systematic authors, and described by Degger under the name of *Iule d <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-QUEUE">queue</a> pinceuse*. It is a very small creature, of rather singular aspect. Our magnified representation <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> referred to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the necessity of descriptive details. Its early organization is less complicated than that of the adult state; that is, the young consist of fewer segments and a less number of legs. We know little of its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> habits. It occurs in the clefts of walls, and beneath the bark of old trees. **Order II.—Chilopoda.** Lat. This division of the Myriapoda bears nearly the same relation to the unrestricted genus *Scolopendra* of Linnaeus, --- 1 Règne Animal, iv. 332. 2 See Osservazioni per servire <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ALLA">alla</a> storia di una specie di Iulus communissima, reprinted in Memorie Scientifiche, Pisa, 1824. 3 Linn. Trans. xi. 377. 4 Kirby and Spence's Introduction to Entomology, vol. i. p. 123. 5 Voyage, vol. i. p. 61. 6 Mémoires, t. vii. pl. 36. as the preceding does to the genus *Julus* of the Swedish naturalist. The antennae become slender towards the extremity, and are composed of fourteen articulations and upwards. The mouth is composed of two mandibles, each furnished with a small palpitiform appendage, and exhibiting in their centre the appearance of a jointing, and ending in a spoon-shaped termination, with toothed edges. The labium is quadrifid, with the two lateral divisions larger than the others, transversely ringed, and resembling the membranous feet of caterpillars. This labium is analogous to the lower lip of the chilognathous kinds, which represents in Latreille's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> the tongue of the crustaceous tribes, but possesses also the functions of maxilla. It is what Savigny names the first auxiliary lip. Besides these parts, there are two palpi or minute feet, united at the base, and unguiculated at the point; a second labium (*seconda lèvre auxiliaire de Savigny*), formed by a second pair of feet dilated and joined at their origin, and terminated by a strong hook, moveable, and pierced at the extremity, for the transmission of a venomous or acrid liquid. The body of these unseemly creatures is depressed and membranous. Each ring or segment is covered by a coriaceous plate, and usually bears only a single pair of legs; and the terminal segment is generally thrown backwards, and elongated into a kind of tail. The organs of respiration are composed, either in whole or in part, of tubular tracheae. The sexual parts are interior, and placed at the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> extremity of the body, as in the generality of insects properly so called. The stigmata are more obvious than in the preceding family, and are either lateral or dorsal. The species of this division are of much more nimble habits than those of the preceding; and the peculiar <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> in which the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> produces an undulating lateral motion. They are of carnivorous habits, and, avoiding strong light, usually conceal themselves under stones or old timber, beneath the bark of trees, &c. They are held in some dread by the inhabitants of tropical countries, where they attain a great size, and are consequently capable of inflicting dangerous wounds. But the majority of travelers seem agreed that, although the bite is more painful than that of a scorpion, it is never attended by fatal consequences. In more northern countries they are quite harmless, though disliked in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their repulsive aspect. Our common centipede (*Scolopendra fuscicollis* of Linn.) so frequent in this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> under stones, may be mentioned as a familiar example. Leeuwenhoek, the great Dutch microscopic observer, has described the perforation of the books, through which the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POISON">poison</a> is supposed to flow. This order (which corresponds to the *Syngnatha* of Latreille's earlier works, the title adhered to by Dr Leach) is divided into the following genera. The first two have only fifteen pair of legs; and their bodies, when viewed from above, seem to present fewer segments than when examined from below. **Genus Scutigera**, Lamarck. Body covered by eight plates or shields, beneath each of which are two pneumatic pouches or vesicular tracheae, which receive the air, and communicate with lateral and inferior tracheae of a tubular form. The under surface is divided into fifteen semi-segments, each <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> a pair of feet terminated by an extremely long, slender, and minutely articulated <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TARSUS">tarsus</a>. The terminal legs are long, and seem to increase in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> from the foremost to the hindmost pair. The eyes are comparatively <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and reticulated. The antennae are very long and slender, and the palpi projecting and spinous. The species keep themselves concealed during the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in barns, or the unrequited parts of houses, lying between old planks, or sometimes under stones. They are seen at night running on the outside walls with great velocity, feeding on insects, and various insects. They seem to pierce their prey with their mouth-hooks, and infuse into them a poisonous fluid, which immediately deprives them of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. These Myriapodes make their appearance in great numbers, chiefly in rainy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. According to Illiger, they are greatly dreaded by the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. The best known European species is the *S. aracoides* (Plate CCXXXIX, fig. 4). It is the *Scolopendra coleopterata* of Linn. and Fab. Pallas asserts that it was taken by a friend of his among some fuci in the sea; but as all analogy is against its natural occurrence in such a locality, we may infer that it had fallen accidentally from the timbers of a vessel. **Genus Lithobius**, Leach. Body divided into an equal number of segments both above and below, each bearing a pair of legs. The dorsal plates are alternately long and short. The stigmatic openings are lateral. We have figured our most common species, *L. forficata* (Plate CCXXXIX, fig. 6), a familiarly-known Linnæan scolopendra, as an example of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> genus. It occurs almost everywhere, throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season, under stones. The anatomical structure of the genus has been described by M. Leon Dufour. The remaining generic groups of this order have at least twenty-one pair of legs, and the segments of the body are of nearly equal size, and of similar number, both above and below. In the genus *Scolopendra*, properly so called, there are eight distinct eyes, four on each side, and the basal joint of the terminal legs is armed with small spines. We have no British species, but the south of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> produces *Scol. cingulata*, which presents almost as formidable an aspect as some of the exotic kinds. The great foreign species (one of which sometimes <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> above a foot in length) have been as yet but ill defined, several kinds being no doubt described under the name of *Scol. morsitans*, a native of South <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> (Plate CCXXXIX, fig. 9). A monstrous species, called *Scol. Plumieri*, is figured in Lister's Journey to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, and appears to be also represented in Seba's Thesaurus, under the name of *Millipeda <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAJOR">major</a> ex Nova Hispana*. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and the great eastern <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, produce some very large species; and scolopendras of alarming size likewise occur on the African continent. The bite of these creatures is said to be dangerous; but it seems that the poison of the wound is allayed by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AMMONIA">ammonia</a>. M. Amoreux is of opinion that no poisonous power is possessed by any of the European species. The whole are carnivorous and voracious, and, all things considered, they may be regarded as among the ugliest of creeping things. Nevertheless they are not without their advantage to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>. "I have seen <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> chil- --- 1 This piece is not attached to the head, but to the anterior extremity of the first semi-segment. The two hooked feet form by the union and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a> of their first article a plate in the form of a labium or mentum, and the same semi-segment bears the two first ordinary feet. (*Régne Animal*, iv. 336.) 2 Latreille and others have adopted Lamarck's designation, although the title of *Ceratiola* had at a prior period been assigned to this generic group by Illiger. See Rossi's *Fauna Etruria*, t. ii. p. 299. 3 *Spicilegia Zoologica*, fascic. 9, tab. 4, fig. 16. 4 *Bulletin de la Soc. Phil.* <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1824, p. 24. 5 *Annales des Sciences Nat.* ii. 81. 6 *Insect. Venim.* p. 277.

MYRISTICA

Pages 664-665

the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUTMEG">Nutmeg</a> Tree. The seeds <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> kernels called nutmegs are well known, as they have <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> been used both for culinary and medicinal purposes. Distilled with <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, they yield a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of essential <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, resembling in flavour the spice itself; after the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> an insipid sebaceous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is found <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> on the water; and the decoction inspissated gives an extract of an unctuous, very slightly bitterish <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and with little or no astringency. Rectified spirit extracts the whole virtue of nutmegs by infusion, and elevates very little of it in distillation; hence the spirituous extract possesses the flavour of the spice in an eminent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. Nutmegs, when heated, yield to the press a considerable quantity of limpid <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> oil, which, on cooling, concretes into a sebaceous consistence. In the shops we meet with three sorts of unctuous substances, called oil of mace, though really expressed from the nutmeg. The best, which is brought from the East Indies in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> jars, is of a thick consistence, of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of mace, and has an agreeable fragrant smell; the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> sort, which is of a paler colour, and much inferior in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, comes from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> masses, generally flat, and of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; the third, which is the worst of all, and usually called <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> oil of mace, is an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of sevum, palm oil, and the like, flavoured with a little genuine oil of nutmeg. When the fruit is ripe, the natives ascend the trees, and gather it by pulling the branches to them with long hooks. Some are employed in opening them immediately, and in taking off the green shell or first rind, which is laid together in a heap in the woods, where in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> it putrefies. As soon as the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> has taken <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, there <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MUSHROOMS">mushrooms</a> called boleti moschatynis, of a blackish colour, and much valued by the natives, who consider them as delicate eating. When the nuts are stripped of their first rind they are carried home, and the mace is carefully taken off with a small <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>. The mace, which is of a beautiful <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a>, but afterwards assumes a darkish or reddish colour, is laid to dry in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> for the space of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and is then removed to a place less exposed to his rays, where it remains for eight days, that it may soften a little. It is afterwards moistened with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> water, to prevent it from drying too much, or from losing its oil; but the people are careful not to employ too much water, lest it should become putrid, and be devoured by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. It is last of all put into small bags, and squeezed very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. The nuts, which are still covered with their ligneous shell, are for three days exposed to the sun, and afterwards dried before a fire till they emit a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> when they are shaken; they then <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> them with small sticks, in order to remove their shell, which flies off in pieces. These nuts are distributed into three parcels, the first of which contains the largest and most beautiful, which are destined for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; the second contains such as are reserved for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the inhabitants; and the third contains the smallest, which are <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> or unripe. These last are burned; and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the rest is employed for procuring oil by pressure. A <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of them <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> gives three ounces of oil, which has the consistence of tallow, and the taste of nutmeg. Both the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> and mace, when distilled, afford an essential, transparent, and volatile oil, of an excellent flavour. The nutmegs which have thus been selected would soon corrupt <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were not watered, or rather pickled, with lime-water made from calcined shell-fish, which is diluted with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a> water till it attain the consistence of fluid pap. Into this mixture are plunged the nutmegs, contained in small baskets, two or three times, till they are completely covered over with the liquor. They are afterwards laid in a heap, where they <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and lose their superfluous moisture by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>. When they have sweated sufficiently, they are then properly prepared, and fit for a sea voyage. In the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Banda, the fruit of the nutmeg-tree is preserved entire in the following manner. When it is almost ripe, but previous to its opening, it is boiled in water and pierced with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>. It is next laid in water to soak for ten days, till it has lost its sour and sharp taste, and then it is boiled gently in a syrup of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, to which, if they wish it to be hard, a little lime is added. This operation is repeated for eight days, and each time the syrup is renewed. The fruit, when thus preserved, is put for the last time into a pretty thick syrup, and is kept in earthen pots closely shut.

MYRMIDONS

Pages 665-665

MYRMIDONES, in Antiquity, a people in the southern borders of Thessaly, who accompanied <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a> to the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>. They received their name from Myrmidon, a son of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Eurymedusa, who married one of the daughters of Æolus, son of Helen. His son <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTOR">Actor</a> married Ægina, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Æopos, and gave his name to his subjects, who dwelt near the river Peneus in Thessaly. According to some, the Myrmidons received their name from their having arisen from ants <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> pismires, upon a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> put up for that purpose by Æacus to Jupiter, after his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> had been dispeopled by a severe pestilence. According to Strabo, they received it from their industry, because they imitated the diligence of the ants, being like them indefatigable, and continually employed in cultivating the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. MYRMILLONES were gladiators of a certain kind at Rome, who fought against the Retiarii. Their arms were a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, head-piece, and shield. On the top of the head-piece they wore a fish embossed, called myrmillones, whence their name is by some supposed to be derived. The Retiarii, in their engagements, made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NET">net</a>, in which they endeavoured to entangle their adversaries; and sung during the fight, Non te peto, piscem peto; quid me figis, Gallo? "I aim not at thee, but I aim at thy fish; why dost thou shun me, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>?" The Myrmillones were called Gallic, because they wore Gallic armour; and they were also named <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECUTORES">Secutores</a>. This kind of gladiators was suppressed by Caligula. --- 1 Personal Narrative, vol. ii. p. 205. 2 Zoological Miscellany, vol. iii. 3 Histoire des Insectes, t. ii. p. 676, n. 5. 4 Iunn. Trans. xi. 384.

MYROBALANS

Pages 665-666

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of medicinal fruit brought from the Indies, of which there are five kinds, viz. the citrine of a yellowish <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, hard, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, and the size of an olive; the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> myrobalan, of the size of an acorn, wrinkled and without a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; chebulic myrobalans, of the size of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, pointed at the end, and of a yellowish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; emblic, which are round, rough, of the size of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GALL">gall</a>, and of a dark brown; and balleric, which are hard, round, of the size of an ordinary prune, less angular than the rest, and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. They are all slightly purgative and astringent. The word comes from the Greek μυρον, ointment, and βακτρον, acorn, from their being in the form of acorns, and used in medicine.

MYRON

Pages 666-666

an excellent Grecian statuary, who flourished 442 years before Christ. The cow he represented in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> was an admirable piece of workmanship, and proved the occasion of many fine epigrams in Greek.

MYRRH

Pages 666-666

a gummy, resinous, concrete juice, which is brought from the East Indies <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>. It is affirmed by some that the myrrh we have at present is not equal in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to that of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and has not that exquisite smell which all authors ascribe to the latter. With it they aromatized their most delicious wines; and it was presented as a very valuable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a> to our <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> whilst he lay in a manger. It was this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> also which was mingled with the wine given him to drink at his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, to deaden his pains, and produce a stupor. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GALL">gall</a> mentioned on the same occasion by St Matthew is probably the same with myrrh; for any thing bitter was usually distinguished by the name of gall. The Hebrews were accustomed to give those who were executed some stupefying draught. The difficulty which arises from the seeming <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the two evangelists, some have solved by saying that St Matthew, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> in Syriac, made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the word μαρρα, which signifies myrrh, bitterness, or gall; but that the Greek translator has taken it for gall, and St Mark for myrrh. Others think that our Saviour's drink was mingled with myrrh as a stupefying drug, but suppose that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, out of a wanton cruelty and inhumanity, infused gall; which was the reason, according to them, why, when he had tasted, he refused to drink.

MYRTOUN MARE

Pages 666-666

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Ægean <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, lying between Euboea, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>. It receives this name from Myrto, a woman; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MYRTUS">Myrtus</a>, a small <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the neighbourhood; or from Myrtilus the son of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, who was drowned therein.

MYRTUS

Pages 666-666

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a small <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> near Carystus, in Euboea, which gave name to the Mare Myrtoum. Strabo extends this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, Argia, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>. Pausanias, making it commence at Euboea, joins it at Helena, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> island, with the Ægean Sea; but <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> carries it to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>; and Pliny says that the Cyclades and Sporades are bounded on the west by the Myrtoan coast of Attica.

MYSCHEKIN

Pages 666-666

a circle of the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> Jaroslav, between 37° 33' and 38° 46' east <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and 57° 25' and 58° 4' <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. It contains one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and 701 villages, distributed into fifty-five parishes. It is watered by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Wolga, Karasitschina, Kadka, and Sudka, and is moderately fertile, maintaining a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of 71,390 persons. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, of the same name, is situated on the Wolga, 450 miles from St Petersburg, with some little trade by that river. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 56° 5' E. Lat. 57° 47' N.

MYSLENICZER

Pages 666-666

a circle of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, extending over 825 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, and comprehending twelve cities and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and 339 villages, with 37,143 houses, and 144,077 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, situated on the river Raba, with 286 houses, and 2075 inhabitants. MYSOLE <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">ISLE</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is situated in the Eastern Seas, about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of south latitude, midway between the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of Ceram and Papua. It is fifty miles in length by fifteen in breadth, and is inhabited on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> chiefly by Mahommendans, and in the interior by the natives. On the east coast is a harbour, formed by a small island, on which fresh <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> may be procured in abundance without risk, as the harbour is landlocked. The island is frequented by birds of paradise in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> flocks at certain seasons of the year, when they are caught with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>-lime, and afterwards dried with the feathers on as they are seen in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> loory, a very scarce bird, may also be purchased here. The trade is inconsiderable, consisting chiefly of biche de mer, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBERGRIS">ambergris</a>, pearls, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; the imports are coarse piece goods, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTLERY">cutlery</a>, beads, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> in bars, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">china</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, looking-glasses, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>-wire.

MYSON

Pages 666-666

a native of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> wise men of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. When Anacharsis consulted the oracle of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, to know which was the wisest <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> in Greece, he received for answer, he who is now ploughing his fields. This was Myson.

MYSORE

Pages 666-683

MAHESURA, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> MAISOOR, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in the south of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, situated principally between the eleventh and fifteenth degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and now surrounded by the British territories subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MADRAS">Madras</a> presidency. Its length is estimated at 210 miles, and its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> breadth at 140. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> consists of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, enclosed between the Eastern and the Western Ghauts, and elevated 3000 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, from which rise numerous lofty hills, containing the sources of many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, such as the Cavery, Toombudra, Vedawati, Bhadri, Penar, and others. The elevation of this inland plain varies at different places. The highest mountain of Mysore namely, Sivagunga, is 4600 feet; at the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">Pass</a> of Peddannak Durgum, the height is 1907 feet, according to barometrical observations; at Baitamangalam, 2435; at Bangalore, 2807; at Hurrypur, 1831. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is mitigated by the height of the ground, and the climate throughout the whole of this extensive tract is remarkably temperate and healthy. This country has another peculiar advantage, namely, that it is sheltered by the Ghaut <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a> from the violence of the monsoons, which <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a> along the lower plains, and deluge with torrents of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> the coasts of Coromandel and Malabar. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> which are driven on the land from the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> Ocean by the south-west monsoon are opposed by the mountain wall of the Western Ghauts; and although the higher and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> clouds make their way into the plains, and occasion frequent, and sometimes heavy showers, which refresh the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> and the ground, yet they are seldom of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance. Occasional showers, however, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> at other seasons, and preserve the verdure of the fields throughout the year. The country of Mysore, from its elevation and its temperate climate, not only produces all the other grains and vegetables of other parts of India, but also many of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It appears to have been formerly in a much higher state of cultivation than at present; but has been <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">Mysteries</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>, in its original form, was simple and intelligible. It was intended for the instruction and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of all ranks of men, and of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> its doctrines were on a level with vulgar capacities. The Jewish dispensation was openly practised; nothing was performed in secret; every article was plain, open, and accessible. The divine Author of the Christian economy commanded his disciples to preach his doctrine in the most public manner: "What ye have heard in secret," says he, "preach openly; and what I have taught you in private, teach ye publicly; and proclaim it on the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-tops." Such are the charms of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and such the character of that religion which came <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from heaven, that they, as it were, "delight, and lift up their <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the streets, and cry in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> places of concourse." But such is the depravity of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>, that the noblest institutions degenerate in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Religion itself, originally pure, simple, and amiable, under his management has often been transformed into pollution, perplexity, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a>. The ministers of religion, whose province it was to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the sacred deposit, and to secure it from foreign and spurious intermixtures, have generally been the first innovators, and the first and most industrious agents in corrupting its integrity and tarnishing its <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. Avarice and ambition prompted that class of men to deviate from the original plainness and simplicity of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> institutions, and to introduce <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>, and usages, which might furnish them with opportunities of gratifying these unhallowed and insatiable passions. Hence distinctions unknown to pure and undefiled religion were fabricated, and that heavenly <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, heretofore one, simple, indissoluble, was divided into two partitions; the one popular and public; the other dark, secret, and mysterious. The latter of these we intend as the subject of this article. The English word mystery is derived from the Greek μυστήριον, and, in its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> acceptation, imports something beyond <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> intelligence, something awfully obscure and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a>, and enigmatical; anything artfully made difficult; the secret of any business or profession. The word is often used by <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, the founder of the Christian religion, and more frequently by his apostles, especially St Paul. In these <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, it generally signifies those doctrines of Christianity which the Jews, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the advent of the Messiah, either did not or could not understand. The Trinity in Unity and the Unity in Trinity, the incarnation of the Son of God, the union of two natures in one and the same person, &c., we generally call mysteries, because they are infinitely above human comprehension. All these significations are out of Mysteries: the question at present. Our intention in this article is to lay before our readers the fullest and fairest account we have been able to collect, of those mysteries, or secret rites, of the Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, which were carefully concealed from the knowledge of the vulgar, and which are universally known under the denomination of mysteries. The word μυστήρια is evidently deduced from μυστήριον; but the origin of this last term is not altogether so obvious. The etymologies of it exhibited by the learned are various; some of them absurd and inconsistent, others foolish and futile. Instead of fatiguing our readers with a detail of these, which would be equally unentertaining and uninteresting, we shall only produce one, which to us appears to come nearest the truth. The mysteries under consideration at present were certainly imported into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> from the East. In those regions, then, we ought of course to look for the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the word. Mistor or mistrur, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, signifies “any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> or thing hidden or concealed.” As this word implies a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of the nature of the thing intended, and as it is one of the excellencies of original languages to apply vocables with this propriety, we find ourselves strongly inclined to assign the word mistrur as the root of the term μυστήρια, mystér. We have already observed, that the avarice and ambition of the Pagan priesthood probably gave birth to the institution of the mysteries. To this observation we may now add, that the ministers of that superstition might possibly imagine, that some articles of their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a> were too profound to be comprehended by the vulgar; others, too sacred to be communicated to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of men whom the institutions of civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> had placed in a situation not only subordinate, but even contemptible. It was imagined, that things sacred and venerable would have contracted a taint and pollution by an intercourse with sordid and untutored souls. These appear to us the most probable motives for making that odious and pernicious distinction between the popular religion and that contained in the sacred and mysterious ritual. Bishop Warburton is positive that the mysteries of the Pagan religion were the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of legislators and other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> personages, whom fortune or their own merit had placed at the head of those civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> which were formed in the earliest ages in different parts of the world. It is with reluctance, and indeed with diffidence, that we presume to differ in our sentiments from such respectable authority. Whatever <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> this prelate had once adopted, so extensive was his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-READING">reading</a>, and so exuberant his intellectual resources, that he found little difficulty in defending it by an appearance of plausibility, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not of rational argumentation. The large quotations he has adduced from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> and Cicero do indeed prove that the sages and legislators of antiquity sometimes availed themselves of the influence derived from the doctrines of the mysteries, and from the authority they acquired by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of their having been initiated in them; but that those men were the inventors and fabricators of them, is a position for which his quotations do not furnish the most slender presumption. At the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> we think it not altogether certain that the doctrine of a divine <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, and a future state of rewards and punishments, were revealed in the mysteries with all the clearness and cogency which is pretended by his lordship. But, granting that the fabric was raised by the hands of sages and legislators, we imagine it would be rather difficult to discover what emolument that description of men could propose to derive from the enterprise. The institution was evidently, and indeed confessedly, devised to conceal from the million those very doctrines and maxims which, had they known and embraced them, would have contributed most effectually to dispose them to submit to those wise regulations which their governors and legislators wished most ardently to establish. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a> has taught that nothing has a more commanding influence on the minds of the vulgar than those very dogmas which, according to the bishop, were communicated to the initiated. A conviction of the unity of the deity, of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, power, goodness, omnipresence, &c. the steady <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the human <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and of a future state of rewards and punishments, have in all ages and in all countries proved the firmest supports of legal authority. The very same doctrines, in the dawn of Christianity, contributed, of all other methods, the most effectually to tame and civilize the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> inhabitants of the northern regions of Europe. Supposing those principles to have been inculcated by the mysteries, the most prudent <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> legislators could have adopted would have been to publish them to all mankind. They ought to have sent forth apostles to preach them to the savages whom they had undertaken to civilize. According to the learned prelate, they pursued the opposite course, and deprived themselves of those very arms by which they might have encountered and overthrown all the armies of savagism. Of all the legislators of antiquity, the Cretan alone was prudent enough to foresee and adopt this rational plan. Of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELEUSIS">Eleusis</a> Diodorus the Sicilian informs us that the mysteries of Eleusis, Samothracia, and other places, which were elsewhere buried in profound darkness, were amongst the Creteans taught publicly, and communicated to all the world. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a>, however, was a successful <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>, and his intercourse with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Ideus extended his influence and established his authority. He was not under the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of calling in the mysteries to his assistance; on the contrary, it is highly probable that the universal knowledge of the doctrines of the mysteries among his countrymen contributed in a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to facilitate his labour and ensure his success. The divine Author of the Christian economy, viewed in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of a human legislator, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the propriety of this procedure. Nothing was concealed in his institutions; nothing was veiled with mystery, or buried in darkness. The success was answerable to the wisdom of the plan. The million flocked to the evangelical standard; the gospel was preached to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, to the illiterate, and the vulgar; and the meanest of mankind eagerly embraced its maxims. Wherever it prevailed it produced civilization, morality, sobriety, loyalty, and every other private and social virtue. Upon the supposition that the mysteries had contained and inculcated the principles and practices which the prelate supposes they did, the civilizers of mankind, legislators, magistrates, and princes, ought to have combined to make them public for the sake of their own tranquillity, and the more effectual support of their authority and influence. Upon the whole, we are inclined to believe that the mysteries were the offspring of Egyptian priestcraft. They were instituted with a view to aggrandize that order of sprung men, to extend their influence, and enlarge their revenues. To accomplish these selfish projects, they applied every artifice towards besetting the multitude with superstition ed by logic and enthusiasm. They taught them to believe that themselves were the distinguished favourites of heaven; and that celestial doctrines had been revealed to them, too holy to be communicated to the profane rabble, and too sublime to be comprehended by vulgar capacities. It is, 1 Divine Legation of Moses Demonstrated. 2 The Germans, Russians, and Scandinavians, who were never thoroughly civilized till the gospel was preached among them. Mysteries. We confess, exceedingly probable, that after the mysteries were instituted, and had acquired an exalted reputation in the world, legislators, magistrates, judges, and potentates, joined in the imposture, with the same views and from the same principles. Princes and legislators, who found their advantage in overpowering and humbling the multitude, readily adopted a plan which they found so artfully fabricated to answer these very purposes.
