He is said to have contrived an instrument of torture in the form of a statue of a beautiful woman, whose rich dress concealed a number of iron spikes in her bosom and arms. When any one therefore opposed his demands, he would say, "If I have not talents enough to prevail with you, perhaps my woman Apega may persuade you." Then appeared the statue, which Nabis, taking by the hand, led up to the person, who, being embraced by it, was thus tortured into compliance. To render his tyranny less unpopular, Nabis formed an alliance with Flaminius the Roman general, and pursued, with the most invertebrate enmity, the war which he had undertaken against the Achaeans. He besieged Gythium, and defeated Philopoemen in a naval engagement. But his triumph was short; the general of the Achaeans soon repaired his losses; and Nabis having been defeated in an engagement, was killed as he attempted to save his life by flight, about 194 years before the Christian era.

NABLUM

Pages 695-695

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> Nebel, was an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of music amongst the Jews. It had strings like the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>, was played upon by both <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and in form resembled that of a Greek lyra. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> and Vulgate it is called nubium, psalterion, lyra, and sometimes cithara.

NABO

Pages 695-695
or Nabo, in Mythology, a deity of the Babylonians, who possessed the next rank to Bel or Belus. Vossius apprehends that Nabo was the moon, and Bel the sun; but Grotius supposes that Nabo was some celebrated prophet of the country; and this opinion is confirmed by the etymology of the name, signifying, according to Jerome, "one who presides over prophecy."

NABOB

Pages 695-695

properly Nawab, the plural of Naib, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>. As used in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, this <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> is the same as Nazim.

NABONASSAR

Pages 695-695

first <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Chaldeans <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Babylonians, memorable on account of the Jewish era which bears his name, and which is generally fixed in 3257, beginning on Wednesday, February 26th, in the 3967th of the Julian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, 747 years before Christ. The Babylonians having revolted from the Medes, who had overthrown the Assyrian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, founded under Nabonassar a dominion which was much increased under Nabuchadnezzar. It is probable, that this Nabonassar is the Baladan mentioned in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of Kings (xx. 12), father of Medrosh, who sent ambassadors to Hezekiah.

NABOPOLASSAR

Pages 695-695
king of Babylon, who joined with Astyages the Mede, to destroy the empire of Assyria; which having accomplished, they founded the two empires of the Medes under Astyages, and the Chaldeans under Nabopolassar, 627 years before Christ.

NABUCHADNEZZAR

Pages 695-695
or Nabuchodonosor II. king of Assyria, son of Nabopolassar, and styled the Great, was associated with his father in the empire, 607 years before Christ. The following year he took Jehoahkim king of Judah prisoner, and proposed to carry him and his subjects in captivity into Babylon; but upon his submission, and promising to hold his kingdom under Nabuchodonosor, he was permitted to remain at Jerusalem. About 603 years before Christ, Jehoahkim attempted to shake off the Assyrian yoke, but without success; and this revolt brought on the general captivity. Nabuchadnezzar having subdued the Ethiopians, Arabians, Idumeans, Philistines, Syrians, Persians, Medes, Assyrians, and almost all Asia, and being puffed up with pride, caused a golden statue to be set up, and commanded all to worship it; but Daniel and his companions having refused to do so, they were cast into the fiery furnace. As Nabuchadnezzar was admiring his own magnificence, he was, by divine sentence, driven from men, and in the Scripture style is said to have eaten grass as an ox, that is, he was seized with the disease called by the Greeks liconthropy, which is a kind of madness that causes persons to run into the fields and streets in the night, and sometimes to suppose themselves to have the heads of oxen, or to be made of glass. At the end of seven years his reason returned to him, and he was restored to his throne and his glory. He died 562 B.C. in the forty-third year of his reign; in the fifth of which happened that eclipse of the sun mentioned by Ptolemy, which is the surest foundation of the chronology of his reign.

NACHELO

Pages 695-695
or Nakhilo, a sea-port of Persia, in Laristan, defended by a square fort, flanked by four towers. It is situated at the mouth of a river which falls into the Persian Gulf, where the anchorage would be good if it were not exposed to the north-west winds. This place was for a time under the dominion of the Walabees, driving the prevalence of their power. There is a fishery of pearls in the neighbourhood. It is fifty miles south-south-west of Lar.

NACHITSCHEVAN

Pages 695-695

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Russia in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the circle of Roatow, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Katerinoslaw. It stands on the river <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DON">Don</a>, which here frequently overflows its banks. Its inhabitants are almost exclusively of the Armenian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and, by their eastern costume and manners, they are in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> kept separate from the Russians. The city contains 2400 houses, and about 14,000 inhabitants. In their eastern way they produce much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, having planted more than 20,000 mulberry trees. They also grow much <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>; make <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, cotton, and silk goods; and have <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-works, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>-works, and numerous distilleries. These people were brought from the Crimea.

NACKSHIEVAN

Pages 695-695
or Nuckshieván, a town of Persian Armenia, formerly one of the most magnificent cities of Persia, supposed to have been the ancient Artaxata, now only famous for its magnificent ruins, and containing not above 400 inhabitants. Its ruin was completed by Abbas I, who, in the plenitude of his tyrannical power, removed the inhabitants by force into the interior. It is eighty-five miles south-east of Erivan.

NADED

Pages 695-695

a town in the south of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, situated on the Cavery River, 100 miles above <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYDERABAD">Hyderabad</a>. It is celebrated as the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Goroo Govend, the Sikh <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, who died A.D. 1708.

NADEGADOO

Pages 695-695

a well-watered district on the east side of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ceylon, through which runs the Sinpetto River. It lies between the seventh and eighth degrees of N. lat. and produces chiefly <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>.

NADIM

Pages 695-695

a river of Asiatic Russia, which rises in Lake Toromul, and falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a> of Obi. There is a small town of the name of Nadimskoi at its mouth. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 73. 44. E. Lat. 66. 25. N.

NADIR

Pages 695-695

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, that point of the heavens which is diametrically opposite to the zenith <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> point directly above our heads.

NADONE

Pages 695-695
or Nadoun, a town of Hindustan, in the province of Lahore, being the principal one of the Kangrah country, is situated on the eastern bank of the Beyah river. This place was considered as a respectable fortress in the year 1014, and was taken from the Hindus by Sultan Mahmoud of Ghizni. The Nadone district borders on the Punjab. It is mountainous, and is governed by a Hindu prince, tributary to the Sikhs, who was plundered by the rajah of Nepaul's army. Long. of the town 75. 47. E. Lat. 31. 59. N. NÆNIA, the goddess of funerals at Rome. Her temple was without the gates of the city. The songs which were sung at funerals were also called nemia. They were generally filled with the praises of the deceased; but sometimes they were so unmeaning and improper, that the word became proverbial to signify nonsense.

NAEFELS

Pages 696-696

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of Glaris, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of that canton. It stands on the river Linth, in a fruitful and pleasant district. The small river Rautibach, on its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the Linth, forms a fine, and at times a most copious cascade. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> victory was gained here by the Swiss in 1388, and it is still yearly celebrated with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> ceremonies. The town contains 220 houses, with 1730 inhabitants, who are chiefly employed in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>.

NAERDEN

Pages 695-696

a strong town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, situated at the head of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. The foundations of it were laid by William of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, in 1350. It was taken by the Spaniards in 1572, and by the French in 1672; but it was retaken by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> the next year. It stands at the south end of the Zuyder Zee, in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 5. 3. E. and lat. 51. 22. N. NÆVIUS, Cætius, a tragic and comic poet, was a native of Campania, and flourished about the year 235 B.C., having served in the first Punic <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> (264-241 B.C.), which he celebrated in an epic poem (Gell. xvii. 21, 45; v. 12, 7). He wrote a little before the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Ennius, who was born in 239 B.C. and died in 169. He was younger than <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIVIUS_ANDRONICUS">Livius Andronicus</a>, who exhibited his first play the year before Ennius was born, B.C. 240. Naevius was the author of several tragedies, many of the titles of which have been preserved; and from them it is easy to discover that they were imitations of the Greek writers. But he appears to have earned still higher praise by his labours as a writer of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>. Pursuing the path of the old Attic comedy, he lashed with an unsparing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> the vices of the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>; for which he was driven into exile, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, confined in prison, where he nevertheless seems to have written two tragedies. Such an example of severity could not have but impeded the free development of the comic muse of Rome. All that remains of the comedies of Naevius are the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> names, and a few insignificant fragments. The epic poem on the first Punic war was divided into <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> books by C. Octavius Lamprodius (Sueton. De Illust. Graec. 2). Naevius died in exile at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UTICA">Utica</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, a. c. 201, the very year in which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Punic war terminated. (Eusebius.) The fragments have been published under the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Enni Anni, Fragments et Cn. Naevii Fragm. Leipzig, 1825.

NAGAL

Pages 696-696

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, situated on the east side of the river Ganges. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 78. 10. E. Lat. 29. 43. N.

NAGAMANGATAM

Pages 696-696

a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> mud fort in the south of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MYSORE">Mysore</a>. It contains a square citadel in its centre, in which are two Hindu <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and all the public granaries and store-rooms. The town is said to be 600 years old, having been erected by a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> named Jagadeva Raya, of the same family with the present Mysore rajah. It was taken by the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MAHRATTAS">Mahrattas</a> in 1793; and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of houses was reduced from 1500 to 300; but it has since rapidly recovered its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> and its wealth. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 76. 57. E. Lat. 12. 49. N.

NAGHERY

Pages 696-696

a town of the south of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARNATIC">Carnatic</a>, forty-eight miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west by west from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MADRAS">Madras</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 79. 45. E. Lat. 13. 19. N.

NAGJERY

Pages 696-696

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Khandesh, 32 miles west by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOORHANPOOR">Boorhanpoor</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 75. 50. E. Lat. 21. 25. N.

NAGNE

Pages 696-696

a small river in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUJERAT">Gujerat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, which rises in a range of hills, fourteen miles to the south-east of Lawrin, and, after passing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOANAGUR">Noanagur</a>, falls into the Runn, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTCH">Cutch</a>.

NAGY-BANYA

Pages 696-696

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, of the circle of the Farther Theiss, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a district of the same name. It is situated in the centre of a mining <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, from which much <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> are extracted; and it has an <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the miners. There is a mint, in which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a> produced around it are coined into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. The inhabitants are a mixed <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Germans, Hungarians, and Greeks, and have a Catholic, a Lutheran, a Calvinist, and a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, for the adherents of those several modes of worship; the whole <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> is 5800. Around the city there are some vast woods of chestnut trees, the fruit of which is a valuable article of trade; and there is a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> in corn. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23. 29. E. Lat. 47. 37. N.

NAGY-ENYED

Pages 696-696

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Siebenbergen, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Transylvania, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a Nagy-Karolli, a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of the circle of Szathmar, in the province of Farther Theiss, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. It is situated on a fruitful spot, and has a splendid <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> and gardens belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Karoli, a Catholic, a Calvinist, and a Unitarian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and a Catholic gymnasium. It contains 943 houses, and 7567 inhabitants, amongst whom are many Jews. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 22. 22. 40. E. Lat. 47. 40. 10. N.

NAGY-KOBESCH

Pages 696-696

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, in the district of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PESTH">Pesth</a>. It is composed of 12,000 inhabitants, almost wholly of the original Magyar <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Hungarian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>, who adhere to the Calvinist <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and are chiefly occupied in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, producing good wine, and rearing <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> flocks of sheep. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19. 47. E. Lat. 47. 1. N.

NAHN

Pages 696-696

a district of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, partly situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, on its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-eastern frontier, and partly in Serimgur. It is between the thirteenth and thirty-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> degrees of north latitude, and is bounded on the east by the river Jumna. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is in general woody and mountainous; but is interspersed in the neighbourhood of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> with low hills and extensive wastes, overgrown with wood; yet these wastes might be watered from the Jumna, and brought under cultivation. They are, however, open to the incursions of both the Sikhs and Nepalese, who plunder the country; and hence the peasants have no encouragement to be industrious. The country is possessed by native chiefs, ever jealous of each other, and who plunder the miserable peasantry, and are in their turn plundered by other robbers more powerful than themselves. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, of the same name, is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of considerable strength, being built of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and situated upon the summit of a lofty mountain. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 77. 7. E. Lat. 30. 41. N.

NAHR EL BERD

Pages 696-696

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, in the pachalik of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, which falls into the Mediterranean, about <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Tripoli.

NAHR EL HOUALL

Pages 696-696

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRAK">Irak</a> Arabi, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Hermes, which rises in Mount Marius, passes by the ruins of Nisibis, and, after a short course, falls into the Khbour.

NAHR EL KEBIR

Pages 696-696

a considerable river of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, which rises in Mount Libanus, and, after a winding course, falls into the Mediterranean, twenty miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>.

NAHR ELTEMASIEH

Pages 696-696

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, which falls into the Mediterranean, six miles south of Tortosa.

NAHR GEBAL

Pages 696-696

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, which falls into the Mediterranean, four miles south of Latakieh.

NAIADES

Pages 696-696

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, certain inferior deities who presided over <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, and fountains. The Naiades generally inhabited the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and resorted to the woods <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> meadows near the stream over which they presided. They are represented as young and beautiful virgins, each leaning upon an urn, from which flows a stream of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Eagle was, according to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, the fairest of the Naiades. Their name appears to be derived from naios, to flow. They were held in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> veneration amongst the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; and often sacrifices of goats and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a> were offered to them, with libations of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. Sometimes they received only offerings of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, fruit, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>.

NAIANT

Pages 696-696

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLAZONING">blazoning</a> fishes, when borne in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> posture, as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>.

NAIN

Pages 696-697
Lewis Sebastian de, a French critic and historian, was son of a master of the requests, and was born at Paris in 1637. At ten years old he went to school at Port-Royal, and became one of the best writers of that in- Sacy, his intimate friend and counsellor, prevailed with him in 1676 to receive the priesthood; which, it seems, his great humility would not before suffer him to aspire to. This virtue he seems to have possessed in the extreme; so that Bossuet, seeing one of his letters to Father Dami, with whom he had some little dispute, sought him merrily "not to be always upon his knees before his adversary, but to raise himself up now and then." He was solicited to push himself forward in the church; and Buzanval, bishop of Beauvais, wished to have him for his successor; but Nain, regardless of dignities, wished for nothing but retirement, so that he might indulge in the mortifications of a religious life and the indefatigable cultivation of letters. He died in 1698, aged sixty-one. His principal works are, 1. Memoirs on the Ecclesiastical History of the first six ages of the Church, in sixteen vols. 4to; and, 2. The History of the Emperors, in six vols. 4to. These works are deduced from original sources, and composed with fidelity and accuracy.

NAIRNSHIRE

Pages 697-698

a small <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in Scotland. It is situated between 57° 22' and 57° 40' <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and 3° 47' west <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, having the Moray Frith on the north, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MORAYSHIRE">Morayshire</a> on the east and south, and the county of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a> on the west. Its <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> from north to south is from twelve to twenty miles, and from east to west from ten to thirteen; and its contents are 198 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> 126,720 English acres, of which only about a fourth <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is in cultivation, the rest consisting principally of waste and moor ground, with about 8000 acres of wood, chiefly planted, about two square miles of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and a small proportion of moss. It has only four entire parishes, Nairn, Auldearn, Cawdor, and Ardelach, and portions of other five, which belong to the counties of Moray, Ross, and Inverness. Two detached districts, Ferintosh and Dunninglass, belong to Nairnshire; the former lying near <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DINGWALL">Dingwall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROSS_SHIRE">Ross-shire</a>, and the latter at the head of Strathnairn in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INVERNESS_SHIRE">Inverness-shire</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> shore of Nairnshire is low, bare, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>; and the approaches to it from the Moray Frith are all beset by numerous sand-banks, especially from Fort George to Whiteness Point, where the free channel is narrow, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> intricate and dangerous. To the eastward the sand has been drifted into hillocks and even hills of sand, the parents, it is believed, of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> sand floods which have buried the estate of Culbin, below Forres. Near to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> there rises to the height of about ninety feet a bluff terrace-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, from the top of which the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> deflects back in several gentle undulations to the slopes of the first chain of hills on the south side of the river Nairn, the undulating plain being from one to four or five miles <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The terrace-bank is part of a general one which encircles the Moray Frith, and which, with the waving cultivated grounds behind, consists of a great deposit of sand and gravel, the rolled débris in part of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and also, most likely, of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rocks which at one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> filled up the basin of the frith. Owing to this preponderance of sand in the subsoil, the alluvial covering of Nairnshire is in general extremely slight, sandy, and porous; and as the gravel beds are deep, rocks in situ are but seldom seen (with the exception, however, of some about the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town, and Boath, which form good <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a>) till we reach the south-western bank of the river Nairn. There the nearest chains of hills, which, rising gradually from the east to an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a>, on the confines of Inverness-shire towards the west, of perhaps 1500 feet, are skirted by a narrow strip of the old <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> sandstone formation, with its associated coarse conglomerate, dip beneath the gravel beds. Immediately behind, the whole country, extending from the river Nairn to the Findhorn, and in one part beyond it to Duthel in Strathspey, consists of primitive rocks, the only stratified member of which is gray gneiss, with a few occasional beds of bluish granular Nairnshire <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>. All the rest are varieties of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, the most abundant variety being a red or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-coloured and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>-grained granite, which about <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PARK">Park</a> is beautifully porphyritic, with large crystals of felspar. All the rocks, as well as those of the sandstone deposits on the north, as of the primary masses in the interior, exhibit undoubted and very extensive indications, in their shattered and uplifted positions, of several great granitic eruptions having occurred at different times. On the Findhorn the scenery is in general wild and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>; the hills above are moorish, lumpish, and unbroken in their outlines; the banks of the Nairn, excepting the short distance they are enlivened by the contiguous <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> grounds attached to the several seats of Kilravock Holm and Contry, are tame and uninteresting; but along the course of the streams traversing the sandstone rocks, we meet scenes of simple picturesque <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. Such especially is the burn of Cawdor, which, for about two miles above the Castle of Cawdor, has cut <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the conglomerate rocks into most beautiful pyramidal curves, the deep dells stretching around them being clothed with the most luxuriant vegetation, from either side of which a fine old oak forest, and more recent plantations of pines and oaks, cover for miles the lower slopes of the hills constituting the beautiful grounds of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Cawdor. Nairnshire cannot boast of a peculiar Flora; but some rare <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> occur, as potamogeton prairea in Loch Leece, and along with nymphea <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALBA">alba</a> in Loch Littie; gagea lutea and ranunculus auricomus near Blackhills; carex vesicaria and lycomus europaeus near Millhill; salicornia herbacea, teesalda nudicaulis, and carex incurva, about Nairn; milium effusum, festuca calamaris, convallaria majalis, lycomus europaeus, listera ovata, goodyera repens, scolopendrium vulgare, lycopodium inundatum, about Cawdor. The territory of Nairnshire, exclusive of the lands belonging to and held of the burgh of Nairn, is divided into fifteen estates, of which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> are under the valuation of L.500 Scots, other three under L.2000, and the remaining three above L.2000. The valued rent is L.15,062. 15s. 1d. Scots, of which about one fourth is entailed. The real rent is now (1837) supposed to be fully L.16,000. The principal residences are, Cawdor Castle, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Cawdor; Kilravock Castle, Rose; Lethen <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> and Coulmony, Brodie; Kinsteary, Gordon; Boath, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUNBAR">Dunbar</a>; and Geddes, Mackintosh. This county is further subdivided into farms, in general small and unclosed. Although it is far behind the neighbouring counties of Moray and Ross in its <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, yet the gradual introduction of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of lime along with the turnip husbandry is fast ameliorating the appearance of the cultivated districts of the county. Its live stock presents nothing worthy of particular notice; the cattle are generally small and puny, a sort of mongrel breed intermediate between the Highland and the Morayshire, but inferior to both. This county sends a member to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> along with Elginshire; and the town of Nairn joins with Inverness, Forres, and Fortrose, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of a member for these burghs. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of county electors is 116, and those of the burgh amount to seventy-one. The counties of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ELGIN">Elgin</a> and Nairn are under the jurisdiction of the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, who has a substitute for the latter county in the town of Nairn. Nairnshire formed a part of the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Moray. A few miles to the east of Nairn, at a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> called Harmuir, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MACBETH">Macbeth</a>, according to Shakspeare, met the witches on his way to Forres. Near to the village of Auldearn, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONTROSE">Montrose</a> obtained a great victory over the Covenanters in 1645. The county contains the ruins of several castles, and other remains of an early <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The castles of Nairn, the county town, and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> burgh, is a place of considerable antiquity, pleasantly situated on the northern bank of the Nairn, near its mouth. It has no <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and but little trade, and contains about 2000 inhabitants. The National Bank and the British <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">Linen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> have opened branches here, and an academy has lately been erected by subscription. Nairn has an excellent inn, with hot and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>; and from the dryness and salubrity of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, it is much resorted to in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> for sea-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>.

NAISSANT

Pages 698-698

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is usually applied to any animal issuing out of the midst of some ordinary, and showing only his head, shoulders, fore feet, and legs, with the tip of his tail, the rest of his body being hid in the shield, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> upon it. In this it differs from issuant, which denotes a living creature arising out of the bottom of any ordinary or charge.

NAJOO

Pages 698-698

a small <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Eastern Seas, near to the west <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the island of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CELEBES">Celebes</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 124. 25. E. Lat. 129. S.

NAMACUL

Pages 698-698

a town of the south of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and district of Baramahl, subject to the British. It has a strong fort, situated on a rock of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 78. 5. E. Lat. 11. 22. N.

NAMAGANG

Pages 698-698

a small <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Eastern Seas, situated in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 123. E. and lat. 6. 45. N.

NAMBOODY

Pages 698-698

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AURUNGABAD">Aurungabad</a>. It belongs to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MAHRATTAS">Mahrattas</a>, and is sixteen miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from Ahmednuggur. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 73. 3. E. Lat. 19. 15. N.

NAME

Pages 698-699

E denotes a word by which men have agreed to express some idea, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> which serves to denote or signify a thing or a subject spoken of. This the grammarians usually call a noun, nomen, though their noun is not of quite so much <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> as our name. Seneca (de Beneficiis, lib. ii.) observes, that there are a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of things which have no name, and which, therefore, we are forced to call by other borrowed names. Iugens est, says he, rerum copia sine nomine, quas cum propriis appellatibibus signare non possumus, alienis accommodatis utimur; which may show why, in the course of this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, we frequently give various senses to the same word. Names are distinguished into proper and appellative. Proper names are those which represent some individual thing or person, so as to distinguish it from all other things of the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; as <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, which represents a certain <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. Appellative or general names are those which signify <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, or which are common to several individuals of the same species; as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, animal, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>, oak, and the like. Proper names are either called Christian, as being given at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, or surnames; the first being imposed for distinction of persons, answering to the Roman praenomen; the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, for the distinction of families, answering to the nomen of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and the patronymicum of the Greeks. Originally every person had but one name, as amongst the Jews, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>; amongst the Egyptians, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUSIRIS">Busiris</a>; amongst the Chaldees, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINUS">Ninus</a>; the Medes, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ASTYAGES">Astyages</a>; the Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a>; the Romans, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>; the Gauls, Divitius; the Germans, Ariovistus; the Britons, Cassibelannus; the English, Hengist, &c.; and so of other nations, except the savages of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, whom Pliny and Marcellinus represent as anonymi, or nameless. The Jews gave the name at the circumcision, viz. eight days after the birth; the Romans, to females on the eighth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to males on the ninth; at which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> they held a feast, called nominalia. Since Christianity has obtained, most nations have followed the Jews, baptizing and giving the name on the eighth day after the birth; excepting our English <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, who, until recently, baptized and gave the name on the birthday. The first imposition of names was founded on different views, amongst different people; the most common was to mark the good wishes of the parents, or to entitle the children to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> which a happy name seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>. Hence Victor, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a>, Faustus, Statorius, Probus, and the like. Accordingly, we find that such names, by Cicero called <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BONA">bona</a> nomina, and by Tacitus, fausta nomina, were first enrolled and ranged in the Roman musters, because those <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> them were first called to serve at the sacrifices, in the foundation of colonies, &c. And, on the contrary, Livy calls Atreus Umbra, abominandi omnis nomen; whilst Plautus, on occasion of mentioning a person named Lyco, or greedy <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>, says, Vosmet nunc facite conjecturam ceterum Quid id sit hominis, cui Lyco nomen fiet. Hence <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> recommends it to men to be careful in giving happy names; and the Pythagoreans taught expressly, that the minds, actions, and successes of men were according to their names, genius, and fate. Thus Panormitan, ex bono nomine oritur bona praesumptio; and the common proverb, Bonum nomen bonum <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>; and hence the foundation of the onomomantia. It is an observation deserving <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, says the Abbé Barthélemy, that the greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of names found in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> are marks of distinction, and appear to have been given in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the qualities most esteemed in the heroic ages. From the word polemos, which signifies <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, have been formed Tlepolemus and Archepolemus, the names of two heroes mentioned in the Iliad. The former name signifies able to support, and the latter, able to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, the labours of war. By adding to the word maché, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, certain prepositions and different parts of speech, which modify the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> in a manner always <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>, are composed the names Amphimachus, Antimachus, Promachus, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-TELEMACHUS">Telemachus</a>. Proceeding in the same way, with the word strength or intrepidity, they formed the names Agapenor, "he who esteems valour," and Agenor, "he who directs it." From thoes, swift, are derived Alca- thoes, Panthoes, Perithoes, &c.; from nous, mind or intelligence, come Astynoe, Arsinoes, Autones; from medes, counsel, Agamemnon, Bumetes, Ixomedes, Thrasybodes; and from chos, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, Amphicles, Agacles, Iphicles, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a>, Cleobulus, and many others. Hence Camden takes it for granted, that the names, in all nations and languages, are significative, and not simple sounds for <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> distinction's sake. This holds not only amongst the Jews, Greeks, and Latins, but even amongst the Turks, with whom Abdallah signifies God's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, Soliman, peaceable, Mahommmed, glorified, &c.; and also amongst the savages of Hispaniola, and throughout <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, who, in their languages, name their children Glittering <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>, Bright, Fine <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>, &c.; whilst those of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONGO">Congo</a> call them by the names of precious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, &c. To suppose names given without any meaning, however their signification may be lost by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, that learned author thinks is to reproach our ancestors, and that too contrary to the sense of all <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers. Porphyry remarks, that the barbarous names, as he calls them, were very emphatical, and very concise; and accordingly it was esteemed a duty to be sagacious, or sui nominis homines. Hence Severus, Probus, and Aurelius, are called sui nominis imperatores. It was the usual way of giving names, to wish the children might discharge their names. Thus, when Gunthera <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-KING">king</a> of France named Clotharius at the font, he said, Crescat puer, et hujus sit nominis executor. The ancient Britons, Camden says, generally took their names from colours, because they painted themselves; but these names are now lost, or remain hid amongst the Welsh. When they were subdued by the Romans, they took Roman names, some of which still remain corrupted; though the greater part became extinct upon the admission of the English Saxons, who introduced the German names, as Crida, Pendda, Oscaed, Edwaed, and the like. The Danes, too, brought with them their names; as Swayne, Harold, Knute, &c. The Normans, at the Conquest, brought in other German names, having originally used the German tongue; such as Robert, William, Richard, Henry, Hugh, &c., in the same manner as the Greek names Aspasius, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a>, Symmachus, &c. were introduced into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the empire. After the Conquest, our <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, which had ever been averse to foreign names, as deeming them unlucky, began to take <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> names; as Matthew, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, Samson, &c. Camden mentions it as an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the practice of giving surnames for Christian names first began in the reign of Edward VI. and was observed by such as would be godfathers, when they were more than half fathers; upon which some were persuaded to change their names at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>, which seems to have been usual in other countries. Thus, two sons of Henry II. of France, christened Alexander and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, changed them at confirmation into Henry and Francis. In monasteries, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> assume new names at their admission, to show that they are about to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a new <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and have renounced the world, their family, and even their name; as, for instance, sister <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> of the Incarnation, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Henry of the Holy Sacrament, and the like. The popes also changed their names at their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXALTATION">exaltation</a> to the pontificate; a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> first introduced by Pope Sergius, whose name till then, as Platin informs us, was Svisne's Snout. But Onuphrius refers it to John XII. or XIII. and at the same time adds a reason for the change different from that of Platin, namely, that it was done in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and St Paul, who were first called Simon and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>. Amongst the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, those deified by the heathen consecrations had new names given them; thus, Romulus was called Quirinus; Melicertes, Portunus or Portumus, &c. New names were also given in adoptions, and sometimes by <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>. Thus L. Emilius, adopted by Scipio, took the name of Scipio Africanus; and Augustus, who was at first called C. Octavius Thurinus, being adopted by the testament of Julius Cesar into his name and family, took the name of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Julius Cesar Octavianus. Names were also changed at enfranchisements into new cities. Thus, Lucumo, on his first being made free of Rome, took the name Lucius Tarquinius Priscus; and slaves, when made free, usually assumed the names of their masters. Those called to the equestrian order, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had base names, were always new-named, nominibus ingemorum veterumque Romanorum. And amongst the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, it was the practice to change the names of the catechumens; thus, the renegade <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LUCIANUS">Lucianus</a>, till his baptism, was called Lucius. Towards the middle of the fifteenth century, it was the fancy of the wits and the learned men of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, particularly in Italy, to change their baptismal names for classical ones; as Sanzarius, for instance, who altered his own plain name of Jacopo to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIUS">Actius</a> Synecrus. Numbers did the same, and, amongst the rest, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PLATINA">Platina</a> the historian at Rome, who, not without a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a>, took the name of Callimachus, instead of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>. Pope Paul II. who reigned about the same time, unluckily chanced to be suspicious, illiterate, and obtuse in comprehension. He had no idea that persons could wish to alter their names unless they had some bad <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; and actually scrupled not to employ imprisonment and other violent methods to discover the fancied mystery. On this frivolous pretence, Platina was most cruelly tortured; but he had nothing to confess, and so the pope, after endeavouring in vain to convict him of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, sedition, and other crimes, released him after a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> imprisonment.

NAMPTWICH

Pages 699-699
or NANTWICH, a market-town of the hundred of its own name, in the county of Chester, an hundred and sixty-five miles from London. It is situated on the banks of the river Weaver, and has by canals good water communication in all directions. It is one of the largest and best-built towns in the county, with regular streets and handsome houses. It was known to the Romans by the name of Saltinis, and must at all times have been a place of importance, from the vast quantities of salt procured from its vicinity. This product is partly made from brine springs highly saturated; and prodigious masses of rock-salt are drawn from mines, or rather quarries, near the town. These mines are many acres in extent. The roofs are supported by pillars, both of the same substance; and the translucent nature of the salt affords a pleasing and picturesque appearance. Many thousands of tons of this rock-salt are annually exported from Liverpool to the ports of Prussia, Russia, and Sweden, on the Baltic Sea. The country around yields a large portion of the best Cheshire cheese; and the trade in that article is carried on upon a very extensive scale, especially with London. The making of shoes is one source of employment; and many of them are sent to the metropolis and other parts of England. There is a well-supplied market, which is held on Saturday. The population of the town amounted in 1801 to 3463, in 1811 to 3999, in 1821 to 4661, and in 1831 to 4886; but the parish includes five other townships, which, by the last census, appear to make the inhabitants of the whole 5357.

NAMUR

Pages 699-700

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>. It is formed out of a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portion of the French department of the Sambre and the Meuse, of parts of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Namur, of some parcels of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, Luxemburg, and Brabant, and of the cantons of Philipville and Couvin, ceded to the Netherlands by the peace of 1815. It extends in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude from 49° 47' to 50° 49' and in east <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> from 4° 15' to 5° 13'. It is 1342 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; it is formed into three circles, fifteen cantons, and 313 communes; and it contains 165,000 inhabitants. The surface is covered with hills and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, with many valleys between them, in which channels are formed for numerous <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>. There are scarcely any ex- <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol14.html#article-NANCOWRY">Nancowry</a> tensive plains; but the lower hills, not exceeding 360 feet in height, are for the most <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> covered with woods. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in the northern <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> is of moderate fertility, but in the south it is stony, chalky, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> slaty, being almost destitute of mould, and covered with heath or scrubby woods. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> is well conducted in the arrondissement of Namur, but neglected in other parts; so that, with the help of potatoes, which are extensively cultivated, the province barely furnishes corn sufficient for its scanty <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, rye and winter barley being the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of grain chiefly grown. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-FLAX">Flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RAPE">rape</a>-seed are produced, but in small quantities. Fruit is abundant, especially walnuts. The vine is but partially cultivated, the whole of the vineyards not exceeding thirty acres. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINES">Mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and coal are found in several parts, and worked to such an extent, that about 10,000 tons of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> and wrought iron are procured, and soon converted into utensils. There are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of glass, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, besides many breweries and distilleries. The inhabitants are of the Walloon <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>, and much attached to the old customs and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; they for the most part speak only their peculiar patois, and are almost entirely destitute of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. The two <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, the Sambre and the Meuse, serve to carry off the waters of the numerous small streams, and, when united, become navigable, but only for small craft. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Namur is the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, as well of the arrondissement as of the province. It is situated between two hills, in a valley, on the left <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Meuse, where that river is joined by the Sambre and the Boderin. It is strongly fortified, and has a powerful citadel, commanding the city, as well as the passage over the river. It is a well-built <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, though with no buildings of a remarkable character. It contains 16,800 inhabitants, who are the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> manufacturers of the province. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 45'. E. Lat. 50° 28'. N.

NAN-HIUNG

Pages 700-700
or Nan-yong, a large and populous city of China, in the province of Quangtong, on the northern side of a mountain, which crosses the great road between Pekin and Canton.

NAN-NING

Pages 701-701

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, in Quangsee, situated in the midst of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and small <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> containing <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 107. 44. E. Lat. 22. 44. N.

NANDAPRAYAGA

Pages 700-700

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Hindu worship in Northern <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, being situated in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Serinagar, at the confluence of the Alcananda with the Nandacni. This is one of the most northerly places of Hindu worship. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 79° 22'. E. Lat. 30° 22'. N.

NANDERE

Pages 700-700

a district of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECCAN">Deccan</a>, 150 miles in length, and about 35 in breadth, being intersected by the river <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol10.html#article-GODAVERY">Godavery</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is fertile, well watered, and capable of being much improved. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is of the same name, and contains a good fortress built of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which is garrisoned by the nizam's troops. It is situated in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>. 77° 35'. E. and lat. 19° 6'. N.

NANDOOR

Pages 700-700

a town of the south of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Circars, seventy-four miles south-west by south from <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIZAGAPATAM">Vizagapatam</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 82° 25'. E. Lat. 17° 27'. N.

NANGASAKI

Pages 700-700

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-ports of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, at the south-western extremity of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Ximo, and one of the largest commercial sea-ports in the island. It is the only point of the empire at which Europeans are permitted to trade; and this permission is confined to the Dutch. The island of Ximo is separated from Nangasaki only by a ditch. It has two gates, one of which, looking to the town, is shut at night upon the Dutch, and is guarded by the Japanese. The other looks to the harbour, which is three miles in length and one in breadth. The Dutch town is built lengthwise, and contains several <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> storehouses, which have been made fire-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. The other houses are built of wood, clay, and tiles, with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> windows, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>-mats of straw. The Japanese interpreters have a large <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and also the Ottomans, who are a sort of spies, and report all that they see to the governor. The Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> pay fifteen per cent. and private traders seventy-five per cent. on all goods imported. Nangasaki, the Japanese town, is built at the head of the harbour, and has neither walls nor fortifications. There are two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>; the inner, which contains twenty-six, and the outer, which contains sixty-one streets. These streets are neither straight nor spacious, although many <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and artificers reside in them. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is watered by three rivulets, descending from the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. The most handsome houses are the palaces of the two resident governors, and of other princes and grandees. There are sixty-two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> built on eminences, serving for worship, and also for recreation. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 130° 12'. E. Lat. 32° 48'. N.

NANI

Pages 700-701

John Baptist, was born in 1616. His father was procurator of St Mark, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> to Rome. He was educated with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and made considerable improvement. Urban VIII., a good judge of merit, soon perceived that of young Nani. He was admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of senators in 1641, and was shortly afterwards nominated ambassador to France, where he signalized himself by his complaisant manners. He procured considerable succours for the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> of Candia against the Turks, and, after his return to Venice, became superintendent of the war-office and of finances. He was subsequently ambassador to the empire, where he rendered those services to his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which, as a zealous and intelligent citizen, he was so well qualified to discharge. He was again sent to France in the year 1660, to solicit fresh succours for Candia, and on his return was appointed procurator of St Mark. He died on the 5th of November 1768, at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of sixty-three, much regretted by his countrymen. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> had appointed him to write the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Republic, which he executed to the satisfaction of the Venetians, although the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> has not been admired by foreigners. This history was printed at Venice in 1662 and 1679, in two vols. 4to. NANKA <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">ISLANDS</a> are three in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and are situated near the west <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Bunca. They produce wood for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, and excellent <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 105. 41. E. Lat. 2. 22. S.

NANKANG

Pages 701-701

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, of the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, in Kiangsu. It is situated on a branch of the Poyang Lake. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 115. 39. E. Lat. 29. 33. N.

NANKING

Pages 701-701

a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, and at one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the southern <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the empire; but, since Pekin became the seat of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, it has lost its former importance, and its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> has also diminished. Nanking is situated on the southern <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YANG_TSE_KIANG">Yang-tse-Kiang</a>; it was formerly visited by vessels of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> burden, and still communicates by smaller barks with all the interior of the empire, and with Pekin by the great canal. It has fine <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, which are considered as its staple; and also plain and flowered satins, besides thin woollen stuffs. It is considered as a seat of Chinese learning, being the residence of many great doctors; and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BOOKSELLERS">booksellers</a>' shops are better furnished than any in the empire. The city is kept very clean, though the streets are narrower than those of Pekin. The public eating-houses are numerous, and well supplied. Formerly Nanking had a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, which was destroyed in 1643, by the Mantchoo Tartars. It is still adorned with lofty and splendid gateways, and with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> attached to them. It has also a very curious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> tower. This celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAGODA">pagoda</a> is of an octagonal form, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> stories in height, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the structure is 1411. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 118. 34. E. Lat. 32. 4. N.

NANPAREH

Pages 701-701

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in the territories of the Nabob of Oude, eighty miles <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-north-east from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUCKNOW">Lucknow</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 81. 30. E. Lat. 27. 52. N.

NANTES

Pages 701-701

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the arrondissement of the same name, in the department of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>. It is one of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-ports of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and owes much of its importance to its local situation. It stands in a fine <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river Loire, about thirty miles from its mouth, and opposite to the point where the river Sèvre falls into that stream. The entrance to the Loire is very dangerous, on account of the many sunken rocks near its mouth. Of these, the most remarkable are, Le Turque, uncovered at low <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>; La Couronne, a most dangerous reef, having ten fathoms of water <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to it; and the Lamborde, a rock <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the water at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>. These are all on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west side of the entrance; but on the south-west side the dangers to be avoided are, the Leven, a rock nearly covered at half tide; Pierre Percée, an islet, elevated about thirty feet above low water; the Baguehard, another rock nearly covered at half tide, upon which a bank of sand is visible; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Charpentier, Petit Charpentier, and La Vieille, three rocks of nearly equal height, and even with the sea at neap tides; and Les Morées and La Truye, appearing about eight feet above the water at neap tides. The commercial importance of Nantes depends in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> upon the length of the river Loire, which is nearly 500 miles, and the means afforded, by the help of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, which connect it with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>, and the Soane, of conveying to its harbour a portion of the productions of every department in France. The trade by sea is shown by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and tonnage of vessels which entered the port in the year 1831; the one being 3344, and the other 146,258 tons. Of the foreign ships, seventeen were British, estimated at 1780 tons. The amount of duty on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> and importation, including that on <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, which is very heavy, was, in 1831, 15,100,374 francs, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> L575,000; in 1832 it amounted to 13,907,400 francs, or L522,000. Nantes is also a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of considerable manufacturing industry. One of the most prominent branches is ship-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, including the fabrication of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>, cordage, sailcloth, and anchors, with other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> made of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WEAVING">Weaving</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> of woollen, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, cotton, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, occupy a great number of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. Glass and earthen <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a> are also made, and many <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, and much <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> of all kinds. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, and other engines used in the sugar colonies, are extensively prepared, and the refining of sugar is a vast branch of trade. There are also many distilleries, in which the most delicious cordials are prepared, and possess great celebrity. Nantes is finely situated on the banks of the river, some <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in which are covered with houses. Though many of the buildings are old and not regular, some are handsome, especially in the parts recently erected. The fortifications have been destroyed, and are now formed into fine promenades. The river, which is very wide, is crossed by a succession of bridges connecting the five islands, and the passage over them is nearly three miles. The city has seventeen churches, and several other public buildings, amongst which is the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> built in the Gothic style. There is a university, a lyceum, an anatomical and naval school, a public library, a botanic garden, and a cabinet of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. There is likewise a <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. This place is remarkable in history for the edict which gave freedom to Protestantism, and for the horrible cruelties perpetrated in it during the Revolution, by means of the noyades. The city contains 87,500 inhabitants. The arrondissement in which it is situated extends over 776 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, and is divided into seventeen cantons, and sixty-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> communes, containing 205,627 inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 22. 44. W. Lat. 47. 13. N.

NANTUA

Pages 701-701

an arrondissement of the department of the Ain, in France, 310 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. It comprehends six cantons, divided into sixty-one communes, and contains 51,500 inhabitants. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the same name, situated in a narrow valley between two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, on the border of the lake of Nantua. It has 340 houses, and 3860 inhabitants, who carry on several tanneries, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SILK">silk</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, and make <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a> and cotton goods. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 33. E. Lat. 46. 8. N.

NANYANG

Pages 701-701

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, of the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, in Honan. It is situated in a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, where <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> are cheap. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 112. 14. E. Lat. 33. 36. N.

NAPAKIANG

Pages 701-701
